div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
[BY REDCAP.]
FEEDING MENU.

In the following article I will give you the details of a general feeding menu. I say general because under certain conditions and for certain purposes the genetal rule has to be altered and modified. This menu is for use with utility stock. THE MORNING MASH.

The morning mash should be given as early as possible and should consist of the following ingredients: Biscuit meal, two parts ; Kavaris, according to directions; thirds or bran (good quality), in sufficient quantities to make the whole into a crumbly mass. Preparation: mix the biscuit meal and Kavaris together while dry, and then pour on to this sufficient boiling water to just cover the surface. After this has stood for 15 minutes, add the thirds or bran as stated above. Only give (your fowls what they eat up greedily. Never leave any food lying about, fowls do far better a little underfed rather than overfed; especially does this apply with the morning `meal.

div.head: MID-DAY MEAL.
div.p: MID-DAY MEAL.

The mid-day meal should consist of house scraps, green food in some form, such as chopped clover, cabbages, lettuce or sprouted oats. The latter form of green food is not so well known. It is. however, a 'very good food and one which gives good results with laying and breeding stock. The oats can be produced in the following manner :—Take a shallow box about two inches deep. In this put a layer of fine ashes and sand, then on the top of the sand and ashes place a good layer of cats about an inch deep. Then mix the whole together,place in a warm temperature and where it is dark. With frequent watering the oats soon sprout and are ready for use when the sprouts are about one inch long. It should be observed that the water used for propagation must be warm; this hastens the growth. it is advisable to have several boxes in use at the same time, so that you keep the fowls with a constant supply.

div.head: EVENING MEAL.
div.p: EVENING MEAL.

The evening meal should consistof grain and be given always as late as daylight will allow. Always remember that fowls go to roost early. The night is a long one, and a substantial meal is necessary. The best grains for general use are undoubtedly good sound wheat and heavy cats. Other useful grains are white Canadian peas, maize, barley and buck-wheat. These latter can be given s a e]ange of diet, with the excep- tion of maize, which should only be given in very severe weather. lam often asked, wlitit is the right quantity of grain to give to a fowl ? A good handful of corn just about fil's the crop of a fowl. Therefore, if you measure your evening meal in a like manner you will not get far wrong. CHICKEN FEEDING.

This is an important matter and one that will be of service if dealt with at the present moment. As I have often pointed out, chickens need neither food nor water for the first 24 hours of their existence at least. Prior to their emergence from the shell they absorb the contents of the yolk bag and this supplies them with sufficient nutriment for the period stated. No serious harm will accrue if they are allowed to go without food for an even longer period, so do not be over anxious in helping them to their first meal. It is dangerous to do so. They will instinctively help themselves as nature demands. The first meal should consist of hard boiled eggs chopped very fine, this should be given fi,r the next two or three days, then for the next two or three days hard boiled eggs mixed with stale bread crumbs, then you can put them on to bread and milk for the morning meal with a feed of chicken meal for dinner and supper. As they advance in growth you may substitute the evening meal of soft food for dry-chick food. For the first two weeks chickens should be fed as often as they will eat their meal greedily. It is hardly possible to give you a time table, but the oftener they are fed (and not overfed) the better they will thrive. A very important feature is the last meal. The first meal of course should be given as soon as it is day- light, but the evening meal should be given by the assistance of a light. Very young chicks are unable to withstand the long cold nights of early spring unless they are well nurtured ; therefore, it is essential to go to a little trouble in this direction. GRIT.

Just as adult fowls need grit so must the chickens be supplied. Thio can be given in the form of good sharp sea sand. In some parts this is difficult to obtain, a good substitute however, is found in ordinary building sand. Take a shovel full of sand, spread it over an old tray and put it into the oven to thoroughly dry. When this is thrown down in the coops the chicks will sort out of it, those little pebbles so easily discerned when the sand is dry. Clean water as well as grit is an essential, so also is green food. The best form of green food for yourg chicks is a nice green sod, these can be peeled off the road side, and by just ordinary selection you are able to get a sod with plenty of young clover growing thereon. 'A further advantage also is Ihe fact that often enough these sods are full of grit. The rain washes the sand &c., off of the road, this in turn washes into the channels and when dry the wind blows a quantity into the grass, where it remains. MARCH JOTTINGS. Let me remind my readers that this is the most important month in the breeding season. If you want a winter laving stack you mu,t hatch chickens in the month of March. Therefore special attention should be paid to the breeding pens. keep the laying stcck well supplied with a plentiful supply of clean water. Laying hens drink a lot of water, and unless this is clean disease will follow. And you all know how important it is to keep the breeding stock healthy. Be careful not to get the breeders over-fat. Keep a ben in good condition and she will give you a better supply of eggs. Not only so, but the eggs from over- fat stock hens are not as fertile. A good supply of clean water, plenty of sharp flint grit, a supply of old mortar in the scratching shed, and p!enty of fresh green food, these are the salient features of keeping your breeding stcck in good 'buckle.' QUERIES.

"Constant Reader" says that he has got half a dozen White Orpington pullets, and wants to know what is the best cross for the production of an all round fowl from these ? Answer: I should mate the Wbite Orpingt,u pullets with a vigorous Houdan Cock. Later on in the season you could mate them again with an Indian Game cock. Thus you would get from the first mating pullets that would make good layers and the cockerels, good table birds. From the second mating, you would get table birds almost par -excellence. The pullets from these also would prove not bad winter layers even if you did not want to kill them for culinary purposes. " Backyarder " wants to know which are the best varieties for the town run were there is no grass ? He states that they will have an almost free run but only on a practically cindered run. Answer : It is always advisable to have a dark- feathered variety, because if ycu run white plumaged fowls on a town run they soon look dirty and unsightly. I should recommend any of the following varieties : Black Minorcas, Andalusians, Croad Lang- shans, Black Leghorns, or Black Wyandottes. Thanks for your kindly remaras about the poultry column. It is always open for the free use of my readers. You cannot ask too many questions. It is a pleasure to be of some little service to readers of this column.- " Town Hall Ward Novice" sends along the follow- ng very interesting balance sheet of his year's work-

div.head: RECORD YEAR.
div.p: A RECORD YEAR.
MESSRS. RICHMONDS' CONTINUED PROSPERITY.

A record turnover was the outstanding feature of the past year's work of the Richmond Gas Stove and Aleter Co., Ltd., which was under review at the annual meeting of the Company, held at the offices, Academy- street, Warrington, on Thursday. Mr Thomas Dwerryhouse (chairman of the company) presided, and was supported by the following directors : Messrs Horace M Thornton (vice-chairman and managing director), John Coxon, J F Atkins, MB., John A Ransome,(managing director),J W Glover and J W Slack (secretary.) Among others present were : —Aldermen J Smethurst and A Bennett, Messrs F A Frost, W Duff, J Booth, C Jackson Holmes, Segar Owen, E J Hall and L A Voisey (auditor).

div.head: DIRECTOR'S REPORT.
div.p: THE DIRECTOR'S REPORT.

In their report the directors stated that the balance standing to the credit of profit and loss account (less debenture interest and contingent reserve) including the amount brought forward %/SS £35,024 Os 3d which the directors recommended be appropriated as follows: —Depreciation an buildings, plant, patterns, fixtures, etc., £5,612 16s Gd ; dividend on preference capital at the rate of 6 per cent per annum (less income tax), £5,881 12s 5d ; dividend (frte of income tax), on the ordinary shares at the rate of 10 per cent per annum, £8,161 12s ;bonus of 6d per share on the ordinary shares £2,010 8s ; reserve fund (bringing this amount up to, £50,000), £5,000 ; total £26,696 Ss lid ; balance to next account subject to directors' reniuneration,.£B,327 us-id. After placing the entire cost of advertising as in former years against revenue, the Directors recommended a dividend at the rate of 10 par cent, per annum and a bonus of Gd per share on the ordinary shares. The Company's w;orks at Academy-street, Grappenhall and branches had, as usual, been kept in good condition and maintained out of revenue. To meet the growing demand for the company's goods, it has again been found necessary to make further extensions at Grappenhall, and additional fitting shops, etc., would be completed at an early date. The retiring directors were Mr J A Ransoms and Mr J F Atkins. Their re-election by the hoard was reported in accordance with the company's articles of association. Mr Jas W Slack had been elected a director of the company.

div.head: COMPANY'S STRONG POSITION.
div.p: THE COMPANY'S STRONG POSITION.

The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report and statement of accounts, congratulated the Company on a prosperous year's work. When they met in that room twelve months ago and talked over their prospects for the coming year, with the coal strike on nand and further disasters impending, he was sure it was not in anyone's mind that they would surmount their difficulties and improve their position, as corn- pared with the previous year, to the extent they had done. There were two influences which bad to be taken into account before profits could be thought of. There was the miners' strike which nearly ruined some manufacturers but which left that company compara- tively free, as they looked tar ahead and did not really require any fuel until about a week before the collapse. He was not quite sure that,as manufacturers, they did not gain something by the coal strike, as he believedamany people took to gas cookers and tires at that time, because of their great difficulty in securing coal. The other trouble was the strike of railway workers aiming at the stoppage of all railway traffic. That caused considerable trouble, but eventually the country settled down and for the remainder of the year the company bad a very busy time. Their orders since the commencement of the year had been good and, as the year progressed, they increased very considerably,so much so that they were again compelled to erect more buildings at Grappenhisll. He expected they would have to keep on adding buildingsaccording to their vvants,and in accordance with the plans lain down, until the entire works was completed. Of course, that would be carried out gradually, and might be the work of considerable time. The additions recently made were found invalu- able during the high pressure of last year. With regard to the supplies of raw materials, they had been fortunate in buying early and the market, as it happened, was a rising one. What the future would bring forth it remained to be seen. It was risky buying on a falling market, and it was possible the market might be in that position soon. References were made at the last meet- Ina to the engagement of Mr Hartley, their chemical expert, and they were glad to say his services and experience had been and were of great benefit to the company. The Chairman next briefly alluded to the striking developments which had taken place of late years with regard to the designs and workmanship of gas fires, the result being that the firm now produced fires which were fit to be installed in the best class of houses, as well as catering for the humbler dwellings. They could claim to be in the very front rank in that class of business. Reviewing the balance sheet in detail, the Chairman emphasised the fact that the reserve fund was being raised to £50,000 which, on a capital of £BO,OOO, he considered was is good sum. (Hear, hear.) During the year they had added to their assets in respect of works and buildings no less a sum than £18,531. Depreciation had, of course, to be deducted trow that, leaving a net increase of £13,000 The same applied to their trade stocks at their various works. They had rather prided themselves on keeping their stocks down, but the increase of trade had altered all that, and their stocks showed an increase of £13,303 on last year. The directors had taken an important step in deciding to inaugurate a contingency fund which would obviate any necessity to withdraw from the reserve fund, under exceptional circumstances, and would steady the 41ividends, thus,in turn, steadying the price of shares. Speculators like to see shares fluctuating because they made something out of it, but the investor preferred that they should remain at a steady, valuable rate. (Hear, hear.) The amount owing to the company from sundry debtors was £62,449, as against £50,000 last year. The fact was, however that they had done such a very much larger volume Of trade that debtors, creditors, stocks and everything else showed an increase. Some shareholders might object to the carrying forward of £8,327, which represented almost 10 per cent on the capital, but taking everything into consideration, he thought it was the safest course to adopt, as they never knew what the future might have in store, and it was well not to view the prospects in too rosy a light but to be prepared for any emergency. (Applause). Mr H M TiioalsTost, in seconding, said 1912 had proved a record year for turn-over, and as a result of that greater business their profit was also larger and, as the balance sheet showed, their financial position had been materially strengthened by additions to their reserve and depreciation funds. There were several reasons for their continued prosperity, but primarily they might attribute it to the work done by them for many years in the way of advertising, not only of their own particular manufactures, but also the educational work they had accomplished by means of gas exhibitions canvassing, showrooms, etc., which had brought prominently before the public the many uses of gas for cepking, beating, industrial and other purposes. An additional factor which had been responsible for the larger business was the British Commercial Gas Mao- oiation, which was formed in 1911, with the object of advertising the uses of gas for all purposes. This bringing together of both sides of tbe industry had proved to be is great power for good. It had broken down prejudices, improved the relations of buyer and seller, and had been responsible for an enthusiasm for the advancement of the industry which augured well , for the future and which had astonished even those who were most optimistic in the formation of the associa- tion. One other reason for their present prosperity was the recognition in the gas world which they bad obtained for theproduction of reliable and scientifically I constructed goods. In that connection, the growth of their research work had been so considerable that Dr , Colman, who had been their consulting chernist and who had a very large practice, felt he must relinquish the position and strongly recommended them, in view of the growth of the work, to appoint a fully qualified ofiemist to take control of their laboratories and to devote the whole of his time to analytical and research work. This had been done and Mr Harold Hartley, Master of Science, late Gas Research Fellow, Leeds University, and Gartside Scholar, Manchester University, was now with them and they felt fully satisfleld they had been fortunate in securing his services. The responsibilities and importance of the position would be realised when he mentioned that an even more rigid and exacting standard had been estab- lished in their laboratories and throughout their works to ensure that everything they placed on the market e ould give the utmost satisfaction, not only to the buyer, but to the consumer who used it. A further contribution to the success of their business was was the addition in recent years of departments for the manufacture of gas apparatus other than cookers and gas fires, for which they had already a world-wide reputation. One of the most successful of these departments was that con earned with the manufacture of industrial appliances Another department to which they were looking to give them a considerable business was that of appli- ances for water heating. They were quite satisfied that the progress they had made had brought them right to the front and, as the further demand developed, they were confithint they would obtain a full share of the extra business that would come.lt would be seen,there- fore, that they were fully alive to the possibilities and requirements of the gas industry and were thoroughly equipped and well organised to take a leading part in all further developments. They were very gratified at the continued growth and prosperity, but the success of a business like theiriasub- ject as they were to keen competition, depended on the capacity, industry and example of those appointed to control it. Speaking for the management and the whole of the stall, and also for those gentlemen who represented them so ably in various parts of the coun- try and the countries across the water, he knew their interests a 3 shareholders were well served and it was to their loyalty and earnest endeavours, coupled with the continual care with which the directors watched over the general policy of their business, that they were able to present a balance sheet showing such steady and satisfactory progress. (applause.) The resolution was unanimously agreed to..
THE DIVIDEND.

The CHAIRMAN moved that a dividend at the rate of 10 per cent, per annum (less 5 per cent already paid) and a bonus of 6d per share for the year ended December 31st, 1912 (tree of income tax) be now declared and paid. Mr J CoxoN seconded and said that, never since his association with the company, had he seen the business look in a healthier condition than to-day. Although they were always subject to keen competition, he thought the shareholders might look forward with con- fidence to the future prosperity of the business. He also wished to refer with pride and a great amount of gratitude to the two managing directors, the secretary and members of the staff who had so ably managed their respective departments. Toe resolution was passed. DIRECTORS' REMUNERATION.

Mr W DUFF moved: That the sum of £8.50 (free of income tax) be placed at the divosal of the directors for their services during the year. He said de amount was a little increase, but be was sure the shareholders would agree that the directors were worthy of it. Mr BOOTH, in seconding, said the statement for the past year was eminently satisfactory and exceeded the anticipations of many of them. The proposition was agreed to. THE AUDITOR.

Alderman SMETHURST moved the re-appointment of Mr Louis A Voisey, as auditor at a remuneration of £l5O. He kept bringing out a better balance sheet each year and tie hoped that would continue for a long time to come. (Hear, hear.) Mr E J HALL seconded. He also took occasion to congratulate the Board, the company and Mr Slack on his appointment as a director. (Hear, hear). The appointment v.as approved and Mr VoisEY, in returning thanks, said it afforded him great pleasure to append his name to such a solid and sound balance sheet as had been submitted that day. (Applause).
The Examiner, Saturday, March 8, 1913.

div.head: GENERAL PROSPERITY OF NOVA scarm.
div.p: GENERAL PROSPERITY OF NOVA scarm.

The value of the yield of the farms, forests, fisheries, mines and factories of Nova Scotia for 1912 was 27 millions sterling. This is the largest reached within the history of the Province, and betokens universal prosperity and progress. The business situation may be characterised as one of general buoyancy, and there is confidence in every quarter that the present year will witness even further improvements. The popula- tion of Nova Scotia continues to increase. British emigrants are settling there in considerable numbers. and many of the Dative-born who left the Province years ago are returning. Wealth is not centralised in Nova Scotia. The growth of industries has been general and widespread. The unemployed problem aoes not exist. Practically every man has a living wage, and, as a natural consequence, social conditions are excellent, and there is a g3neral feeling of contentment.

div.head: THANKING THE STAFF.
div.p: THANKING THE STAFF.

Dr ATKINS moved a vote of thanks to the managing directors, secretary and staff for their efficient services during the past year. He said that, although the past bear had been a very good one, and a record in some respects, they must not lose sight of the fact that it hen been a trying year, and the profits and not been easily earned. Keen competition in some cases involved cut prices which, in turn, necessitated a larger turnover to keep up the profits. Extra work was thus necessarily thrown upon the management of their manufacturing cepartments. Air 10 A Frost, in seconding, said the Board and the staff reminded him of the organ and the tune that was got out of it. The Board might manipulate the keys as ably as possible, but unless the men behind put wind into the instrument, there would not be much tune. (Laughter and hear, hear.) He was very pleased that his fellow townsman, Mr Slack, had been appointed a director. One always liked to see fellow-townsmen progressing in that way. (Hear, hear). Tee vote was heartily accorded. Mr RAN6om F:, in returning thanks, said he could assure the shareholders that the management and the staff which they had working for them were second to none in the country. (Hear, hear.) I hey had at the head of their departments—of which there was a growing number in the works—men who were not only thoroughly capable, but earnest and willing. They had not been entirely with- out their labour troubles during the year—no businets in the country had—but he believed that the very fact that their men knew they had a straight deal that the company expected the best they could do and in return was prepared to treat them in a reasonable and fair way, induced them to give whole-hearted co-operation. Mr Ransome briefly alluded to the death of his brother who in the early years of the company was one of its most ardent and enthusiastic workers.
PURIFYING THE ATMOSPHERE. Mr SEGAR OWEN moved a vote of thanks to tha Chairman.

Alderman BENNETT, in seconding, said it must be a source of great gratification to Mr DNerryhouse to preside over the affairs of a company which not only showed such admirable financial results, but which was doing a peat deal to help to cleanse the atmosphere and conduce to the convenience of tne population, not only in Warrington, but in every large centre. If the shade of Dr Priestley ever revisited " the pale glimpses of the moon" he must be very proud to feel that his old residence was put to such an appropriate use.
The vote having been passed the CHAIRMAN, in responding, said the staff and workmen of the firm were as tine a lot of men as he ever came across. (Applause.)

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Described as the acme of refinement and originality in vaudeville, the vocal act presented by Betty Barclay and a Baritone at the Ilippcdrcme this week has proved a great attraction. There is an air of homely simplicity about the turn which at once appeals to the audience who are not slow to show their appreciation of the charming manner in which the couple render their items. In the duet "Call round on a rainy afternoon" they were highly successful and the baritone pleased immensely with his rendition of " Little man." The Three Brothers Huater

are clever acro-pantomimical humorists, and appear in the sketch "Languid Energy" with a large amount of success. One of the trio affects a continual desire for rest but, when called upon by the other two, he performs the most daring and smart feats of jump- ing and vaulting, but immediately afterwards he assumes the same languid mood. Miss Gwennie Llewellyn charms the audience with her singing of well-known songs. She puts plenty of spirit into her numbers and sings uncommonly well. Fi ed Evans presenis a novel turn, "A dream of Oliver Twist." Under Mr Evans' treatment the characters, Fagin and Bill Sykes are most realistic, and one marvels at the rapidity with which he effects his "changes. Couqelli is a clever mimic, and created much laughter with his representation of a squalling babe. The Fitzroys appear in a refined gymnastic act, and prove themselves to be smart trapeze aitistes. They perform the most intricate and daring feats with an ease and grace which is astonishing. The Two Canadians (Ida Grahame and Dorothy Gibson) are clever instrumentalists. They manipulate the trom- bone in a skilful manner and the turn goes with a catchy swing. Sims Woolley is as popular as ever with his stole of humorous stories which he tells in his inimitable style to the delight of the audience. The Sisters Reeve, refined vocalists, also appear. The pictures " Wonderful fruits " and " Dr Brian Pellie and the secret despatch" are shown on the bioscope.

At Canterbury Diocesan Conference on June 13tb, the subject of " Moral Responsibility " will be intro- duced by Mr lan Malcolm, M.P., and that of "The Position of Women in the Church" by Lord Robert Cecil, M.P.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL TOPICS. THE ETERNAL BRIDGE QUESTION. Tramway Employes' Wages.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL TOPICS. THE ETERNAL BRIDGE QUESTION. Tramway Employes' Wages.
TIME AND A QUARTER FOR SUNDAY WORK.

In addition to the uproarious proceedings reported elsewhere, there were several topics of interest under discussion a', the monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Coun- cillor Dr Joseph) presided and there were also present : —The Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), Aldermen T Burton,A Bennett John Evans,W Pierpoint,J Smethurst, D Tinnion, Councillors G Archer, T Birtles, J Broad- hurst, J Chrimes, E Cunnington, E Chantler. J G Craik, J Dickinson, S Gough, J Hawthorn, J Halliwell, R Henshall, F Lindley, .1 T Locker, F T Lashford, Dr McKee, E Osborne, J Pemberton,P Peacock,H Roberts, .1 Shaw, J Wilkinson, Messrs J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), A T Hallaway (deputy-town clerk). .1 Fairhurst (borough treasurer), A M Ker (borough surveyor), Dr J Coote Hibbert (medical officer of heilth), Dr G W N Joseph(assistant medical otticer),W T telood(inspector of nuisances),F V L Mathias (electrical engineer),J Moore Murray (director of education) R B Roberts (assistant director), and J Gray (water engineer). THE COST OF EDUCATION. Councillor ROBERTS, in submitting the minutes of the Education Committee, said that in view of the con- siderable expenditure on new schools, the Council and the town were to be congratulated on the fact that it was not proposed to take any larger sum from the rates for educational purposes in the coming year than was levied during the past twelve mouths. Councillor BIRTLES seconded. Councillor PEMBERTON said the Council ought to make some real and serious protest to the Education Depart- ment in view of the small amount contributed from the National Exchequer for educational purposes He rlforred to the ever-increasing burden which was being placed on the municipalities in an insidious way, and said it was time a strong stand was made against it. The MAYOR : I quite sympathise with what Coun- cillor Pemberton says, but I don't think that, without combined action on the part of municipalities, the pro- test of one Corporation will have much effect. The minutes were approved. BATH -6 AND BOWLING GREEN.

When the minutes of the Town Hall, Parks and Bath Committee were under consideration, Councillor PEMBERTON asked when the baths exten- sion would be completed. The work seemed to be going on very slowly and summer was approaching. According to the terms of contract, the jou ought to have been finished some time ago. Councillor PEACOCK called attention to a resolution of the committee instructing the Borough Surveyor to obtain tenders for the laying-out of the bowling green to be constructed at Grace's Pottery. So far back as 1905, he said, definite instructions were given to the late Borough Surveyor to obtain tenders for the work, and they were repeated in April 1909, and again in April, 1910. in June of lust year the Council obtained the sanction of the Local Government Board to the borrowing of the money, but nothing had been done up to now. Such inaction was a disgrace to the Council and an insult to the ratepayers of the ward. Councillor DICKENSON said the baths extension was being pushed on as rapidly as possible. He partly blamed Councillor Pemberton for the non-completion of the contract, for he was appointed a member of the committee but when he came and saw the work that was going on be retired from it. (Laughter). Councillor Dickenson repeated the statement he made at the last meeting of the Council that the baths would be finished before Warrington Bridge. (Alderman Smethurst : "Question.") As to the bowling green in Winwick-road, it had been in hand for eight years and it was certainly high time it was brought to an issue.

div.head: MOTOR BUSES.
div.p: MOTOR BUSES.

Alderman SMETHURST, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee, said the tender of Messrs W A Stevens Ltd. of Maidstone, for the supply of three motor buses had been accepted. The firm had undertaken to deliver them within twelve weeks and he hoped that the expenditure involved would be recouped by the support of the public. He had a doubt with regard to one district, but he hoped the residents would be induced to patronise the 'buses sufficiently to make them pay. Councillor WILKINSON said he had every faith that the motor 'buses would pay. In reply to Councillor Chantler, Alderman SMETHURST said the routes on which the 'buses would be placed had not been fixed.

"TIME AND A QUARTER " FOR SUNDAY WORK The Electricity and Tramways Committee resolved that the men employed in the car sheds be entitled to time and a quarter for Sunday work. In reply to Councillor Osborne, Alderman Sm ETITURST said the resolution meant that the men would be paid at the rate of time and a quarter. Councillor BROADHURST asked for the resolution to be withdrawn. It was an injustice to ask men to wcrk on Sunday for such a miserable pittance when private firmq paid at the rate of time and a half or even double time. The Corporation should be model employers and he admitted that they were generous in other respects. Councillor PEACOCK, as a member of the Electricity Committee, stoutly maintained that they were generous and model employers who did justice to the workmen, even in preference to the officials. All the men asked for was time and a quarter and they were perfectly satisfied. They worked very little time on Sunday. Councillor PEMBERTON said he understood the stand- ing orders laid it down that all Corporation workmen should receive the standard rate of pay. It was a well established fact that men employed on Sunday should be paid time and a half. Corporation workmen had to be moderate in what they asked and thankful for small mercies. Councillor DICKENSON moved and Councillor OsnortNE seconded an amendment that the minute be referred back. Alderman SMETHURST said he would back the wages of the Warrington tramway employes against those paid in any Lancashire town of similar population and with a like number of workmen. The committee had constantly raised wages. The men asked for time and a quarter and they had received it. Councillor DICKENSON : They are not satisfied. Alderman SMETHURST : We granted the rEquest signed by all the men. Councillor DICKENSON : It is a miserable thing to ask any man to work on Sunday for time and a quarter. Alderman SMETHURST : lam as much in favour of the workingman as any man in this room. Since I have been chairman of the committee—for eight or nine years—we have not had a single dispute with our men.

Councillor LASHFORD : Alderman Smethurst says he is greatly in favour of the workingmen with regard to wages. We have only his word for it, and his votes here. I beg to differ from Alderman Smethurst. He is not in favour of the workingman having a fair wage, or he would talk and act differently from what he does. One would have thought that when the men asksd for time and a quarter he would have thought it was not enough and proposed time and a' half. Alderman BURTON said it would be unjust to the rate- payers to thrust more money upon the men tban they asked for, when they were quite satisfied with what had been conceded. He questioned whether Councillor Dickenson would act in a similar way with regard to workmen of his own. .

Councillor BROADHURST : We have the moral right to show to the Council that these men, unfortunately for themselves, dare not ask for more, yet the trade union laws of this town, hich every councillor is willing to acknowledge, provide for titue and a half on Sunday. In reply to Councillor Chrimes, Alderman SMETHURST said about ten cleaners and Litters were employed on Sunday. Their wages averaged over 30s. a week and the miority of them were men whom the Corporation had taken off the streets. The voting was as follows :—For the amendment : _
Councillor; Broadhurst. OsbornA, Dickenson, Chantler, Gough, Chrimes, Pemberton, Cunnington and Lashford-9. --

Against : Tho Mayor, Aldermen Fore haw, Smethurst John Evans end Burton, Councillors Birtles, Wilkinson Halliwell, Peacock, Lindley, Archer, and Hawthorn-12 The amendment was lost and the minutes were approved.

div.head: BRIDGE AGAIN.
div.p: THE BRIDGE AGAIN.

Alderman SMETHURST, in proposing the minutes of the Bridges Committee, said he Mies not in the habit of betting but, if he were, he would be willing to wager something that one portion of Warrington Bridge would be opened before any portion cf the new baths. Councillor DicKENAoN : I think a portion of War- rington Bridge has already been opened, and it has cost £3OO extras for it. Alderman SMETHURST said the site of Messrs Fair- dough's property was now in the hands of the con- taactor, and piles for the training wall on that side of the river were being driven. He hoped the work would now go on pretty quickly. The MAYOR seconded the minutes.

Councillor PEMBERTON said be would not have minded taking up Alderman Smethurst's bet, hut be had given up that bad habit years ago. (Laughter). The MAYOR : We are not taking any bets here. Alderman SMETHURST : I would not take the bet on. Councillor PEMBERTON moved an amendment that certain accounts due for bridge works be not paid. He said a great deal remained to be done before one third of the bridge was completed. Unless the Committee made a stand and stopped the payments the work would probably be hanging on for years, whereas the time stipulated in the contract would shortly expire. Councillor Broadhurst had challenged him on the matter. VEO other members he was fond of making challenges when he (Councillor Pemberton) had not the right of reply.

Councillor BROADHURST rose to a point of order but the Mayor called upon him to resume his se%t. Councillor PEmitEaToN said the Council ought to call upon the engineer to see that the contractor carried on the work more expeditiously. They had two clerks of the works and the Council should require them to pre- sent weekly reports on the progress which had been made,mentioning the time which had been lost through conditions which they could not control. The Council should also insist that a proper number of men should be kept on the job. The way in which the work was being dilly-dallied with was a disgrace to the Corporation. There was no seconder of the amendment and when Councillor WILKINSON sarcastically suggested that Councillor LA.SHFORD should step into the breach, the latter remarked : Oh, he (Councillor Pemberton) is not particular about it. The MAYOR: I think this is a deliberate waste of time. It is a mean transaction. _

Councillor BROADHURST : -Councillor Pemberton's attack requires no answer, Mr Mayor. The MAYOR : NO, it is not worthy of one. There was some laughter from certain members whereupon the MAYOR retorted: I would laugh at something nobler than that. Alderman SMETHURST characterised Councillor Pemberton's attitude as ridiculous. He knew very well that when the engineer gave a certificate for a certain amount the Council must pay it, or the following day the contractor could issue a writ. It was a shame that the Council's time should be repeatedly wasted in that manner. "the minutes were then approved.

div.head: INCREASING MANGOLD AND OAT CROPS,
div.p: INCREASING MANGOLD AND OAT CROPS,

Mr Ernest Parke's eleventh annual report on manurial trials on the arable part a his farm at Kineton, in Warickshire, has just been issned. The mangold crop, grown after wheat, was a heavy one where well manured. The unmanured portion of the field grew only 16 tons per acre. This was increased to 25 tons by a dressing of superphosphate. Different portions of the field had, in addition, dressings of nitrate of soda in quantities of 2 cwt., 4 cwt., and 6 cwt. per acre, and in these cases the yield of rnangolds. was 32 tons, 37 tons, and 43 tons per acre. Deducting the yield of the unmanured land, the increase, when both superphos- phate and nitrate were used, averaged 21 tons of man- golds per acre, and, as the average cost of the fertilisers was only about 60s. per acre the cost of the extra 21 tons of roots was only 3s. I.er ton. As the consuming value of mangolds is usually assumed to be nearer lOs a ton, the result appears to show a handsome profit. The responsive nature, under manurial treatment, of this naturally poor soil—which is typical of much in this neighbourhood—is again illustrated by the oat crop, which followed roots of the year before. An unmanured plot gave 46 bmhels of oats per acre. Where man.ured with 3 cwt. of super- phosphate and 1 cwt. of nitrate of soda the crop was 59 bushels per acre, and with a second hundredweight of nitrate it was raised to 77 bushels, making a total increase, due to fertilisers, of nearly 4 quarters of oats per acre, worth, at the present price of English oats, about £4, the cost of the fertilisers responsible for the increase being only about 355,

The draw for the second round ties will be made at six o'clock this evening at the Fleece Hotel, St, Helens. Now what can have attracted the Northern Union officials to St. Helens?

Warrington's Cup team gave an excellent account of themselves in the pi elimitiary encounter with Bull last Saturday. The Third Porters have yet to gain their fist victory on Warrington soil and, clever as they are, I don't think they will ever succeed. They had the chance offered them by the Fates on Saturday.. Warrington were only leading by 5 points to ml, when they lost the services of Tranter and R Thomas, and for the whole of the last 25 minutes they had to resist the full strength of the visitors with only four forwards in the pack. Even then, Hull could only pet one try, and Warrington added to their discomfiture by a dropped goal from the foot of young Douglas in the last minute. It was a fine, fast game, from start to finish, with Warrington certainly the superior team. Our forwards were heroic, and the tackling all round was a treat. The worst feature of the match was Darmody's persistent obstruction as a wing-forward. He roused the ire of the crowd, was cautioned by the referee, and did his own side no good. If he has no better football in him than we saw on Saturday he might as well go back to the Antipodes.

The "A " team will indulge in a " friendly" at home to-day with Pendleton. A capital side has been selected including Bradley, a nineteen-year-old brother of the famous Wigan wing, who is anxious for a trial with the Wirepullers. If he is anything like his brother he will be an acquisition.
The team is : J Brown,full back; Bardsley, Davies, Berry, and Bradley, three-quarters; A Brown and Jordan, half backs; Gibbs, Fletcher, Bevan, Clark, Blundell and Sankey, forwards.
Ile Works Competition preliminaries are being rapidly pu=hA forward. Entries have to be in the hands of the club secretary by Monday the 17th inst. and the draw will take place the following night.

A variation of the rules specifies that any works may enter more than one team, or any works not able to provide a full complement of players may combine with any other works not taking part in the competi- tion, subject to permission from the Club Committee. This is a concession which should enable smaller works to co-operative to advantage in raising a respectable thirteen to enter the competition.

div.head: Warrington Defeat Hull.
div.p: Warrington Defeat Hull.

The Hull match is one of the most popular on the Warrington card and the attendance of only about 5,000 last Saturday was disappointing. A fine, dry day favoured the game and both sides were well represented, the visitors team including the two famous Australians Gilbert and Darmody. arrington gave another trial to Douglas at half back and he fully satisfied the critics. Teams : Warrington.—Jolley ; Brookes, Tranter, Berry and Bradshaw; Nicholas and Douglas; George Thomas, Caesters, Naylor, Fearnley, Cox and R Thomas. Hull .—E Rogers ; Francis, Gilbert, Smith and Nolan ; G Rogers and Anderson ; Kerridge, Holder, Merry, Darmody, Allen and Taylor. Referee, J H Whiteley, Wakefield Trinity. Touch judges, H Mainwaring. Salford and H Yates, Runcorn. Play opened in lively fashion. with Hull somewhat in the ascendant. Gilbert received from Anderson and made a strong burst on the right but was well held by Fearnley. Nicholas and Douglas soon changed the venue with smart tactics and the Hull goal was hotly assailed. Cox was tackled just outside, and then Tranter missed a pass when well placed. The Warring- ton forwards were in brilliant form and f oon took the ball over, but R Thomas was judged off-side. Hull were having a hot time on the defence, and a smart move by Douglas nearly brought about a score. The half back got away smartly on the right and then gave Berry a reverse pass. The inside man went strongly for the line but lack of pace resulted in his capture by E Rogers a yard short. NVarrington cantinually forced matters, and before Hull could clear, Nicholas secured the ball close in and dodged over smartly near the posts. Brooks added an easy goal. A penalty shot by G Thomas for an infringement by Darmody fell short of the desired haven, and then a groan of disappointment went up when Nicholas broke away and his pass to Cox was not accepted. Anderson tried hard to make an impression on the home defence,but Jolley maintained his brilliant form and forced matters within a few yards of the Hull line. Naylor and Cheaters were prominent in one determined rush and Nicholas again dashing away from a pack sent on the pass to Berry, who was pulled up when only a yard short of the line. A tall kick by Anderson was not of much service to his side and had the Warrington forwards controlled the ball a little better the score must have been augmented. Gilbert got the Tykes out of a tight corner, and several com- mendable dashes by him were the medium of Hull reaching the Warrington quarters. Danger was speedily averted by Tranter and Jolley, and once more the scene of operations was at the Hull end, where Brookes and Bradshaw in succession made futile efforts to break through. Rogers cleared to half-way and this move brought about the interval with Warrington leading by one goal and one try (five points) to Hull, nothing. Warrington resumed in the same aggresive spirit,and Rogers was kept busy clearing his lines. Anderson was tackled near the line,aud Warrington passed across smartly, Berry missing the ball when he had a clear course. Keeping up the attack, Warrington again handled smartly, and Bradshaw made a commendable effort on the right, hut was forced over the corner flag by E Rogers. Before Hull could clear, Jolley took a drop at goal which went near the mark, and then a serious mishap hefel the homesters. Tranter came into violent collision with a visiting player and was assisted from the field of play, taking no further part in the game. Cheaters was drafted into the threequarter line and Brooks played at centre. Even with their forces weakened the Warringtonians lontinued to have the best of it and any attempts by 'rancis to evade Cheaters were soon frustrated,for the ,orward made no mistake when any tackling had to be lone. Warrington bore down on the pavilion goal and ,he ball trevelled to G Rogers, but Brookes brought off

great tackle and the visitors continued to be hard ,ressed. Then R Thomas was hurt, and though he was stole to resume he did not last long and was compelled to retire for good. Meanwhile Hull were threatening the Warrington line and after Gilbert had made one splendid attempt, the Hull backs got working on the right wing and the return pass being taken by Anderson, the Warrington line was crossed. E Rogers missed the goal. Warrington continued to play a plucky game with only four forwards. In the closing stages the " Wire- pullers" made a splendid rally, and in the last few seconds hot work was witnessed on the Hull line. From a psck about fifteen yards from the touch line Douglas secured, and before Hull could realise their position a smart drop sent the ball sailing over the cross-bar, this success of Warrington being bailed with loud cheers. Result: —Warrington, two goals one try (seven points) ; Hull, one try (three points).

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday March 8, 1913.
CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
NORTHERN CHAMPIONSHIP. WARRINGTON A.C. WIN.

At Stockton-on-Tees on Saturday last the local athletic club added to their already long list of successes, of this season, by a highly meritorious victory in the 31st annual Northern Senior Cross Country Championship, after what may fairly be described as the fastest race of the series, and they have since been the recipients of many hearty con- gratulations whizh included a very cordial letter from the Secretary of the previous holders—HallamshireA.C. Of the 15 qualified teams Wirral,Broughton and Salford did not turn out and 109 individuals represented the other twelve clubs. Details :

The start took place at the one mile two furlongs post with Hallamshire on the inside and Warrington in the centre to the first bend, round which Glover, Wallack, Vose, Breed, Fennah ml Holbrook ,ere in the leading positions and this order was maintained until the winning post was passed for the first time in omins. them The stadting point was passed, 1 mile, 5 furlongs, with the first three close together and well clear of the next batch with the tail about a quarter of a mile long, then a further 300 yards on tbe race- course was covered before the country (?) was reached about 1,000 yards of unmade road, which provided fairly fast grass mining before the plough was encountered, and the plough proved to be about 120 yards of a path between the ploughed land and hedgerow then 1,000 yards up the racecourse, equalled a second lap or 11 miles, a total of 3 miles, time 15min. 27scc., and the only change was that Breed had fallen back and his clubmate Lee, had taken his place, four more laps of miles made up the distance, in the first of these Wallach and Vose were together in this order when a 'one at a time" patch was reached, and with Wallach hanging fire Glover took a 70 yards lead. The start for the junior race was wretched and the local youngsters, who proved to be very poor travellers, were incapable of recovery from the effects of a rough railway ialrney in such a fast run race which was a terrific scramble with G F Roberts, Holmforth, leading all the way and Heaton Harriers team winners.

div.head: WARRINGTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB.

For the first time in its history the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club have a credit balance in hand. This was the encouraging news at the annual meeting which was held on Monday night. at the Lion Hotel. The chair was occupied by Mr W Silcock and there was a good attendance of members. The balanc-, sheet, submitted by Mr R LowE,showed that the subscriptions amounted to £240 Hs. The gate receipts were £l7 8s 9d, and rents receivable £52 10s. On the income side was a donation of £5 from Sir Gilbert Greenall. The deficit of £l5 7s2d at the beginn- ing of the year had been converted into a credit balance of £313 15s.

The Hon Secretary Mr C H 17nsworth pointed out that the present was a unique occasion. He had been con- nected with the club for over 30 years, and the present was the first time they had ended the season with a credit balance. They had made over .£5O profit on the year's working, and he thought the hon. treasurer (Mr Robert Lowe) was to be congratulated on the excellent results shown. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr R T FAIncLouGH congratulated the club on the talance sheet. He had been a member for 47 or 43 years and this was the first time to his knowledge that there had been a balance in hand. There was plenty of room for an improvement of the ground and he hoped the work would be taken in hand. (Hear, hear.) The following officials were re-elected :—President' Sir Gilbert Greenall, Hart ; hon treasurer, Mr Robert Lowe ; assistant treasurer and collector, Mr R Lowe; hon secetary, Mr C H Unsworth ; match secretary, Mr B Silcock ; captain of the first XI, Mr W Richardson, jun ' • second XI, Mr NV Vaurtoe ; deputy captain first XI, Mr S Pertrir,ge ; deputy captain of the second NI, Mr C E Hawthorn; Hzioretary of the tennis cluh, Mr R P Johnson; secretary of the bowling club, Mr T Cu oper ; captain of the bowling club, Mr R 1' Fairclough ; committees : cricket, Messrs B Silcock, NV Richard,on, ajun, W V Turton and H Partridge,; bowling, Messrs (3. NV A Brown, W S Haddock, John Rigby at d E Wallington. A resoluti( nof the Tennis Section that they be allowed four repres-mtations on the general committee was withdrawn and an amendment by Alderman Tinnier] that the tennis section be allowed three representives was passed unanimously. On the prop 'salon of Alderman TINNION seconded by Mr J L PEARSON a vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CENTRE). . .

Although the weather was somewhat cold last week end anglers did not mind. They heard from reports in our local press that roach were being taken at the Gowy, and this being the Warringtonian's favourite ground for specimen species, they turned out in great numbers, despite the cold, some hurrying to catch their train on Saturday at noon, to spend the week-end and try to top the fish that were already weighed in.ln this they were disappointed but one or two put roach over the scales that were well over the 1 lb ; in fact from reports we hear that there was no member from Warring ton who did not kill and some very favourable caCches were taken. One member had ten fish ; they were not weighed but by guess they averaged roach at 12oz and ten roach at 12oz is providing a fair day's sport. According to the quantity taken last week-end anglers from Warrington v.ere extremely unlucky in not having one to beat the lib soz B,lrms as they are all unanimous that they are there to be caught. The report from the canals is almost blank. These waters seemed to fish better before this last week or so and we cannot account for them falling off so suddenly, especially when you view the waters, as they look in fine condition.

div.head: SUCCESS OF THE GOWY.
div.p: THE SUCCESS OF THE GOWY.

The nearer to the close season this water gets, the better it seems to fish, and for quantity last week end surpassed all records this year. Mr T Jolley ereeled the heaviest with a fine roach of 110 loz 14dr' Mr J Green coming next with one of Ilb Ooz 10dr sod both members bad roach ranging from Soz up to llb. It was most surprising to members that not one roach was taken to reach the top one. However a party are con- sidering to pay a visit here during the week, with the expectation of upsetting caLulations. We shall soon hear if they do so as information of this kind is most pleasant to anglers, and there is a looking through line books to prepare for the week end, (as they say they are on at." Brook ") and when news of this kind get noised about. it would take more than uasettled weather to keep them away.

div.head: CANALS.
div.p: THE CANALS.

The Shropshire Union Canal was a blank last week end, and I once beards remark that this water was a hot water canal (meaning a summer fishery) and accord log to results up to the present their is borne truth in the statement. Norton also is fishing very poor several members who paid a visit on Thursday last returned without having a stir.

div.head: ULSTER WILL NOT FIGHT.
div.p: ULSTER WILL NOT FIGHT.
" A Faked and Artificial Campaign."

"The Ulster opposition to Home Rule is a faked and artificial campaign " declared Mr J F Lacey, of New Brighton, in an address on •` Home Rule and Ulster problems" before the members of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association on Monday evening. Mr P H Brown presided over a good attendance and the meeting was undoubtedly one of the most interesting of the successful series promoted by the Association. The CHAIRMAN said that Home Rule might already be regarded as an accomplished fact. Referring to the opposition of the Orange faction in Ulster, he said it simply meant that they wanted their own way and did not want anybody else to have theirs. If they could not have just wht..t they liked, they threatened to fight. However, whtn Ireland had settled down to the administration of hsr own iiffairs the Ulster problem, like a great many To, y bogeys, would dissolve and Ulster would worts amicably with the rest of Ireland for the benefit of the race. :kir Brown further submitted that Home Rule would tend to greater amity between other nations and ourselves. The Irish difficulty had stood in the way of a rapprochement between this country and the United States, and he believed it was an acknowledged fact that a great arbitration treaty was remaining to be signed, but for the opposition of the United States, which was solely due to the Irish cu3stion. The Irish dominated politics in practically the whole of our colonies, and also in a special degree in the United States. Liberal statesmen had therefore wisely recognised that, for the safety and peace of the world, the first essential was the grant- ing of Home Rule to Ireland. (Applause). Mr LACEY, in the course of a comprel,iniive and stirring address, said that to-day Ireland was a land of poverty, yet she was fertilt., had a good climate, and large undeveloped resources. The Irish race succeeded wherever it wei t but in its own cuuntry it could do nothing, because it was misgoverned sod mismangged. The Act of Union had proved a failure, but even if it were as good as it was bad, the Irish would still claim Home Rule as a nation's right—as a moral duty to rule itself. (Applause.) The

div.head: RECOGNITION OF NATIONALITY
div.p: RECOGNITION OF NATIONALITY

and the responsibility of Government were necessary to nourish and stimulate those qualities of perseverance and industry which had withered under centuries of persecution, servitude and misgovernment. Suppose the English people were governed by a German Chief Secretary,responsible to a Parliament in Berlin—would not all those present be members of a young-England movement, designed to set up an English Parliament? The message he brought from young Ireland to young Liberals was a request that they should, in Mr Gladstone's words, view the question as if, instead of being Englishmen, they were Irishmen. Dealing with the Ulster problem, Mr Lacey said it was difficult to et anything but vague hints from that province as to why it should be allowed to dominate the rest of Ireland. The suggestion was made that the Irish were unfit to manage their own affairs, but surely the nation which gave Lord Lansdowne and Sir Edward Carson to the Tory party could not be accused of unfit- ness for self-government ! (Laughter and applause) Mr Balfour had said that the Irish party was toe reost brilliant in the House of Commons. Ireland had been not inaptly termed the only place in the English- speaking world which the Irish did not govern. He regarded no insult as so great as the insinuation that Irish Catholics were intolerant in the matter of religion. If Home Rule meant Rome Rule—if it were for the benefit of the Catholic Church alone—surely the English Catholics would be in favour of it ! But they found the great majority of English Catholics, led by the Duke of Norfolk, were against Home Rule and that in 1893 they actually signed a petition against it on the ground that it would he harmful to tne Catholic Church. The Protestants who said they wonld he persecuted all came from the north east corner of Ulster, where Protestants were in a majority. But let them ask the Protestants in the south and west, where they were in a hopeless minority, whether they were afraid of Catholic intoleranco and they would reply in one voice " No." It was ascendancy which the Ulster Tories were afraid to give up. He believed

div.head: MR. HAROLD SMITH
div.p: MR. HAROLD SMITH

had used the argument in Warrington that the industries of Ulster would be taxed out of existence under Home Rule. To begin with, Ulster was not the richest province in Ireland, it was not the province of law and education and it was not the best province in Irelend, by any means. If, as they were told, Ulster wee necessary to Home hula because otherwise Home Rule would lie financially impossible,how silly it would be of them to tax its industries out of existence and thus rob themselves of their best means of income ! There were thousands of pounds of the money of Irish Catholics invested in the industries of Belfast and Ulster. %Vete they going to ruin those industries and at the same time ruin their Catholic fellow-countrymen, as well as the Protestants ? There were thousands of Irish Catholics employed in the Ulster industries. Were they going to throw them out of work ? Mr Lacey referred to Belfast commercial magnates, notably Lord Pine, who welcomed Home Rule and were not hesitating to spend large sums en extending their concerns. They were told that" Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right, " but he said that " Ulster will fight for the right "—and Derry echoed that. (Applause.) The Orangenaenof North-Ea3t Ulster were fanatical bigots, and the value of their loyalty was evidenced by the fact hat &ring the recent Belfast demonstrations against Home Rule, oae placard read :—" If England won't help us Germany will." Whenever a meisure had been introduced for the betterment of Ireland, the Orange bigots hair threatened rebellion. Mr Lacey referred to the out- rages perpetrated on Home Rulers by the Orangemen of Belfast, but said their riots and misbehaviour shotild not keep the rest of Ireland in subjection. Ulster was not really prosperous. Under English rule, the popula- tion of Ulster had been more than halved, industry after industry had been wiped out and tax had been piled upon tax. To-day they were asked to believe that Ulster would rise in insurrection if England did not continue to fleece her. Belfast had more to gain from Home Rule than any other city in Ireland. It was a melancholy fact that the conditions of labour in Belfast were worse than in any other place in these islands. The Ulster opposition to Home Rule was a faked and artificial campaign engineered by rack-rent landlords and sweating employers. Sir Edward Carson went to Belfast and raved about the Pope and the Church of Rome, but did he tell the toilers of Ulster that he r voted against the Old Age Pensions Act? The Ulster Tories had always striven to keep the workers down : they were the most reactionary element in the Imperial Parliament. Mr Lacey concluded by saying that the Home Rulers wanted the help of every Irish- man in building up a new Ireland. (Applause). Mr E LLOYD JONES said the basis of the demand for Home Rule was to be found in the fact that Ireland was a nation and, on that account, she desired to govern herself. The Ulster problem would solve itself when the measure actually came into operation.

Mr G TOULMIN said one could not help contrasting Mr Lacey's speech with the tirades against Home Rule to which they were treated in Warriagton. The latter were full of animosity against Ireland and talk about wallowing in the blood of their fellow-countrymen. They were also told about 10,000 men who web ° drilling in preparation to fight if Home Rule were granted. What a refreshing contrast it was to hear the true national sentiments to which Mr Lacey had given expreseion ! At the next election they would not have to trouble themselves about Home Rule or Welsh Disestablish- ment, but about something nearer home. Mr P DELANEY, Jon, and Mr J HUGHES also spoke and a v.:AA Gf thanks was passed to Mr Lacey.
In reply, Mr LACEY said that if plural voting were abolished, the Nationalists would win four more seats in Ulster. (Applituse).

div.head: Exa,rriner Saturday, March 8, 1913.
div.p: The Exa,rriner Saturday, March 8, 1913.

Warrington Photographic Society. Perhaps the brightest of all the season's evenings is the One spent by the members in recalling by means of word and picture the previous summer's outings. On Tuesday, Mr W Burrell (assistant secretary) entertained over 40 listeners with accounts of the nine excursions undertaken last summer, among them Hoylake, Lincoln and Amsterdam. The 195 pictures had been made by :natty members, and occasioned endless interest and merriment, Colborne-street Baptist Church. - •

Thursday next will he a long tioked-for day in the history of the Baptist community in Warrington, for it will witness the opening of the extension of Golborne-street Baptist Church. The new facade is certainly one of the finest of its kind in the town and reflects great credit upon the architfct (Mr W H Matley, of MancLester) and the builder (Mr George Wallington). To complete the effect of the improve- ment it only remains for the Town Council to pr,..->ceed with the widening of the street. At the opening service en Thursday (particulars of which are advertised) the preacher will be the Rev William Owen, of Manchester. The Mayor will preside at the evening meeting.

Crosfleld 01,eratic Society. On the invitation of an admirer, the members of th e Crosfield Operatic Society who took part in the recent successful production of "Paul Jones" partook ( f a hot-pot supper at the Patten Arms Hotel on Monday. A com- pany numbering about 40 spent a most agreeable evening. During the evening, Mr W Percy Taylor, the hon. secretai yto the socisty in proposing the •health of the host said the members were greatly encouraged by the kindness which had been extended to them, and it was a pleasure to know that among their supporters they had such a warm and large hearted admirer. The toast was accorded musical honours. Instrumental selections, songs, humorous items and recitations were contributed by Messrs R Ellison, F Sedgley, W Brobbin, H Creamer, J Newns, A Davies, Hughes, G Dean, W Thornton, Jennings, W Lawton, G Harding and Williams.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Who tolled the bell? I," said Cock Robin " I tolled the bell." * * Most bells are tolled, but if they were told all that the Stockton Heath councillors have been told this week, they would crack and blush for very shame. * * * Somewhere or other the proprietor of that popular drama "The Still alarm" is going about sublimely ignorant of the fact that he is missing the chance of a life time. If pro- duced at Stockton Heath the play would just now, draw the whole population of the " heathen" district.

* Our contributor Mr A Mounfield will commence in our next issue a series of three or four articles on "Children's Marriage Games" which we think will prove of decided interest. These evill be followed by articles on other of the traditional games of children. *

Tramway-conductor Horton has r assed through a trying ordeal this week, but his acquittal has restored public confidence in an obliging and exceptionally well-conducted body of public servants. One hesitates to think that there are any men wearing the uniform of public service in Warrington who would sink so low as to pilfer pennies. * "We know now that the traditional 'Lady Bountiful' is only a witch and that her potions and charms, her groceries and tracts may do as much harm as good."—Mr. Walter Milledge at the annual meeting of the Warrington Citizens' Guild of .Help.

* * * People who bewail the "expatriation" of British capital do not realise how much of it is used to develop the resources of our Empire abroad. In 1910 921/2 millions, in 1911 65 millions, and in 1912 721/2 millions were raised by public subscription in this country for the use of our Dominions abroad. Of these sums Canada (for whom, according to Tariff Reformers, we do nothing) has secured the giant's share, her total borrowings from the Mother Country in 1912 amounting to no less than 47 millions. * * * Much of the ill-health among the poorer classes of the community can be traced to the purchase of unsuitable food and the lack of proper cooking. With the object of initiating some practical educational work on the subject, the May or is calling an open conference to be held in the Council Chamber on Thursday afternoon next at 4 o'clock. A special invitation is extended to ladies who are in touch with organizations which could help to stimulate interest in the question of cooking amongst the wage-earners. * *

The commercial and industrial prosperity of the past year is reflected ,in a striking degree, in the experience of one of our most prosperous local undertakings, the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd. Even the coal strike was a blessing in disguise to this firm, for the scarcity of fuel led many people to make use of gas cookers and fires to an unaccustomed extent. Like everyone else, the Richmond company participated in the great boom which succeeded the strike, and, by the consistent adoption of scientific methods in all branches of their business, they have equipped themselves to share to the full in the ever-increasing demand for their class of production. A dividend of 10 per cent. a bonus of 6d. per share, and a reserve fund of £50,000, are outstanding factors in the present exceedingly sound position of the concern. * *

* - The proposition to appoint an official short- hand writer to the Corporation was more favourably received on Tuesday than the adverse vote indicates. A free discussion revealed the admitted fact that even an important minute sometimes gets omitted from the records of committee proceedings under the present system, and anyone familiar with Town Council business knows how frequently there is complete contradic- tion between members as to what actually transpired in committee. There were some extravagant estimates of the cost to the town which might be involved by obtaining a verbatim record of the various meetings. One was as high as £1,500--equal to a rate of 11Ad. in the X--but we should be prepared to substantiate the assertion that the work could be reliably and systematically under- taken for £5OO a year. It would be worth that to the Council individually and collec- tively. We hope to see Councillor Osborne's proposal reconsidered at an early date. It has much to recommend at!

- As a change of representation is strongly desired by many of the residents in Padgate and Fearnhead, Mr. E. England is being nominated for the position of District Coun- cillor and has consented to stand. The office carries with it a seat on the Board of Guardians. The present Councillor is Mr. George Mather, who sprang somewhat into notoriety by claiming to be "boss of the show" at a Board of Guardians' meeting Mr. E. England has had considerable experi- ence in public work. When resident in Stockton Heath he was a prominent member of the Parish Council and Parochial Com- mittee where it was generally acknowledged he rendered excellent service. He led the movement for increased school accommoda- tion which was sorely needed at the time and which ultimately led to the new Council schools being built. He was also Elective Auditor for seven years for the Borough of Warrington, fighting three elections success- fully and being twice returned unopposed. A genuine progressive he is a warm advocate of all improvements which make for the betterment and health of the people and is a strong supporter of that far-reaching measure, the Town Planning Act.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School.

A concert and entertainment were given in the schoolroom on Thursday evening, in aid of the school's contribution to the forthcoming bazaar. Mr Hedley H Taylor presided, and in his opening remarks referred to his long connection with the school. He commended all connected with the Bold-street Sunday school for the ambition they were displaying in con- tributing their share to the forthcoming Circuit Bazaar, which was for the purpose of rais- ing funds for the new chapel in Norris-street. The Artistes who contributed to the evenings enter- tainment were: Miss Emily Taylor, songs; Miss Parkinson, accomp mist ; M!ss Lockerbie, violin solos; Messrs E A Saucers and A Dutton, recitations; and a song by Mr It Ellisoa. Limelight views of some of the beauty spots of England and Wales were also shown by Mr T Prince, and a description of same, illustrating scenes on the Thames from Oxford to London, as vt ell as North Wales, and some of the noted Cathedrals and Castles of England, was given by Mr J C Holland. The singing of the National Anthem, brought a very enjoyable evening to a close, St. Helens Cable and Rubber Co.'s Recreation Club.

The third annual dinner and smoking concert in connection with the above was held at the Royal Oak Hotel, on Ssturday evening last, u hen about 90 members and friends were pres,-nt, with Mr Seymour (works manager) in the chair. Dinner was served in Mr Sangster's usual A 1 manner and was thoroughly appreciated by all present. After the usual toasts the concert was proceeded with, and consisted of glees by the works quartette (Messrs Bull, Richardson, Hayes and Ford) ; French horn solos, Mr W D Bond ; violin solos, Mr L Wood ; concertina selections, Mr Sam Aukland ; and songs, Messrs Watson and Bellfield, the latter being the only artists to receive anything at ttie time of singing to show how much he was appreciated. The humorist was Mr \V Moores, whose characters "Ginger and the " Beauty of the Gliards" vvers heartily encored. Mr W Morris, of Chester, who is an exceptionally clever ventriloquist deserves special mention, for he was undoubtedly the star of the even- ing, keeping the audience, with the aid of his dummy partner in a continuous roar of laughter. The pianist, Mr Bert Smith carried out his arduous duties in a most efficient manner.

Benefit Building Society. A bighty successful year was under review at the 40th annual meeting of the Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society held under the presidency of Mr W -J Shaw, in the Cairo-street schoolroom, on Wednesday evening. The Chairman said the balance sheet was of a character which they had not bad since the society was formed. The society was now in an unique position so far as actual money in hand was concerned. The interests of the shareholders was always looked after in the best possible manner. The directors report stated the year had been a most successful one, and although 'withdrawals through death and other causes had been large, all claims had been promptly paid. It was pleasing to report a marked increase in subscriptions and general business and the directors confidently looked forward to the co-operation of shareholders in introducing new members. The reserve funds of the society now exceeded 1,2.000. The net profit on the year's working amounts to ,C.,710 12s, and the amount brought forward from last rar's account is £54 Os id, making a total profit of :£.705 is id for distribution, out of which the directors prop,sed to pay a dividend of Piper cent (free of income tax', and to carry the balance forward to next year's account. The report and balance sheet were adopted Mr Woodcock remarking that the society as a whole stood for progress. The following are the officials of the society : President, Mr W J Shaw ; directors, Megsrs Thomas Critchlev, S W Dallow, C H Hibbert, Thomas Trice, F A Milling, T Partridge, Richard Shackleton, F Timperley ; treasurer, Mr Aquila Cook ; surveyor, Mr Willism Twiss ; solicitor, Mr A J Willett : auditors, Mr Edwin Bradshaw, F C.A., Mr W H Woodcock, A S.A.A. ; secretary, Mr A H Clive, 43, , Egypt-street, Warrington. A vote of thanks to the Ichait man and officials concluded the meeting.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDING.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDING.
Sinith—Sutton.

A very pretty and interesting wedding took place at St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath, on Thursday March 6th. Mr Alexander Smith of " Clapton " London, was married to Miss Maggie Sutton of " Ivy Dene, ' GrappAnhall-road, Stockton Heath. The cere- mony was performed by the Vicar, Rev J Collins, M.A. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr Walter Sutton. Her dress of ivory silk trimmed with pearls and guiper point lace was much admired, and she carried a large bouquet of white carnations and lilies. Her attendants included one little page, Master Smalley, and three bridesmaids, Misses. McKenzie, cousins of the bride (Southport), Miss Daisy Cathleen Hollows niece of the bride (Manchester.) They carried bouquet of pink carnations. The bride's mother looked charming in saxe blue velvet robe trimmed with sable. The bridegroom was supported by Mr Leonard Sutton as his best man. Mr John Sutton was grooms man. Mr Sbarrocks presided at the organ. A reception was afterwards held at the Wintnarlegh Cafe Sankey-street, Warrington. After receiving the hearty congratulations of their many friends the bride and bridegroom left for Folkestone where they will spend the honeym:on, the bride going away in a dress of pale grey and satin charmeuse with hat plumed with grey and white feathers. The wedding presents were very numerous.

div.head: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
div.p: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.

MILITANCY CONDEMNED BY SUFFRAGISTS The National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies the oldest and biggest organisation for obtaining the Parliamentary Franchise for Women, held its half yearly Council meeting in London last week. Between 700 and SOO delegates, representing 42.000 members were present and the proceedings lasted two days. Mrs Fawcett, who was in the chair, moved a resolu- tion protesting against militant methods, which was passed unanimously, and one of the speakers said that the union regarded these methods with " whole hearted loathing." A reception was given ti the delegates by the London Society at which Mrs Fawcett was presented with a neck ornament composed of rubies, diamonds and emeralds (red white and green being the colours of the Union) in recognition of her 40 years service in the Women's Suffrage cause. Remarkable evidence was given of the growth in popularity of the non-militant suffrage cause by the fact that during the last year members have been joining the union at the rate of 1,000 a month and that the money bandit(' by the 'Treasurer am ,unted to over £43,000.

THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY MARCH 8, 1913.

There is no sign of a THE SLUMP IN recovery from the TARIFF REFORM. slump in Tariff Reform which began with Lord Lansdowne's repudiation—endorsed by Mr Bonar Law—of the Referendum pledge and Was. accentuated by Mr. Bonar Law's Edinburgh announcement that food-taxes Will not be an issue at the next General Election. And the significance of that slump lies more particularly in the fact that it supervened upon a falling market. To the man in the street" the manceuvres of the Tory leaders on this question are susceptible of only one explanation. Lord Lansdowne and Mr. Bonar Law made a bolt in one direction because they were driven by the " whole-hoggers," who Wanted a plain statement before the next General Election. They promptly doubled back when they found that the section of their party which will not have food-taxes, not always so much because they dislike them as because they fear the election- eering handicap, were just as firm and much Inor numerous. Mr Balfour in effect said to the British public: "Don't make food-taxes a test-question at the polls; they will not be I.lllPosed without a Referendum." Mr. Bonar Law says: "Put food-taxes out of your Mind when you go to vote." And there are Tariff Reformers who are quite angry at the suggestion that Mr. Bonar Law has dropped tbod-taxes from the party programme. " We will be no party," the Farmers' Union declares," to any change in our fiscal P°licY which excludes agriculture from its btenefits." In other words, the Farmers' nion takes its stand on the ground—" No 'ood Taxes, then No lariff Reform." Why, the farmers ask themselves, should they ,suPPort a policy which would make all we nuy dearer, and give us no higher prices for What We sell? Oh, but, Mr. Law pleads, the Tory Party will raise the money in some Other way and give the farmers "equivalent _reject e d nenefits." The Farmers' Union sternley the bait of " equivalent benefits." T_hey not know what is meant, and they do not believe that they would get them.
