Guardian" the report shak 'in that "Cambridge after 1-- g off the last (or nearly the last) of ological tests, is now proposing to replace them by military tests of an TOnlParably more disgraceful kind.'' _ ,e esteemed Principal' of Didsbury ,L)oilege, in the course of his article, says : 'I venture to think it is time that right-

thinking people woke up to the importance of rousing public opinion as to this insidious conspiracy of the militarists against our freedom of conscience. It is well that we should recognise that we havelto do with an enemy constitutionally unscrupulous. Com- pulsion, of course, involves even personally honourable men in methods which in any other cause would be reprobated. Under the plausible pretext of defehding our country we are to demoralise our boys by familiarising them with the notion that organised slaughter is a respectable and even glorious object. And if we refuse, the splendid example of our Antipodean colonies will show by what methods we may be coerced. We may be deprived of our degrees,our votes,our liberty; we may bear the title of haters of our country and all the other pretty names that the " maffickers " threw at us a few years ago. We may have to refuse to pay income tax and take whatever consequences may follow. Be it so. The war party must do more than that before we will bow down before the idol they worshipped last autumn in the Free Trade Hall, or admit that a I` great nation' is to be applauded if it goes forth to deluge Europe with blood and tears and ruin, not even on some pretext of intolerable wrong, but simply because the hour has struck' for a cynical and barbarous aggression."

In aid of St Benedict's schools,an illustrated lecture on "The Passion Play at Oberammergau" will be given by the Rev Father C Jackson, 0.8.8. at the Hippodrome on Sunday, March :6th, Musical Society's Concert. Our readers are reminded that the final subscrip- tion concert of the season in connection with the Musical Society will be held at the Parr Hall on Wednesday evening next. The principal work to be Presented is Haydn s " Creation" (parts 1 and 2).

Infirmary Workingmen's Committee. The annual meeting of the Workingmen's Infirmary Committee, will he held at the Town Hall, on Saturday next, at three o'clock in the afternoon. Representa- tives are specially invited to attend. Toe Ilayor (Councillor Dr Joseph) has kindly promised to preside.

The Queen's Nurses. The thirteenth annual conference of Queen's Nurs- ing Superintendents (North of England District) will be held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday next. There will be a reception at 12 o'clock noon. The Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph) will preside, and all sub- scribers and friends and all persons interested in district nursing are invited to be present.
The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Ltd.—Half -Year's Dividend.

The directors of this Company, have declared the usual half-year's dividend at the rate of six per cent. per annum, on both the preference and Second prefer- ence shales, also an interim dividend at the rate of six per cent. per annum on the ordinary shares, all lees tax.

Infirmary and Dispensary. On Monday March 17 at 3 pm. the general annual meeting of the governors of the Infirma-y and Dis- pensary will be held to transact the ordinary business of the annual meeting arid to consider the recommenda- tion by the Board of Management that Dr E J Fox be appointed hon. ophthalmic surgeon of the institution in addition to his position as an hon. surgeon.

Spring Cleaning. Try the Daisy VACULTNI CLEANER price 42/-, 63/-, 84/-.--J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55,Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Choked at a Meal. A labourer named David Savage (49), 54, Old-road, Warrington, died on Thursday evening, from the effects of choking. He was employed by Masan Pearson and Knowles, at Irlam. In the course of a meal he choked, and his wife's efforts to relieve him were unavailing. Dr Ogilvie was sent for and succeeded in dislodging a piece of meat from the man's throat, but death had taken place. Confirmation Service. A confirmation service was held at the Church of the Sacred Heart, Bank Quay, on Sunday, when 134 candidates were presented to Archbishop Whiteside, of Liverpool, for confirmation. The Archbishop preachsd at both the morning and evening services and commended the congregation upon the advance which had been made in all departments of Church work. He was extremely satisfied with the progress which had been made.

Next Week at the Hippodrome The management have been fortunate in securing the great Darracq to head a big bill for next week. Darracq will whiz the wheel in a motor carat a speed of over 80 miles per hour. The act is described as the sensation of sensations. J F Elliston will also present The Meymotts, tsupported by Miss Itoehie Websmith, in a new comedy playlet "In the future" or " What we are coming to." Numerous other capital variety turns will also appear. Picturedrome. The star picture for Monday, Tuesday and Wednes- day is "The Traitor," a splendid story of the time of Napoleon. The management has exclusive rights for this film in Warrington. On Thursday, Friday and Saturday a Vitagraph Drama entitled "'rue Dawning" will be the chief attraction. This fine picture portrays the encouragement of woman's vanity by mankind. The booking plans for "Les Miserables ' are now 'open. VACUUM CLEANERS. Free trial at home. Price 42/- 63/-, 84/.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Army Pensioner's Suicide. James Totrilioson, an army pensioner, living at 16, Gilbert-street, committed suicide yesterday afternoon. His two children on returning from school, could not enter the house as the door was locked. John Harrison, a neighbour, burst open the door and on going upstairs found deceased hanging from his bed- room door by means of his belt which he had attached to a skipping rope. Life was extinct. Deceased was a widower, his wife having met her death, under tragic circumstances, a few years ago.

Liberal Bowling Competition. - There was a large gathering of representatives of the various wards at the Liberal Club, on Wednesday evening to make arrangements for the coming season's competition for the Peter Peac,ck Challenge Cup. The following officers were elected: Chairman, Mr It H Holford ; deputy-chairman, Mr S H Walker; hon treasurer, Mr G T Rushton; assistant hon treasurer, Mr A Hoyle; hon secretary, Mr E A Sanders; assistant hon secretary, Mr vE G Hughes. Great interest was shown in the prospects for the season and over 290 entries were handed in. We are requested to announce that entries close on April 10th. " 13AvAn.o" CARS.—See the 8 h.p. 4 cylinder, two seater model, £l97.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, iridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Male Choral Union. A successful social promoted by the Warrington Male Choral Union was held at the King's Cafe, on Monday evening. There was an attendance of about 90 The first part of the evening was devoted to a whist drive, the prizes being won by the following : Ladies : 1, Miss Crawford ; 2, Mrs Baker ; con- solation, Miss Bell. Gentlemen : 1, Mr G Parr ;2, Mr J Poole ; consolation, Mr C Sinclair. Dancing was afterwards engaged in, Mr E Griffiths dis- charging the duties of M.C. A musical programtn3 was also submitted, including selections by the choir (under the conductorship of Mr F Atkinson), songs by Mrs Hannan, Mr E Walker, and Mr J Gibson, and a pianoforte solo by Mr H J Iddon. Mr 3 Foster acted as accompanist and also played for dancing.

Death of Mr Joseph Eastwood. One who of late years bad been a familiar and respected figure in local Liberal circles—Mr Joseph Eastwood—passed away on Wednesday at the residence of bi 3 son-in-law,Councillor Firth Lindley, 4, Bewsey-road. Mr Eastwood, who was 80 years of age, was a native of Kirkheaton, near Huddersfield. For twenty years he rendered faithful arvice as a police sergeant at Hebden Bridge, Yorkshire, retiring on pension about twenty years ago. He then went to live at Stanley, near Wakefield, until about six years ago when he came to Warrington. He was a convinced and ardent Radical and frequently testified, from his own experience, to the hardships undergone by the workers in the 'hungry forties." He took a great interest in current politics and attended the meeting held in the Parr Hall when Mr Birrell was the chief speaker. The funeral will take place to-day (Saturday at Stanley, near Wakefield. Tradesman at Law. - -

The hearing was resumed at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Stanger, K.C., of the action in which James Atkinson, draper 78, Bridge-street,sued James Parkinson,photographer) who has a atudio over Mr Atkinson's shop,for £lB 10s for trespass; he asked for an injunction perpetually to restrain the defendant from the alleged trespass. Mr A Brown appeared for tbe plaintiff and Mr W B Forshaw for the defendant It was stated that the defendant's show case on the wall of the passage leading to the stairs by which the studio was reached caused an obstruction in the passage by the people it attracted and prevented the plaintiff from using the Wall for the purpose of his business. Both parties contended that they lia4 I received permission from the landlord (Mr H Thornton) to use the wall, but this was denied. On Thursday his Honour visited the premises and, on returning, it was announced that the case was with- drawn on terms„ which were not divulged.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT.
div.p: ROYAL VISIT.
FULL DETAILS OF ARRANGEMENTS. "A SPECIAL PAYOUT-TO WARRINGTON."

The arrangements for the Royal visit to Warrington on Monday, July 7th, are such as will give complete sat,sfaction to the townspeople. His Majesty has generously expressed a desire to honour the town in a special degree, in view of the disappointment experi- enced on the occasion of the visit of the late King Edward VII., and the drive through the streets, the ceremonies at the Town Hall and the inspection of Messrs Crosfields' works have all been so arrangedeas to all ,rd the townspeople every opportunity of seeing their Majesties. It is expected that the function at the Town Hall will last a quarter of an hour and that the visit to Messrs Crosfields' works will occupy three-quarters of an hour. The Mayor has been good enough to furnish us with the following official statement of the arrangements. At the request of Lord Derby, his Worship convened a meeting at the Town Hall on Wednesday morning of representatives from the boroughs and urban districts on the line of route between Warington and Knowsley. Lord Derby attended the meeting at which were present the Mayor, Town Clerk, the Borough Surveyor and Chief Constable of Warringtoh, the Mayor, Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor of Widnes, the Chief Constable of Lancashire, Mr t chofield (Csainty Surveyor), the Chairmen and Surveyors of the Urban Distrtct Councils of Huyton and Prescot, the Surveyor of the Warrington Rural District Council, Major Green (C.O. 8111 and 40th Rea. District), Lieut-Colouel Fairclough, Captain Crosfield and Mr J J Ciosfield.

div.head: ARRIVAL.
div.p: THE ARRIVAL.

Lord Derby explained that the Royal Visit would commence at Warrington, their Majesties leaving London at 11.20 and arriving here at 3 o'ciock. Some little doubt remains as to the station at which the Royal train will draw up, but it is almost certain that Arpley station will be selected as it is considered by the railway officials to be the most convenient, and there is Do doubt that the wide open space in front of the station will give a large concourse of people the opportunity of seeing the Royal Group.

div.head: PROCESSION.
div.p: THE PROCESSION.

In any case the procession will pass Arpley station to Warrington Bridge, and travel up Bridge-street and along Sankey-street to the front of the Town Hall. AT THE TOWN HALL.. On arriving at the Town Hall their Majesties and their suite will alight and ascend the platform which will ba erected in front of the Town Hall. The plat- form will be a high one to enable the people assembled to have a full view of their Majesties and the pro- ceedings, and it will necessarily be a long one in order that their Majesties and those in attendance on them may alight simultaneously and assemble in the positions assigned for the interesting ceremony. At no place visited will their Majesties enter the Town Hall, the ceremonies at each place being in the open. No addresses must be presented, and no bouquets will be accepted. The presentations to their Majesties (in boroughs ' only) mutt not exceed twenty and the list of names will be settled by Lord Derby. His Lordship suggested that in each case the selection should be mace, after the Mayor and Town Clerk,from the Free- men, the ex-Mayors, and the Members of Parliament, and in the case of Warrington, he specially named Sir Gilbert Greenall. 'We are informed that the Mayor has decided also to submit the name of Mr A 11 Crosfield.

div.head: VISIT UNOFFICIAL.
div.p: THE VISIT UNOFFICIAL.

His Lordship stated that the visit of his Majesty was purely unofficial, and that he would not appear in uniform. After the presentations the Queen will again enter the carriage and his Majesty will inspect the Guard of Honour which will be drawn up in front of the Tr,wn Hall, and be formed by the local Territorials. The Royal procession will proceed at a slow trot through the towns ; but in passing from town to town the speed will be accelerated, and his Lordshiptsaid that the people should be warned that if they witlhed to see their Majesties they must be in the towns. THE DECORATIONS.

Lord Derby stated that it was his Majesty's desire that money should not be spent in expensive decora- tions, and that he should preter to rely upon individual displays. . ESCORT AND LINING OF STREETS.

His Lordship also expressed the wish that the Boy Scouts and the Church Lads' Brigade should be invited to take part in lining the streets or in any other way on the day of the visit, and he said that he felt sure that it would be gratifying to his Majesty if the Territorials turned out in good numbers. The arrangements for the escort, the lining of the streets, and maintaining order will be left in the hands of Major Green, Lieut.-Col. Fairclough and the Chief Constable.

div.head: "SPECIAL FAVOUR TO WARRINGTON."
div.p: "SPECIAL FAVOUR TO WARRINGTON."

Subsequently Lord Derby asked the Mayor to state to the people of Warrington that he WAS personally mindful of the great disappointment suffered on the laF4 Royal Visit when their Majesties, the late King Edward and Queen Alexandra, were compelled to travel through the town in closed carriages and unable to alight at the Town Hall in consequence of the serious and regrettable indisposition of Her Majesty on that occasion, and that he had personally explained the circumstances to His Majesty who had been graciously pleased to honour Warrington by travel- bug through the streets with Her Majesty in an open carriage. His Lordship added that it must be con- sidered as a " special favour Warrington." His Lordship is himself providing the carriages for their Majesties' use. AT MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S WORKS.

After the ceremony at the Town Hall, their Majesties will drive thrcugh the West gate to Messrs Crobfield's works. where the carriages will be dismissed, and after an inspection of the works, the Royal party will leave in motor cars en route for Widnes.

div.head: LORD WINNIARLEIGH. PORTRAIT TO-I3E-HUNG IN THE
div.p: LORD WINNIARLEIGH. PORTRAIT TO-I3E-HUNG IN THE
TOWN HALL.

A pleasing announcement was made by the Afayor at the opening of the Town Council meeting on Tuesday evening when he read a letter from Messrs H B White and Sons, solicitors, stating that they were instructed by the trustees of the will of the late Lord Winmarleigh and by the Hon. Mrs Lumley to inquire whether the Corporation would allow a life-size paint- ing of the late Lord Winmarleigh, in the uniform of colonel of Militia (presented to him in 857 by the inhabitants of Warrington, as the result of a resolu- tion passed at a public meeting) to hang in the Town Hall. By the terms of the late Lord Winmarleigh's will the portrait was considered to be an heirloom. The MLYOR, in moving that the offer be accepted, said it was most appropriate that the portrait should be deposited in that building, if only as a loan. ft was probable that during Lird Winmarleigh's resi- dence there, the portrait was hung in the room now used as the Council Chamber.

Alderman BENNETT seconded. He said Lord Wintnarleigh was an ideal English gentleman, and his close association with the town made it peculiarly appropriate that the painting should hang in the hall where he lived for many years. Councillor BIIZTLES supported and referred to the late Lord VVinmarleigh's great interest in the School of Art in the days when he (Councillor Birtles) was a student.
The Proposition was unanimously agreed to.

Domestic Tact.—An amusing feature of this year's Simple Life Exhibition, which is to be held at Caxton Hall in London, next month, will be the competition for the Domestic Tact Championship. It is intended as a lesson how to avoid irritability and bad temper in the home. A lady will occupy the stage representing "a wife" wbo has been expecting her husband home for an hour or more. The dinner spoiled and the evening upset, there is cause for trouble and it is for "the husband" to show how best to get over it. " Husbands " will be forthcoming from the audience, and each one will be judged by those present, and awarded marks according to how he more or less successfully or unsuccessfully "faces the music." As it is probable that some of the ladies to appear on the stage will be popular actresses, well accustomed to play the part of the outraged wife, it will want some courage as well as tact on the part of 'the husband " to tackle the problem. The reversed situation, when it, is" the husband " who has been waiting, and " the wife" making calls or shopping, is an bour or so late, ivnagte a entertainment sense of and humour may aanydpo a possibly is also to be represented. Whether these " lessons " will be of any practical use is doubtful. They will at ahneyipr othersat e afford t o ot. amusing and take disposition—always two saving qualities in the quest of domestic peace and happiness.

Inquiries must be short, concise, and plainly written, and the name and address of the writer given to show that the inquiry is genuine. The replies are by a member of the profession, and every effort is made to secure accuracy, hut we cannot assume any responsibility for the opinion or advice given. Mark all envelopes containing queries Legal," and address them to the EDITOR," EXAMINER,' . . . . .

WARRINGTON. If you do not wish initials to he used in the reply please suggest a nont-de-pluine. WILL.—A legacy can be given to an Executor with this proviso that such gift may be construed as annexed to the office but the presumption may be
rebutted. D.B.—Yas. No action can be brought after 6 years of the cause of action accruing unless there has . .

been payment on account, or an acknowledgment' and promise to pay iu writing given within that period. DOGGY. No. Proof must be given that the owner knew of the mischievous propensities of the dog. Proof need not he given if the dog has injured cattle (including horses, mules, asses, sheep, goats

and swine). - DESERTED. You can certainly proceed to obtain a verdict for damages for breach of promise of marriage against a man who has left the country, provided the coutzact was made in this country. The trouble, however, is in getting the damages paid. The procedure in such cases is very expensive. J.l.—You can prevent a neighbour from building on his land so as to spoil your view and interfere with your light if your neighbour i 4 under covenant by deed not to do those things. or if you have acquired the right to free access of light and air by long enjoyment—that is for 20 years. F.W.—lf the casual worker is not otherwise in your employ (i.e., a workman sent from your works to clean your windows on an odd occasion) you are not responsible. This being so, no answer to your

second question is necessary. OLD AGE PENSIONS.—We are much obliw.d to the Town Clerk for calling our attention to the proYiEions of the Old Age Pensions Act of 1011, by which the period of disqualification of persons sent to prison without the option of a fine for a period not exceeding six[ weeks has been reduced from ten to two years, and we wish to correct our answer to " Pension " in last week's issue ticcordingly.

div.head: TRAINING COLLEGE CONCERT, A PLEA FOR ENGLISH MUSIC.
div.p: TRAINING COLLEGE CONCERT, A PLEA FOR ENGLISH MUSIC.

It cannct be said of many examinations that they have a pleasurable side, but that advantage can be claimed for a portion, at any rate, of the examination in music at the Warrington Training College. For the choral test of the second year students some classical or standard woik is always selected and its performance is made the occAsion of the annual con- cert which at the invitation of the principal (Rev Canon Morley Stevenson), is attended by many of the townspeople who interest themselves in the College. Owing to the unusually early date, the gathering at the concert on Wednesday evening was not as large as usual, but those who did attend were privileged to hear a most interesting and enjoyable programme. The chorus was nicely balanced, the male voices being provided chiefly from the Parish Church choir. The principal w.rki was Elgar's "Banner of St George," and, not- withstanding the strenuous demands which it makes, an impressive rendering of this vivid and stirring setting of Shapcott Wensley's fine poem, was submitted. Under the guidance of Mr W S Woods,who conducted, the students had evidently made a painstaking study of the intricacies of the composition and their singing was marked by due expression as well as freshness and enthusiasm. Particularly effective was that portion of the broad, majestic epilogue in which the voices are practically unaccompanied. The soprano solos were well taken by Miss Jessie Stubbs. The orchestra which, considering its numerical limitations, did very efficient work, consisted of the following : Ist violin, Mr R H Pearson ; 2nd violin, Mr A Knowles ; viola, Mr J Burrows; violoncello, Mr J Jackson ; double bass, Mr J Stud worth; pianoforte, Miss Hackett; harnaonium, Mr W 11 Payton, Mus. Bac. The senior students also gave a delightful rendering of the part song "The Corall'd Caves of Ocean " (Smart), while the chorus again acquitted itself admirably in the anthem "By Babylon's Wave" (Gounod.) Miss Mabel Pratt, who possesses a mezzo-soprana voice of very pleasing quality, sang "The Ring" and "Green Hat " (Schumann) with tender feeling and dainti- ness. An instrumental trio "Andantino " from " Rosamund " (Schumann) was neatly played by -.lk.ir R. H Pearson, Mr J Jackson and Miss Hackett, and the pianoforte duet " Allegro " from the " Fifth Symphony" (Beethoven) was creditably given by Miss Hackett and Miss Mary Grime. At the close of the concert Mr Geoffry T Shaw, His Majesty's Inspector, gave a short but very interesting address in which he said that in going up and down the country one was immensely struck by the tremendous improvement which had taken place in the choice of music and in the way in which it was sung. Dealing with what he considered the most important element in the teaching of music in schools, Mr Shaw said some people laid great stress on voice production, others on singing at sicht and others on the children being mada in the words of a festival syllabus equally conversant with both notations. AU those things had their definite value, hut it was as well to remember that they were merely a means to an end and that possibly we had for some time been thinking of those means rather than of the end. Touching upon the great influence of music, the speaker said it afforded one of the very !fpw chances that children had for self- expression and engendered a spirit of esprit tic corps among tbem. What were eAucationists going to do for the art of music ? Their aim should be, not merely to make the children proficient in the points he had mentioned, but to give them a genuine and discriminat- ing taste and on appreciation for the best music. How were they to achieve that? Simply and solely by being careful in their choice of music. They might make all the children in England play the piano, or violip, sing or blow some instrument until they were blue in the face, but that did not necessarily mean that they made them musical. There was only one thing that really made a musical man, and that was his taste. First and foremost in their choice of music for use in the schools, they should place the songs of our own country—that splendid heritage left us by our forefathers, and in that respect he thought no nation had quite such a splendid heritage as Great Britain. All the musical education of children should be based on national and folk songs. When we had got really saturated with our own music, then was the time to telt^ to the more artistic forms. Then we might give the children the works of great masters—and every great master had written something suitable for children ; it was a mistake to supsose that their work' was necessarily above a child's head. The keynote of the works of the great masters was simplicity and they., had a very direct appeal. When we accepted the axiom that the very best was just about good enough for the child, we would achieve what we wanted. ii

div.head: COUNCILLOR GOUG
div.p: COUNCILLOR GOUG

The Warrington Town Council has of late become unpleasantly notorious for the uproarious scenes which now invariably mark the transaction of the business of its monthly meetings. The meeting on Tuesday evening, while not quite so disorderly as that of a month ago, was again characterised by some very heated incidents, personalities being freely exchanged. The display of feeling reached boiling point when a majority of the Council united in shouting down Councillor Gough, Nvho had declined to resume his seat when requested to do so by the Mayor. The chief bone of contention on this occasion was a proposition by Councillor Lashford in favour of an altera- tion of the method .of tendering for Corpoiaticn contracts. His resolution evoked strenuous opposi- tion from many members on the ground that it cast a reflection on the honour of the Council, while Coun- cillor Pemberton added fuel to the flames by declaring that " some of the rottenest things ever perpetrated in public work had been done on that Council.' There was another decidedly breezy debate on Councillor Osborne's motion to appoint an official shorthand writer,Alderman Tinnion prutesting sgainst what he stigmatised as " deliberate lies and mis- statements." So protracted were the discussions on these two topics that the Mayor's proposal that a new organ be installed in the Parr Hall was adjourned for a month. A resolution by Councillor Pemberton, pronosing to provide slipper baths for workingmen, shared a similar fate.

div.head: CORPORATION CONTRACTS. ALLEGATIONS OF FAVOURITISII.
div.p: CORPORATION CONTRACTS. ALLEGATIONS OF FAVOURITISII.

Councillor LAsHroan moved: "That any pers-,n or persons tendering to the Corporation shall not put his name on such tender, but shall enclose his Dame and address in a separate envelope, sealed, and place the same with his ter.der in another sealed envelope. The envelope containing the name of the tenderer shall not be opened until the contract is decided." The object of the motion said Councillor Lashford, was to secure to everybody a fair share of competition, so that everyone who tendered would have every con- sideration. More local firms and ratepayers would willingly compete if the system of tendering was carried on in a m.,re business-like manner. All up-to- date public bodies with honourable intentions had adoped such a method of dealing with tenders and the carrying of the motion would save all the bicker - ings and unpleasantness which occurred at the meetings. Further, the adoption of that system would obviate the necessity of going round to ask people to tender. Some years ago, when he was on the Museum Committee, tenders were invited for painting, and the late Borourzh Surveyor went round asking certain people to tender. On that occasion a certain individual was given the work through favouritism, and other tenderers bad practically DO chance. On those grounds he thought it only right and just to bring the motion forward Councillor Gocroli seconded tbe motion, which, he thought, would put an end in some measure to favouritism, and the public would have a chance of doing some business with the Corporation. Alderman FORSHAW asked the Town Clerk if an unsigned tender would be a binding contract? The TOWN CLERK : It would be signed. I think it would be. Councillor BROADHURST was rather surprised to hear that Councillor Lasbford was of the opinion that the general public bad not had fair play in the competi- tions. Since he had been on the Council he bad never seen unfair competition. He was opposed to the resolution, for the reason that all things being equal— price, quality, and reliability—they were under a moral obligation to give the preference to a Warrington firm. Under the system advocated by Councillor Lashford, however, of selecting the lowest tender, irrespective of other considerations, they might be bound to give the work to a man in the South of England, a man who paid not a single farthing to the ratee. Mr Lashford tiad been under the impression ever since a certain Toter in St. John's Ward failed to get a tender for bags that the competition was not fair, but he assured the councillor that the man did get absolute fair play. Ho challenged Councillor Lashford to point to any instance where there had been unfair competition in the business of the Sanitary Works or Health Committee. The motion was practically a vote of censure and an expression of a vant of confidence in every member of the Council. Moreover it would, in some cases, have the effect of depriving Warrington workmen of 'employ meat. "UNCALLED-FOR AND UNTRUTHFUL."

Councillor CRAIK protested against the resolution, which implied an untruth. If the members of the Council were not to be trusted to go through the tenders and do what was right, they should be turned He had been on the Council for some yeeirs, and had yet to learn that favouritism was shown in the selection of tenders by committees on which he sat— and he was a member of seven. The Council ought to reject the motion,which was uncalled-foi and untruthful. Councillor BIRTLES asked what would happen if the tender of a man or straw was decided upon? Would he have the contract? Then very often people tendering made mistakes, and it would be unfair to take advantage of those errors. During his experience he had never known an instance of unfair ,dealing with tenders. The motion was a klander on the men composing the com- mittees. He did not think Mr Lashford had had much experience of tendering in private life. He doubted wriether he had brought forward the motion on his own account, and rather thought somebody was behind him. Independeut of that, the resolution was a step in the wrong direction. Councillor PEACOCK said if the resolution was as simple as it looked on paper he might feel inclined to support it. Already the selection of tenders for the Paving and Sewerage Committee occupied two hours and he doubted whether it would he possible to trans- act the business at all with Councillor Lashford's system in operation. It was not always policy to accept the lowest tender. Alderman SMETHURST declared that during his twenty-one years' experience he had never seen any. undernand work in connection with the tendering, and he defied Councillor Lashford or anyone else to point to an instance. The resolution was an insult to the C ,uncll. It would be an utter impossibility to carry out the work of the Electricity Committee by such a method. He hoped the members would reject a resolution which implied distrust of Councillors who had faithfully served the ratepayers for a large number of years. They could not place their lingers on a single wrongful act by a member. "NOTORIOUS FOR CROOKED WORK."

Councillor PENIBERTON thought a lot of" this talk" was quite uncalled for. It was wonderful what short memories some members bad. One was astounded to hear Alderman Smethurst make the assertions he had done. The amount of crooked work which had teea done on the Council within the Alderman's experience was notorious. It was a farce to represent otherwise to the public,for thousands of Warrington people knew that some of the rottenest things ever perpetrated in public work bad been done on that Council. The MAYOR: I think such assertions as those should not be made without proper proof, Councillor Pemberton. Councillor PEMBERTON : I will give you the proof if you want it, but I don't want to go into personalities. If you ask me, I will give it very quickly. I cannot sit here and allow that sort of assertion to go forward. Councillor GOUGH here ventured an interruption, but what he said was not audible to the Council. The MAYOR (sternly) : Councillor Gough, I must ask you not to interrupt. Councillor Pemberton has got the floor and yrou must kindly keep quiet. Councillor PEMBERTON, resuming his speech, said that a great many tradesmen, feeling that they had not a fair chance, absolutely declined to tender for Council work. He failed to realise how some people bad the cheek to talk in the way they had done. No charges were made when the motion was submitted. He care- fully listened to Councillor Lashford's remarks, and he made no allegations against anybody. The system which was proposed had been adopted in other towns and if everything was straightforward and honest why

div.head: H SHOUTED DOWN.
div.p: H SHOUTED DOWN.

did anybody object to the proposal? He did not resent it nor did he feel insulted. He did not wish to secure any contracts for himself or any of his friends. Every possible precaution could be taken as far as he was concerned. Why could anybody object to proper safeguards ? Every prudent busiuess man, if he saw any way of strengthening and improving his system adopted that method, making sure that there could be no possi- bility of wrong doing ; he did not wait until the wrong was done. Not likely ! He preferred the finest and most perfect system which could be devised. Councillor Broadhurst knew absolutely nothing- Councillor BROADHURST : I know as much as you, and probab'y more. The NI ANOR : Now, Councillor Broadhurst- Councillor PEMBERTON : His experience is absolutely nil. He has only been in business for a few years on his own acconnt. _ _

Councillor BROADHURST : I know toil much for you. The MAYOR: Councillor Broadhurst,l must call you to order. Don't interrupt. Councillor PEMBERTON : To hear a man get up and talk like he does is ridiculous. He talks absolute rot. It makes one wonder whether we are here to do busi- ness or not. The business is too large for Councillor Broadhurst to grasp it. He talks about giving Warring- ton firms a share of the work. Aly experience of the Council has been that wo have always given the Warrington people a chance. Councillor GOUGH : And always will. Councillor PEMBERTON said that in the event of the tender of a man of straw being first recommended, the point was very simple ; don't accept it, but proceed to consider the next. That was the fairest possible way to proceed. It should not be forgotten that each of those present knew something of the particular trade in which he was engaged and of the dodges which could ba employed. He was not going to make specific charges, but the people outside were not the brainless , fools some sup Eel them to be. Because they were ' Councillors, some Of those present thought any assertions they chose to make would he swallowed by the public, whereas they were simply laughed at by pemple of experience. He would vote for the motion because it would secure fair competition and create confidence in the people. They were not obtaining tenders from people in the town, because those people considered that they did not receive the proper sort of treatment. Only a short time ago a contract was let in the town and it was not the lowest. The people in the trade concerned knew the true facts better than the Council, because they were experts, and no amount of subterfuge or equivocation would drive out of their minds what they knew to be right. When inquiries were made, the material was supposed to have been tested. The tenders were opened, the names divulged and the prices scheduled, and then the officials were asked to make a test of the material. If the official had not known the names that would have been a fair test, but when inquiries CAllle to be made it was found that the material for the lowest tender was tested eight weeks before the tender was sent in, and some of it was tested six months before the tender was received. Was that carrying out the resolution of the committee that the stuff should be tested after the tenders had been opened ? Everything in public life onght to be done as fairly as possible. It was most unfair, when anybody introduced motions, to attempt to cast slurs upon them and to impute improper motives, and it was wrong to try to construe remarks into indirect charges against individval members of the Council.

COUNCILLOR ROBERTS'S VIGOROUS REPLY. Councillor ROWIRTS said the proposer of the motion most emphatically gave as the only reason why he thought it necessary to carry his proposal, that, in his opinion, at any rate, there had been very dishonourable conduct on the part of certain committees, which had operated unfairly to lira a tendering for work or the supply of mat-rials. If that was not his whole case, what was ? He did not adduce one single argument or even a thread of a piece of argument in support of the motion other than thmt. " You have been guilty of misconduct, and the public need protection against you," was the charge Councillor hasliford made against the Corporation. He sincerely hoped, with Alderman Smethurst and Councillor Broadhurst, that the Council would act as it ought to act in defence of its honour, and if the resolution could not be supported on better grounds, kick it out with the ignominy it deserved. Councillor Pemberton made a worse suggestion than the other. The suggestion underlying his remarks about the test of certain materials was that not only the members, but the officials also, were corrupt. The members of the Cor- poration had done their drity honestly and fairly. No iustance which justified the suggestions had been quoted, and suggestions were infinitely worse than direct cargee. Suggestions were only msde when direct coarges could not be made, and in default of ability to produce direct evidence in support of allega- tions, compelling resort to filthy insinuations from time to time. What was the meaning of the second part of the mc tion ? What was the good of opening tne envelope when the contract was decided,if they were to decide first and then probably to upset their decision ? They might as well stick to what they were doing, knowing all the circumstances to begin with, and deciding a contract on its merits. It was too late in this 20th century, in view of the publicity which obtained in regard to public work, and in view of the safeguards which the members themselves had imposed,to try to suggest that a Corporation of that magnitude, containing as it did honourable men—in the large majority at any rate— could be possibly guilty of the aoominable and filthy things suggested bv insinuation. Councillor WILKINSON : How much longer is a member of this Council going to be allowed to make suggestions %ithout you, Mr Mayor, demanding from that councillor a concrete case that we can go on ? The MAYOR : That is what I suggested when Councillor Pemberton spoke...

• Councillor WILKINSON said the sooner Councillor Pemberton was pinned down in his rambling statements the better it would be. There was no doubt his sugges- tions would be sucked in by certain filthy-minded people and swallowed as gospel. Until such times as he la's& a direct charge which could he dealt with, the Council ought to put its foot down and stop him. (A voice : "We cannot). It was not to Councillor Peroberton's credit that he should be continually making suggestions that there were dishonourable men in the Council. He had hen in the Council many years, and had yet to find an instance where anything dishonour- able or approaching a shadow of dishonour had been done in contract work. It was not always wise to s,lect the lowest tender. " With reference to the motion "concluded Councillor Wilkinscn "I am so indignant that I will say nothing about it." Alderman TINNION said that, as far as he was con- cerned, he did not care what restrictions were placed upon him. He trusted his character was sufficiently well known and satisfactorily understood in Warring- ton. At the same time, if it were absolutely necessary that the Council should have a new system to enable them to be straightforward, their place was outside. (Hear, hear.) He should like Councillor [Ashford to accuse any individuals or any committee and to prove that it was necessary to have such safeguards to keep them straight. If it was necessary to tackle She ques- tion a committee should be appointed to inquire into the conduct of certain members, and if guilty they should be put outside. He unhesitatingly said, how- ever, that, as far as his c.xperience went, the proposal was absolutely unnecessary and an insult to the Cauncil.

Another interjection by Councillor GOtiGli drew from the MAYOR the remark: I think, Councillor Gough, I have spoken to you before. Alderman TINSION (to Councillor Gough) : I really can't hear what you are chunnering about. If you have anything to say, do tribe your hand away from your mouth and speak up in a manly way. The MAYOR: He has no right to speak at present. Alderman TINNION : If he does be ought to give me the advantage of knowirg what he is saying instead of mumbling through his fingers. _ _
The MAYOR: I Will remonstrate with him.

Alderman TINNION said that self respect and the fear of being found out, apart from the higher aspects which ordinarily kept a man honest, were sufficient guarantee that they could be trusted to deal with the business without binding them down. By passing the motion they would be admitting that they bad been guilty of something which was so shameful and dis- graceful that their proper place ought to be in the building near Bank Quay Station. (Councillor PEMBERTON :—(hear, hear)—and probably—hut he would not say it because one could not be hurt for thinking, and he was "having a very happy think " about some people. Councillor HAwnionN said that Councillor Pember- ton insinuated that certain people would not tender because they thought they had been unfairly treated. After six years experience, he (the speaker) could only say that competition for Corporation tenders was keener than for any other work he could speak of. To-say that people would not tender was absurd.

div.head: MORE RECRIMINATIONS.
div.p: MORE RECRIMINATIONS.
Councillor LASHFORD rose to reply. He said he was sorry the motion had seemed to touch so many members.

Councillor WILKINSoN (warmly) : Drop that. Councillor LASHFORD : Well, it has done. Tha MAYOR: Councillor Wilkinson, no interruptions. Coungillor LAsHFORD : There is no doubt it does not suit a good many of them. With reference to Councillor Broadhust, I could open his eyes. Councillor BROADHURST (sarcastically) : They are closed now, aren't they? Councillor LASHFoRD said he could refer to certain matters at the Health Committee which would open Councillor Broadhurat's eyes. He had a bad memory; be forgot things. Councillor BROADHURST : No, I don't.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 8. 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 8. 1913.

Councillor LASHFORD: There is this about Councillor Broadhurst. He has got into that ring or clique and he cannot possibly get out of it. He must be with them. The MAYOR : I must ask you to avoid personalities I shall call you to order. Councillor LASHFORD : It is not ti personality. The MAYOR : It is a personal matter. It is an insinuation not only against Councillor Broadhurst but against members of the clique, as you call them, whoever. they may be. .
Councillor- LASHFORD : Any man can read between the lines or see a bole through a ladder. The MAYOR : We don't want you to read between the lines, but to speak to the motion before ug.

Councillor LASHFORD : lam not going to satisfy Councillor Broadhurst, at any rate not here to-night. Mr Smethurst said it was a friend of mine who we s tendering for bags to the Sanitary Works Committee. Simply, because an individual in St. John's Ward tenders, it is no interest of mine. His was simply the lowest tender, and I was told by the Superintendent it wss the best bag.

AldermaD JOHN -EVANS : Oh ! Councillor LASHFORD : That is what Alderman John Evans says. Alderman John Evans has alssays stuck up for a certain individual in this town. For nine years in succession he has got the contract, and his was not the lowest tender.
Alderman JOIIN EVANS (wsrmly) : I must object to insinuations of this bort. I think my character is good enough to refute this, but I must ask for your protec- tion.
The MAYOR (to Councillor Lashford) : Did you say that Alderman John Evans had voted for nine years in favour of a certain individual ?
Councillor LASH FORD : I said that Alderman John Evans supported a certain individual in this town who tendered.
The MAYOR : And what is there wrong about that ? Councillor PEMBERTON : It is only a statement of fact.
Councillor LASHFORD : lam speaking about what Alderman Smethurst refers to when he Bays s friend of mine tendered.
Councillor PEMBERTON : Surely on a point of order-

The MAYOR; Let me settle one point of order, first, please. I cannot hear four speeches at once. (To Coun- cillor Lashford ) : I must ask you to avoid all insinua- tions or personalities or otherwise you must resume your seat, and I ask for the support of the Council in enforcing that, so there's an end of it. COUNCILLOR GOUGH IN THE WARS. Councillor GoUGH : But, Mr Mayor. (Cries of " Order" and "chair.") The MAYOR (sharply) : You sit down. Councillor GOUGH : It is a matter of fair play. A scene which the Mayor afterwards termed " indescribable " ensued, members vieing with each other in shouting" Sit down! " and' Chair! " while Councillor Gough endeavoured to address the Council. Eventually Councillor GOUGH was heard to ejaculate: Never mind about chair ! Councillor BROADHURST : Get down! Get down! If you make your voice heard someone else will. I will support the Mayor and shout you down any time. The MAYOR: Disgraceful. Councillor BROADHURST, to Councillor Gough: will fight you with your own weapons. Councillor LASHFORD (continuing his speech) : I don't wish to go into details with regard to friendships. If it had not been for Alderman Smethurst. I should never have mentioned it, but I think I ought to give Alderman Smethurst back what be gave me. The MAYOR : You are not going to give any insinu- ations back. I shall ask you to sit down if you are going to do that. Councillor LASH FORD : I am saying what is abso- lutely true, and what has taken place I can prove. Councillor PEMBERTON : You cannot get away from facts.
COUOCMOr LASTIFORD : Councillor Birtles said a certain individual ruight lose, say £9 on a tender. Tbat is his own look-out. He is a fool if he does-

The MAYOR: Fool is not a parliamentary word here —or not a polite word—and so you must withdraw that word and use some other. Councillor LASIIFORD : If a man tenders he must know what he is tendering for. lam surprised at Councillor Roberts. Fancy a man of his ability—so smart, so very smirt in the Town Council—unable to understand the latter part of the motion. lam not as smart as Councillor Roberts and I can understand it. Councillor ROBERTS : It is a case of these things being hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to babes. (Laughter),
The MAYOR: This is an interruption you know, Councillor Roberts. Councillor LASIIFORD : He is always allowed to interrupt. There% is no doubt that the motion does not suit Councillor Roberts.

Counciliur Ronvers : Oh, yes, it dnes. Councillor LASHFORD: I Eay it does not. He spoke tremendously against it. I know he does not like it. Councillor GOUGH : Not likely he will. Answering the remarks of Alderman Tinnion, Conn- LASIIFORD said that no-one suggested that everything was not straightforward on his committee. The pro- posal was one of the most straightforward which had ever been submitted. The system he advocated worked splendidly in Manchester and there was not a bigger business undertaking than that muni- cipality. He could mention one or two bt.siness rurn in the town—one in ankey-street and one in Bridge- street—who would not tender to a certain committee because they know they had no chance. Alderman TINNION : Which committee?
during the other fortnight. If it could be arranged for the various committee not to clash, it would be a great advantage to the town. ... _

Councillor ROBERTS, while sympathizing with the objects of the proposn and seeonder, said he did not think the. matter had b-3en sufficiently considered to justify the Council in passing it. The overlapping of committees would make it extremely difficult for a proper and full record of the proceedings of the com- mittees to be taken. Then the question arose : Were the verbatim reports to be published, and for whose benefit? Was it intended to take reports of the ccm- mittens only, or of the Council meetings as well? He ventured to suggest that the best thing that could happen, in the iaterests of this Council,and with a view to putting a stop to the somewhat unpleasant scenes, would be the publication occasionally of a literal and verbatim report of everything that transpired. 'lf the people of Warrington could once read a a teally true and complete account of the kind of things that (nu go on at the Council meetings occasionally, he thought the pressure of public opinion would be sufficient to prevent frequent repetition of such incidents. Having pointea out that the re-organization of committees was not included in the resolution, Councillor Roberts said he thought that when the Town Clerk's staff w s complete, attention to thl work of the committees might be divided among the prin- cipal clerks, nearly all of whom were competent short- hand writers and typists. Why should not one of the assistants be attached to a certain number of com- mittees as minute clerk and the work divided in that way? (Hear, hear.) One official shorthand writer could not possibly do all the work of the Council and of the committees.

div.head: Councillor LASH FORD_ : The Health Committee.
div.p: Councillor LASH FORD_ : The Health Committee.

The Mayor : I certainly think these matters ought to be brought before the committees first and not before the Council in the first instance. Councillor LASHFORD : Councillor Broadhurst has challenged me, but I never intended mentioning any- body's name. Councillor BROADHURST : Councillor Lashford has not mentioned the matter I challenged him upon now. We don't know who the tradesman was or what he was tendering for. I chsllenge him again to bring the matter forward, and it will get the greatest investiga- tion. That is a fair challenge. Councillor LASHFORD said he could give the individual names, if desired. He did not suppose the motion would he carried, but there was nothing more straightforward. The vote was then taken and the motion was defeated by 16 votes to thrse. Only Councillors Lashford,Gough and Pemberton voted for tue motion.

div.head: PROPOSED OFFICIAL SHORTHAND WRITER. To Check Irrelevant Speech. ANOTHER LIVELY DEBATE,
div.p: PROPOSED OFFICIAL SHORT- HAND WRITER. To Check Irrelevant Speech. ANOTHER LIVELY DEBATE,

There was another spirited debate on Councillor Osborne's proposal : " That the Town Clerk be instructed to engage a permanent official shorthand writer to take a verbatim report of the proceedings of all committee and other meeting, and that he be authorized to provide such further assistance as may be considered necessary. " Councillor OsnonNE contended that this was a matter of considerable importance. The Chairman of the Finance Committee, at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee—he did not say with malice aforethought—sail the resolu- tion would interfere with the freedom of speech. He (Councillor Osborne) was sure it would not do so ; what it might do, and what he hoped it would do, would be to interfere with irrelevant speech, and in that respect would do the Council con siderable service. It would also enable members to see what their speeches looked like in cold type, and that would he very beneficial. (Laughter.) A great deal was said, both at Council meetings and in com- mittee, which might easily be left unsaid, and the respectability of the Council would be considerably enhanced thereby. If, as one worthy Alderman said, the conduct of the Council was the topic on every tram- car, they ought to do something to make the Council a body to which the electors could look with a certain amount of respect. It was often stated that the most important work was done in committee, and there was, therefore, all the more reason why a verbatim repsrt should be taken. They had it on the authority of the Town Clerk that the minute book was not a complete record of the proceedings of each committee. That, to his mind, was irregular and ought to be remedied. He Lad been reminded that two or three com- mittees sat at the same time, and that, there- fore, it would be impossible for an official reporter to attend them, but it was not impos sible for members of the Council to be appointed on committees which met at the same day, and at the same hour, although the members sat in different rooms. (Laughter.) That was an anomaly that ought to be corrected at once. It was little short of a farce to see a respectable gentleman rushing from one committee room to another, simply popping his head into the room in order that his attendance might be recorded and then going through a similar procedure at another committee meeting. Summarising the advantages of his proposal, Councillor Osborne said it would expedite business, give the mem- bers an opportunity of ascertaining information con- cerning the work of every committee, provide for a complete record of the proceedings for future reference and prevent misunderstanding as to facts. He con- tended that it was a purely business proposition. There was no personality about it. It was quite legitimate and he hoped it would be considered thoroughly and meet with the approval of the Council. (Hear, hear). Councillor PEACOCK seconded. He said that since it had been his privilege to enter the Council for a third time, they had had nothing but uproarious meetings, and if anything would stop the disgraceful scenes which some men were prepared to inflict on the town the motion would. The Councillor alluded to the accidental omission of certain minutes in the rerord of the proceedings of the Street Improvement and Paving and Sewerage Committees as proof of the need for suet' a resolution as that submitted by Councillor Osborne. In the case of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Com- mittee, a contract was actually let against the 'wishes of the committee, but the chairman got out of the difficulty by saying he had misunderstood their decision. If a verbatim record had been taken, there would have been no risk of misunderstanding. The whole of the business of the committees was done in about a fortnight, and the Dotes could be transcribed

div.head: MAYOR AND UPROARIOUS MEETINGS.
div.p: THE MAYOR AND UPROARIOUS MEETINGS.

The MAYOR, after expressing agreement with the greater part of Councillor Roberts's speech, took exception to the reference to uproarions meetings, Elys if they had long been of regular occurrence. There had been a beg interregnum of quiet until the last meeting, and nothing very remarkable bad happened. So much stress should not be laid on uproarious meet- ings having lasted for a long time, as it gave a wrong impression. C )uncillor PEACOCK : I said since I have been here. Alderman TIN.N.toN : A remarkable coincidence. (Laughter). The MAYOR : One swallow does not make a summer. It has been suggested that a verbatim report of the proceedings might lead to better order. I think there is something more than verbatim report required to do that. (Hear, hear and laughter). Alderman TINNION : I would suggest a shot-gun. (Laughter). The MAYOR : I would suggest that some members —I won't be personal—should make good resolutions of internal reform. It would tax the most talented reporter, or even a bevy of reporters to give a frill account of the scene we had at the last Council meeting, and of a portion of this meeting, too. It was absolutely indescribable. You would want a flash- light photograph as well. (Laughter.) As to report- ing the proceedings verbatim, I cannot imagine that any reporter could do it. I appeal to the members, as I did before, to mainta:n better dignity by respecting the chair. lam not speaking in an egotistical sense, but it is from the chair that the dignity of the Council should come in the first instance; and if lam not supported a screw is loose somewhere and the whole Council must go awry. Councillor IlAwnioßN said he had a great deal of sympathy with the motion but he did not thins Coun- cillor Osborne had gone into the question thoroughly. To carry out the proposal in its entirety would require not one shorthand writer,but half-a-dozen. Eighteen com- mittees met twice a month and the transcript of their proceedings would run into thousands of folios, to say nothing ot the coat of printing. It was bad enough to be compelled to listen to all the speeches, and it would he a further indignity to be compelled to read them. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Alderman BURTON suggested that the motion should be withdrawn and an amended one submitted. Councillor LINDLEY said that if the resolution were passed it would penalize the ratepayers without giving compensating advantages. Alderman TaiNtos said the resolution reminded him of bringing a steam hammer to crack a nut. (Laughter.) What gave the final push-off to Councillor Osborne's project was the conduct of Alderman Bolton on the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee. Of course, Councillor Osborne did not know the alderman as well as the other members did—(laughter)—or appre- ciate him at his proper value, or he would not have been offended because the alderman flatly contradicted him. He would contradict himself, if there was no-one else to contradict. (Laughter.) There was no doubt that certain members had been allowed too much liberty, and it was time spades were called spades, and that those who upset the business of the various com- mittees should be taken in hand. He objected to the motion principally on the ground of expense, as from what he had been told by persons connected with the profession the cost would be anything up to £1,500 a year. (Cries of dissent.) Well, the Corporation were not going to engage second-raters. (Hear, hear.) He contended that Councillor Osborne, as the introducer of the motion, had not gone into it sufficiently to be able to tell the CJuncil what the cost would be, or if he had he had kept the information to himself. He suggested it would be well if Councillor Osborne spent some of his time at committee meetings in the day time. Councillor OSBORNE : Mr Mayor-- Alderman TINNEON : Mr Mayor, I object to give way to his interruptions. Councillor OSBORNE : This is a point of explanation. Alderman TiNNioN : I object to hearing your explanation. The MAYOR (to Councillor Osborne) : Make your explanation avterwards. Alderman TINNtoN, continuing, said he objected to the Town Clerk engaging a permanent official shorthand writer. The Council would not let him engage a clerk at 234 a week. (Laughter.) Let the Council be con- sistent. The alderman characterised Conucillor Osborne's proposal as cumbersome and far too expensive. _
Councillor CHANTLER asked if a similar recolution had been passer: by 'any other County Borough Council. The TOWN CLERK I never heard of one.

Councillor BROADEtrEIST appealed to Councillor Osborne to withdraw the motion, as the cost of carry- ing it out would mean an increase of the rates to the extent of lid. and that would raise the rents of the work ing-clas.ses.
Councillor CHRIMES : What would the cost per annum 1)e if the motion is carried ?
The TOWN CLERK : I have not made A y inquiries, but lam told that, it will cost at least £l,ouo per annum.

Councillor WILKIFSON said he should oppose the motion, because neither the proposer nor the seconder and the few supporters had given any idea as to the cost. He knew from his experience of the late inquiry at the Town Hall that the issuing of verbatim reports was a costly thing. He could honestly say that the cost of carrying out the motion would not be less than £l,OOO a year or a penny on the rates.

div.head: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON TN CONFLICT WITH
div.p: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON TN CONFLICT WITH
THE CHAIR.

Councillor PEMBERTON said it would not cost any such ridiculous sum, and if the motion were carried the committees could be organized to facilitate its work- ing. No one would think of having all the leports printed and sent to each member. It was freely admitted that the work of the Council was done in a very irregular and haphazard way through the over- lapping of committees. If it were not for the serious- ness of it, the position would be worthy of comic opera. If the recent inquiry cost so much money it was well spent. Councillor WILKINSON : Question about that. The MAYOR : GO on with your speech. Continue your speech, Councillor Pemberton. Councillor PEMBERTON : I did not ask him to interrupt me. The MAYOR: And I did not ask you to follow him in his interruption. Go on with your speech. Councillor PEMBERTON : I claim the right to reply to interruptions. _ _
The MAYOR: Do you claim the right to obey the chair?
Councillor PEMBERTON : Yes, hut 'claim the right also to represent the public, and I want the chair to be fair to me.

The MAYOR : Do you infer am not fair ? lam trying to be fair. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERTON : If you say I cannot answer anyone who interrupts me, I say it is nnfair. I must have some freedom. I am not, going to be entirely muzzled. If that is attempted, I shall walk out of the place. ' The MAYOR (warmly) : I ask you to go on with your speech or sit down, and I claim to be supported by the Council. (Hear, hear.) Be kind enough to go on with your speech. Councillor PENIBERTON : If you will kindly allow me to make an explanation, but when am interrupted —it may be my misfortune—you tell me in an authoritative voice to go on with my speech. The MAYOR : I have told you to go on with your speech or resume your seat. I say that now. Councillor PEMBERTON : I am explaining why I cannot go on. . . . .
The 1%). AYoR : I don't want your explanation now. Councillor PEMBERTON : When my speech is broken into, I cannot on on. The MAYOR: Go on with it, as soon as you con- veniently can.

Councillor PEMBERTON : That is more like it. Continuing, the Councillor pointed out that some of the committee meetings did not last above ten minutes end one oflicial.shorthand writer would be quite equAl to the work, with occasional assistance. He advocated that the reports should not be printed but type-written.
COUNCILLOR OSI3ORNE AND ALDERMAN TINNION.

Councillor OSBORNE, in replying on the discussion, said his idea was that one copy of the report of each meeting should he typewritten, so as to be available for any member of the Council who wished to consult it. As to the suggested cost of S:1,500, some members must have got confused with the proposed new organ. (Laughter.) His sugges• tion was that it suould not cost a halfpenny more than £soo—in fact a gentleman in this town had told him it could be done for £3OO. Alderman Tinnion took a view of the question which was characteristic of his attitude on most resolutions which he himself did not propose or second. (Laughter.) He was always trotting out such old chestnuts as "Steam hammers to crack nuts." Then he went on to suggest that he (Councillor Osborne) should give some of his time, to Corporation work in the day time. As a matter of fan, he already did so, and and if it had not been for Alder- man Tinnion he would have given more time, because the alderman strongly opposed his getting on a com- mittee to which he would have been of some service. Alderman TINNioN: I did nothing of the sort. I deny that statement. _ _
Councillor OSBoRNE : Now, Mr Mayor. 1 appeal to you. You objected to my getting up sod now he does the same thing.

Alderman fINNION : I must have some opportunity of replying. It is a ruis-.tatement. Councillor OSBORNIC : I protest. The NTayor (to Aldermin Tiunion): You haw, dulled it. You cannot do anything more. Councillor OSBOFtNE : I am prepared to obey the chair, but if Aldermal Tinnion is so smart as to get up when another member wishes to make a point of explanation, he must sit down if I say anything against him.
Alderman TINICION : Would you like to take the chair ?
The MAYOR : I. think these interruptions are very disorderly. Alderman TINNION : Why should he tell me what I should do?
Councillor PEmnEwroN : You objected to Councillor Osborne interrupung you. The MAYOR: This is general disorder.

Councillor OSBORNE : Until Alderman Tinnion spoke there were no personalities introduced in my specco, but if e insists on personalities he must take the consequences. Alderman TINNION : lam quite prepared to. Councillor GSB,IRNE : Well, don't cry out then. Alderman TINNION : But I object to deliberate lies and mis-statements.
Councillor PHMBERTON : That is not a Parliamentary word. (Laughter.). . •

, The MAvort : Things are hopeless. We cannot go on in this manner. 1 cannot compel members to talk properly. C.mncillor EIA wTitonN : it is perhaps a good thing that we are not having a verbatim note taken to-night. (Laughter ) Councillor OSBORNE : My only regret is that a verbatim report was not taken at the first meeting attcnded in this room. It would have shown who it was that prevented me from getting on to the Street Improvement Committee. Councillor LASHFoRD : Hear, hear. They don't like it.

Councillor OSBORNE next turned his attention to Councillor Wilkinson's objection, voicA at a committee meeting, that the proposal would interfere with the freedom of speech. Councillor WILKINSON : Refer to whit I have said to-night. Councillor OSBORNE: It would be idle to do so, because there is nothing in what you said to-night. - Councillor NVILKINSON : Lucky for you ! Councillor OSBORNE : If you ask for it someone can give it, as well as yourself. Councillor ‘NILKINSON : YOU Will get it before long. Counciilor PEACOCK protested that continual inter- ruptions made it impossible for a member to keep to his line of argument. The MAYOR: I have appealed to the members. I cannot make them int o gentlemen. Councillor OSBORNE said be had some sympathy with Councillor Pemberton who was subjected to great interruptions arid yet was expected to continue his speech as if nothing had happened. It might be easy for Councillor Wilkinson, wWI his great auility, to do that. (Laughter from the public). Councillor WILKINSON : WhO'S barking there? (More laughter). Councillor OSBORNE said he hoped the Council would look at the motion as an attempt to remove some of the irregular proceedings—Whet he called irregular pro- ceedings—which existed at the present time. The motion was defeated, seven voting for it and 15 against.

ECZEMA ALL OVER CHILD'S HEAD. 6, Maypole Sq., Alconbury, Hunts, Eng.—" My little boy Vincent had a bad form of eczema all over his head for ten months. He used to scratch it until he made it bleed, then it scabbed over and began to spread round his neck and round to his other ear. It would bleed and discharge until it spread all over his head. I was given a box of--ointment and had to wash the head with soft soap every night and morning and cover it with ointment and sew white rags all over it like a cap. The poor child would scratch outside the rags and it would then discharge and the rags would stick to his bead. It got no better at all, then a friend sent toe a tin of Cuticura Ointment and a tablet of Cuticura Soap, so I started with them. By the third morning the scales were nearly all off. I kept on washing his head with Cuticura Soap and spreading the Cuticura Ointa,ent on each morning until I used up one tin. I sent for another and before I had used half of that his head was as clear as it could be from sores and new hair growing like anything." (Signedi Mrs. Lucy Townsend, May 23,1912. div.p: ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.

At the Liverpool Sessions on Tuesday, j:n3eo, Edward Newton (AP, baker, belonging to Warriugtolh was charged with having assaulted Annie Dickson, ati attendant at Rainbill Asylum, at Cuerdley, on December 28th last. Prisoner pleaded not guilty Mr Woolli, appeA, ed for the prosecution, and Mr Madden defeudea the accused.

For the prosecution, it was stated that Miss Dickson was returning home from Frodshe.m, but having g°!. into the wrong train at Ditton Junction, she left it " Fiddler's Ferry and proceeded to walk back to Widnovt where, she alleged, she was seriously assaulted by the Prisoner. On being alarmed, the man ran away, out i 6 day or two afterwards she dentilled him at ‘Vidnes 1/1 his husky voice and appearance. She also recognised 0, cart he was driving. Prisoner gave evidence, and denied that he had assaulted the woman. He had never see° her before the proceedings were taken. Prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to twelve calencar months' imprisonment with hard labour.

BEER BEFORE WORK.—John Chadwick, 22, Stephee- son-street, was locked up on a warrant tor being .to habitual arunkard, and his wife asked for a separation order.—Complairatut stated that her husband was drunic every week. He came horne and turned her and the children out of the house. They had to go in backs or anywhere they could get. If they aid not give hitt' pint or beer when he wanted one he threatened be would not .go to work.—Mr Firth said there was 0° doubt the wife was persecuted by the prisoner. suggested an adjournment to see if they could do anY; thing in the case. Prisoner promised to be teetotair and the case was adjourned for one month. A HUSBAND'S COMPLAINT.---Joseph Edward Watson, 32, duckeyestreet, was charged with neglecting his tly° children (luring the last six months, thus causing them unnecessary suffering.—He pleaded not guilty.--3,1r Browne, wno prosecuted on behalf of the N.5.P.C.61 said the detenoant was a labourer, formerly employo) at Longford Wire Works and afterwards at Bews.el torg,. He had not worked for a fortnight.—The wlO st Lied that she had brought her husband before 11'9 magistrates for being an habitual drunkard. The familY would not have any food if it were not for the kindnese. of relations and neighbours.—lnspector Wainwright of tue N.S.P.C.O ; said he Mae known the man for three years and had cautioned him several times about We conduct. He had advised him to "dry up " and leave the drink alone. On the 20th February he visited tin house and the prisoner was having his tea. He s!on "I shall get my wages on Saturday and I shall not pg.°, her any as I are off." He (the Inspector) said it he din so. he would get into serious trouble. But for tbe relations and lodgers in the house, there would not' hive be-n any food.—Prisoner said all the bother ice' ori :sed through his wife s uncle living with them. Thei did riot keep theniselves but pulled him hack and 130 had list jots in Warrington through them. One tale was gool until another was told. He had not tasted meat in that house since. the previous Thursday. 11° had eaten more in here (indicating the cells) this morn' ing than he bad done for over a fortnig,ht. His wife gave her uncle the best of everything.—The case weo adjourned for four eeeks. Mr Brawne : Will you 115 j him not to carry out his threats ? He has threatened to stab his wife. Prisoner: I don't know about stabbing, look at this (pointing to nruises on his arnl)• have not married the family. I have married one' I will kiep teetotal. Complainant : I say he cannot k-ep teetital. The Chairman said they were giving tb,B Prisoner a chance. If he did not improve they wouin then know how to deal with him. AN UNEXPECTED VlslTOß.—James Bate, 23, Lold Nilson-street, was charged with burglariously enterieg tie dwelling house 11, Norman-street with intent.to, steal goods, the property of Joseph Taylor.—The Cble' Cons ,able said that at about 1.30 that ruorning,Mr Taylor wes in bed along with his wife,when they were awakened by a noise as if someone was trying to break into tbe Tney went into the kitchen and on striking light, saw two feet protruding from the chimney into, the tire grate. Mr Taylor pulled at the legs au" dragged the prisoner out. Acting Sergeant Newey wng called, and in the meantime Mr Taylor had tied the prisoner up. It was found that three chimney pots and two or three courses of bricks had been removed. TWO other pots had been dislodged from another chimneY stack in the same row. When Mr Taylor asked prisoner what he was doing in the chimney, he replied " Where are those (ion-unionists? I want to get at those non-unionists." He was minus his cap, vest and other articles of clothing and seemed to have had drin.li• The cap and vest were found in another fire grate tri aaother house. (Laughter.) The Clerk: Just as well. In her statement to the magistrates the accused explained that some friends called upon her and the would have her with them. "If I had gone out at the front door I should have been all right," she added, "but I went out at the back and took the wrong tnrn- ing." (More laughter.) The Clerk : Will you be more careful in future ?—The accused: Yes, doctor, will. (Laughter.) She was dismissed after the Mayor had severely cautioned her.

The great interest s/sP, vvorkingmen take in the Association was tnnced by the exceedingly large number of uasiasts who attended at the eleventh annual ts,estice in the Club room, Horse and Jockey, Winsvick- h-5.", on Monday evening. Mr J Willett presided, and os4krs supported by Mr W Patrick (hon secretary), Th"r J A Rushworth (hen treasurer). eic a CIIAIRMAN said they were greatly pleased and 0i "'Ned by the large attendance that thgeht which augured well for the future of f,r association. It made one feel that the fsithcualing season would be a highly success- re from every point of view. (Hear, hear.)
