div.head: iIONOURING FALLEN HEROES.
div.p: iIONOURING FALLEN HEROES.
Impressive Memorial Service in Queen's Gardens.
GENE

With simple but deeply impressive military ceremonial, Warrington on Sunday did honour to the memory of the soldiers of the South Lancashire Regiment who fell in the South African campaign. "Let us now praise famous men" was the inspiring keynote of the memorial service in Queen's Gardens, and those who attended could not but echo the senti- ments of the Rev W Bracecamp when he said the wonder was that such an eminently fitting commemor- ation had never been thought of before. The anni- versary which brought together a huge gathering, representative of civic and military life, was that of the battle of Pieter's Hill, fought on February 27th, 1900, when the gallant Lieut.-Colonel W MacCarthy O'Leary fell white lead- ing the charge. With great pride the admirers of the old " Fighting Fortieth" during those critictl days prior to the relief of Ladysmith read General Buller 's tribute in his dispatch to the War Office : "The enemy's main position was magnificently carried by the South Lancashire Regiment. A graphic descrip- tion of the engagement is given by one who took part in it, T Neligan, of the South Lancashire Regiment, in his book "From Preston to Ladysmith." Ile says : " Onward the men pressed, taking advantage of all cover until the summit of the hill had been reached; then, as if by mutual consent, both officers and men rested for a brief space of time to regain their breath, knowing that in another hour's time the battle would be decided. By th's time, about 4 p.m., the grass within three hundred yards of the enemy's position had caught fire from the blazing of the lyddite shells, and the khaki-clad figures showed up most prominently against the dark and sombre back- ground. When about two hundred and fifty yards from the main position the firing was terrible and the bullets came so thick that my regiment attempted to take cover behind a small rise in the ground, but this proved to be quite inadequate for the purpose. Seeing this, the commanding officer gave the order to fix bayonets and charge, saying at the time, ' Rernen-ber, men, the eyes of Lancashire are watching you to-day l" At his words the whole regiment rose like one man, and the black slope fairly twinkled with the glitter of the bayonets as they flashed in the sun. Like a wall of rock the gallant 40th closed up 'n their foe, and the best disciplined troops in the wide world could not have withstood that irresistible rush. Like demons let loose they charged upon the enemy, who quailed before the contact, and th ,se who were able rushed precipitately away, falling in dozens under the bullets of our men. The Boers who were unable to make their escape sued piteously for quarter, and the Lancashire lads, now as merciful as they had been brave, gave it to them, though with bad grace, as they were burning to avenge the losses they bad already sustained. The colonel fell shortly after he gave the order to charge, whilst leading his regiment on, and Major Hall, the second in command, took charge of the regiment and gallantly conducted the charge unto the end." The centre of interest in Sunday's service was, of course, the regimental memorial in Queen's Gardens and the ceremonial vividly rec tiled the unveiling of the statue by Sir Redvers Buller on February 21st, 1907. The decoratioa of the memorial was under- taken by the non-commissioned officers and men of the Ist, 2nd, and 3rd battalions of the South Lanca- shire Regiment, the work being admirably carried

" Well, you see sir," replied the boy, " I promised father that I would come straight to the ship and report for duty, without stopping in town, so I couldn't very well." "Good boy ! " cried the officer. "If you obey orders as -well in the navy, you should get on capitally. What is your name?" "Horatio Nelson, sir." And the man who, as a boy, had learned to obey orders unflirchingly, later became the great sea hero of England, Horatio Lord Nelson.

DAY BY DAY. Just a little every day, That's the way. Child en learn to read and write Bit by bit and mite by mite; Never any one, I say, Leaps to knowledge and its power. Slowly, slowly, hour by hour That's the way, Just a little every day. —Ella Wheeler Wil ox THIS WEEK'S STORY.

He was not a very smart boy but he knew a few things. He had been told, for instance that if you want the meaning of a big word it is a good thing to break it up into parts. The teacher asked one day " What is adulterated food ? He thought for a minute and then said "Adulterated food is that which can be digested by an adult but not by a child."

div.p: p 1 I CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.

A BOY WHO OBEYED ORDERS. A TRUE STORY. It was on a wet cold October evening that a boy trudged wearily into the seaport town. of Chatham, England, with a bundle on his shoulder. He was covered with mud, and from under the long black locks that fell on his forehead, two big eyes stared out at the world, and his thin cheeks were pinched with cold and wet with rain. He met a sailor as he entered the town's outskirts, and,stopping him, said: "If you please, which way to the docks ? " The sailor directed him, and he went forward down the narrow streets till he came to the waterside. There he wandered around for a time without seeing anyone, for it was supper time; but presently he came upon an old man, and asked: "Are those ships out there warships?" "Aye," replied the man, "they be, sure enough, lad. Be ye a-goin' to the wars ? " And he grinned. " Yes ; but I don't know how to get on board," said the puzzled boy. " Where do the boats land ? " "Right here," and the old man waved his pipe at the landing stage before them. " See ! yon is one a-comin' now." Sure enough, the boat was rowing swiftly in. It drew up to landing stage and an officer stepped out. The boy approached the officer and, touching his cap, said: "Please, sir, can you tell me how to get on board the frigate Raisonnable ?" The officer looked down, and, staring at the thin, pale face with its big eyes and firm mouth, replied: 'Why, that is my ship. But what do you want on board of her ? " "Please, sir, I want to join. Her com- mander, Captain Suckling, is my uncle, and I was to report to him." The officer looked again at the boy. "Well in that case I can take you aboard when I return. But you look cold and hungry, my lad. Have you had supper ? " • "No, sir; I left home early this morning, and have not eaten anything since." "My ! Here you have reported to me. I am a lieutenant on board, so come on up and have something to eat with me. Why didn't you stop in town as you came?"
The Examiner, Saturday, March 8, 1913.

div.head: WISDOM OF GEORGE SHANN.
div.p: THE WISDOM OF GEORGE SHANN.
By Charles E. Parker.

"Who in the world is George Shann asks the reader. I must tell you. Last summer I was invited to an Inter-Denomina- tional Social Congress to be held at The Hayes, Swanwick, Derbyshire. "The Hayes" is a goodly mansion, surrounded with about 20 acres of park land. It was acquired some years ago by the Crossley's, of Manchester, who formed a company, bought the estate, and adapted it for Summer Schools of various characters. Never before had I been to a Summer School, and I went with a good deal of curiosity. What sort of people should I , meet, now would the various denominations including Church of England, Roman Catholic Friends and Free Churchmen,get on together; would the delegates be merely cranks and theorists ; would there be a sufficient number of those who pride themselves on being practical for me to feel at home? At one of the early meals I chanced to sit opposite a young man who challenged interest. He was rough, may be a diamond in the rough. I wondered Nshat had brought such an one to this Conference. On enquiring, I was told his name was George Shann and that he had won, what very few attain to, the right to call himself Master of Arts, that is he held a University degree. Nor was his a case of one who by strenuous temporary effort had specialised on the subjects necessary to take a degree,he was one who had acquired an all round knowledge of men and things. His appear- ance, dress, and speech betokened an upbringing in what we call "humble" sur- roundings. I fancy we will have to alter our nomenclature; because a family lives in poor surroundings I do not think it at all follows that they merit the compliment of being humble, nor does it follow that because a man belongs to those who work with hands and receive a weekly wage that he should be spoken of as belonging to the "lower classes." In like manner I protest against the honourable title of working-man being limited to wage-earners because it suggests that those outside the limitation do not work. The thought of the day is slowly but surely making a revaluation of our values, a revaluation of the ideas out of which such terms arise. But the form often lasts longer than the idea which gave it birth and perhaps it is well that it holds together until a new and more appropriate form is born and is ready to take its place. George Shann was a typical workingman and neither education nor later surroundings had either spoilt him or altered him. There was nothing low about him and nothing particularly humble; he was a typical work- ing man in the best sense. . The paper Mr. Shann gave to the Conference entitled "The Social Life of the Adult Worker" showed an insight from within of industrial life alto- gether refreshing. Many who were at this Conference, although generally specialists in their own lines,viewed social questions largely from the outside ; this man spoke from inside knowledge and experience. It is from his paper (which has only just come to hand in the published Records of the Conference) that I propose to give extracts which appear to me thought-arresting. BETTER HOUSING.

"In Birmingham it was stated without qualification that the avcrage workman's wages do not allow him to pay the cost of a really good house. We should not try to fit the house to a low wage, it is time we fitted the wage to a good house." WOMAN'S POSITION.

"Often the woman works in the faetoi y or in some other way all day as well as the man. But the woman still does all the work of the house, while both the man and the women take it for granted that the man should be
free to rest or to amuse himself. Often the woman herself would resent the suggestion

that the man should do his share of the housework. It would be considered quite infra dig for the man to do any housework. There is a passive acceptance on the part of the woman of a certain inferiority, and there is almost a total lack of comradeship between

the man and the woman. The man seeks his pleasures by himself amongst other men, and it is only occasionally that he and his wife go out together. Dining the summer in work- ing-class districts it is a common sight to see large wagonettes filled with men off for a trip into the country." "In this respect, however, there is a grow- ing improvement, due, I think, not to any initiative on the part of the .men, but rather to a growing self-assertion on the part of the women. Women in all classes are treated by men exactly at the standard at which they value themselves." READING AND THINKING.

"I have already referred to the kind of reading that the adult worker does. His out- look is naturally narrow. He has been taught to read, but the adult man of to-day when he was at school, was not taught what to read. That is to say, he had little opportunity of acquiring any standard oj discrimination. The majority of working men do not under- stand the difference between a good book and a bad, and as yet it is quite a minority of working men who do any serious reading, or who even read good fiction. The standard of their literary taste is seen by a glance at the windows of a newsagent's shop in a workingclass district or by a perusal of the Sunday papers which sell in such enormous numbers. These papers are full of sensation, morbid details, and sentimental incidents, often crossing the line of decency. It is only another side of the same fact to say that the adult worker has not been taught to think. This is true of many other

people besides the workers, but I am dealing now only with the industrial classes. Ths adult has a kind of common sense which gets him along in a wonderful way in his own limited sphere, but he has little faculty for logical thought or for weighing evidence. He is easily moved by rhetoric and rant. It is simply appalling to see the way in which the minds of the workers can be manipulated by the press, and this manipulation of the mind and will of the workers has now become a scientific method."

div.head: Al VIEW OF THE SCENE IN THE GA
div.p: Al VIEW OF THE SCENE IN THE GA

out by Mr E Slater, of Padgate. From the pedestal hung streamers of laurel, while on the front the word, "Jo Memoriam" were formed in violets on a back- ground of white narcissi. Soon after noon, men of the South Lancashb e Regiment beg in t muster in the gardens and form a large circle round, the memorial Five battalions of the S.,uth Lanca- shire Regiment—including the line, special reserve and Territorials—were represented. Major Green who was responsible fir the arrangement of the service, was in command of 150 men from Orford Barracks, led by the band of the depot. The Territorials were about 400 strong, Colonel B Fair- clough having charge of the 4th battalion, while Major Pilkington was present on behalf of the sth battalion (St. Helens). The drum and fife b nd of the local Territorial battalion, together with the buglers, were also in attendance. Special interest att ched to the presence of the members of the Volunteer Active Service Company which wer..t out to South Africa, under Majr F II Appb ton. Many of the men (having since left the battalion) wete in plain clothes and proudly wore the medals gained in the service of their county. The Church Lads' Brigade furnished a strong detachment from its local battalion, Msjor Brookes being in command. The municipality, of course, paid its part in the tribute to the honoured dead Preceded by the mace and sword bearers, the Mayor and Mayoress (Councillor Dr Joseph and Mrs Arnold Nield) entered the gardens just before the hour fixed for service— 12.30—and took up a position close to the statue. Among others pre- sent were :—Aldermen Arthur Bennett, T Burton, J Smethurst and D Tinnion, Councillors J Broadhurst, E Osborne and H Roberts, Mr J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr Martin Nicholls (chief constable), Mr John Fairclough, Mr Arnold Nield, and Dr Peacocke. Thousands of the townspeople assembled in the gardens and adjoining streets and joined reverently in the service which was conducted by Rev. W. Brace camp (chaplain to 4th battalion). The form of service was very brief, but the purpose of the gathering could not have been more feelingly voiced. It opened with the hymn "0 God our Help in ages past," sung to the accompaniment of the combined bands. Then the Rev W Bracecamp offered a number of prayers, one of which sounded the titre imperial note in the words: " May our flag be every- where the sign of truth and justice, of honour, purity and faith." The Lord's Prayer having been sad, the hymn "Fight the good fight" was sung. The Rev. W. MIACECAMP then delivered an address. He expressed his gratitude to Major Green, with whom the idea of the service originated, and went on to say that the wonder was that they had never held such a commemoration before. He sincerely hop d that they would atone for past neglect by making the service an annual event. No doubt many of the people standing round would ask : "What mean ye by this service ?" The answer was to be found in the Book of Ecclesiasticus, "Let us now praise famous men." The preacher referred to several national heroes, including Nelson, Wellington and 'Gordon, and said that latterly we had been deeply touched by the thrilling story of Captain Scott and his Antarctic expedition. As we read of that touching scene when Captain Oates went out into that terrible snowstorm and gave his life, as he thought, for his companions, we could not but subscribe to the simple but expressive elitaph "Hereabouts lies the body of a gallant gentleman." Coming nearer home and to the reason which had called them together that day, they thought of that

div.head: )ENS.
div.p: )ENS.

noble gentleman-Colonel O'Leary -and the brave men who died with him, while fighting for their King and country. Surely the least we could do was to show them a little honour for their gallantry. The preacher went en to emphasise three lens which might be learnt from tl.e service. The first was our duty to God. At the p esent time we were enj ying a cycle of success in trade and he was afraid there was a danger of men forgetting to whom they belonged. If we wanted to be successful as a nation we must do our duty t) cur God. Money and possessions did not make a nation; it was " righteousness that exalteth a nation." lie,xt we could learn from the noble example of the South Lancashire heroes, our duty to our King. Thank God that we in England had been fortunate enough to have splendid Kings to rule over us -Kings who deserved our honour-and it would he a sorry day Ur England when we becarce unpatriotic and disloyal to our King. ' The third du'y was that which we owed to our country. A great many people in these days were !icing selfish lives. When we con- trasted Vie prop )rtio of time which young men gave to football, golf and other amusements- inoocent in themselves- ai compared with that wlich they devoted to the service of their country, it filled us with lv,rror and with very sad thoughts. In this land of the free we enjoyed gl, ricus liberty and yet how few of us were prepared to give up a little time for the country which had done so much for us. A great deal had been said of late about the Territorial Army. Looked at from the numerical standpbiut, it was a failure, for the numbers fell 50,000 short of the required standard. What were the youths of the present day doing? They were certainly cot made of the same kind of stuff as those men whom they were present to honour. They were pr,ud that so many representatives of the Souir Lancashire Regiment were present. At one timo the regiment used to be made up practically of men from Warrington and district, but somehow there were no! so many Warrington men coming forward to swell its ranks to-day. He hoped that in future more of those who entered the army from this district would attach themselves to the South Lancashire Regiment, because it was an honour to belong to a regiment which had such a record of heroic deeds to its credit. Having expresscd pleasure at the presence of the chief magistrate and leading townsmen who no doubt felt they were only doing their duty in attending the service, the preacher concluded " We are here to do honour to Colonel o.Leary and our brothers who laid down their lives for their country. Their bodies now rest in peace on the veldt in South Africa, but their names and their brave deeds will live as long as the world lasts."

The service reached its ctilmina.ing paint in the Vacing of wreaths at the foot of the memorial. While this ceremony was taking place the massed bands and bugles sounded "The Last Post." The wreaths were from the following :—Mrs O'Leary, Mr and Mrs Fish- wick, Mr and M. s Marsh, M:s Hall, (in memory of Lance-Corporal J Fishwick, St Helens), "In loving memory of Piivate W Blackwood," from Officers, N.C.O.'s and men of the sth Battalion," In loving memory of Private J Gerard (3rd Battali( n Grenadier Guards, who died at Bloemfontein) hone father and mother, Kit, Cis. and Harry" Major Appleton (4th Battalion), "In memory from I. Vol. Service Co., Lieut.-Colonel B Fairclough and the officers of the 4th Battalion, Sergt.-Major, Staff-Sergeants, Sergeants, Corporals and Privates of the 4th Battalion.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
209th Quarterly Meeting.

The 209th quarterly meeting of the Warrington Co-operative Soc.ety, was held on Monday. Mr Wadsworth (president), occupying the chair supported by the Committee, about 150 members being present. The minutes of the previous quarterly meeting having been read and confirmed the President moved that the report and balance sheet be taken as read, which was carried. The report for the half year showed that the total sales had been £157,807 an increase of £23,148 over the corresponding period and the sales for the 12 months .002,220, an inereese of £41,027 over 1911, all departments of the society's business having c buted t) the increttee. The membership now stands at 12,547 an increase over 1911 of 1,088. T le nett profit after meeting all expenses including the payment of an interim dividend of 3s 2d in the £ enabled the Committee again to tecommend the ueeal dividend. The share capital of the Society showed an increase of nearly £B,OOO on the 12 months and the nett pr t fit for the year nearly £6,000 over 1911. Mr J GREEN CHAPPeer,(audit. r)attended the meeting and reported that the accounts were all in order and carefully kept and that the Society was in an extremely sound financial condition. After a few questions the report and balance sheet was accepted. Messrs Wright and Seed were elected as members' delegates to the C.W.S. quarterly meetings for the next 12 months. The recommendation of the Committee theta retiring allowance should he given to the late manager of the Stockton Heath branch who had served the society for over 40 years, was caeried by practically unanimous vote. The Committee ad recommended with a view to meeting necessitous cases that they should be empowered to purchase members' checks during the quarter at a rate of 2s fid in the £. It, wee suggested at tee meeting that the amount should be 2s 9i, it being c nsidered that the difference between this and the ordinary dividend would be sufficient to meet the Increased costs of making these arrangements, and the Cemmittee accepted the euggestion, which on being put to the vote was carried by a large mejority. At the suggestion of the Committee the meeting airhorised the investment of £5,000 in Warrington Cor- poration Loans, and also that the Society should in future bear a portion of their own fire risks through the medium of the Insurance Fund carrying the premiums so saved to that fund. The question of the Walking Dey trip was raised, it being reported that the whole of the number that could be at present catered for had been received but that during the course of the next few days an attempt would he made to try and arrange for additional accommodation so that any other members who desire to go with the trip could do so, and the result of this would he communiceted as soon as possible; those interested being asked to enquire at the office. This practically concluded the business, the meeting closing about 9.30.

div.head: SHUNTING FOOD TAXES.
div.p: SHUNTING FOOD TAXES.

The attention of the Earl of Derby having teen drawn by a correspondent to the fact that food taxes for Colonial Preference or other purposes were still being advocated in certain qu‘rters, he has authorised his secretary to reply, under date February 28th, that "he has no doubt whatever that the Tariff Reform League will loyally abide by 'the decision of their leaders, namely, to support the policy laid down by Mr Bonar Law at Edinburgh."

div.head: CLASS BITTERNESS.
div.p: CLASS BITTERNESS.

"A few years ago it would have been true to say that generally the workmen of any class did not hold feelings of bitterness against the rich and better placed. That is not so true to-day. Large numbers of workmen are bitterly impatient. Note the way in which the old leaders in the trade union world are being displaced. It is not that they want to pull the rich and better placed down, they merely want a better place for themselves. But they do not take the rich classes for granted as an institution as they used to do." STANDARD OF SOCIAL AND MORAL

div.head: VALUES.
div.p: VALUES.

"Before dealing, however, with any specific form of amusement or recreation, I wish to protest against the common habit, so prevalent at the present time, of painting the social lot of the worker all in dark colours, and of crediting him with an undue share of original sin.. It is largely a question of the standard of convention and social values from which we start. We may confuse appearances and take surface or outside results without making due allowance for the different circumstances. Remember that

the poor have no margin for mistakes. Many a middle-class man or woman who goes through life without ever being taken to task in any way would have made a fearful mess of things in a working man's home. The standard of social values and even of morality amongst the workers is different from that of any other class. They meet the elemental facts more openly and brutally, and many conventions which are found amongst the middle and other classes are ignored or never thought of, the practical logic of their life and surroundings preventing such conventions and standards being adopted. In speech and thought the worker is more direct ; a spade is called a spade, and although to those whose standard is different and whose form of speech is more euphemistic the direct thought and speech may seem brutal and even appear indecent, it is not necessarily so to the working-man."
THE COMPLEXITY OF PERSONALITY

"All personalities are complex,inconsistent and contradictory. It does riot follow that because a man goes to a public-house or indulges in betting that he is a moral repro- bate. Often he is a strong trade unionist or co-operator or politician, doing his share to improve the lot of his neighbour. Several of the scholars in my adult school admitted that
they visit public-houses and do a little betting, and these same men are very active in various forms of public service, and are kind fathers and good husbands." THE DIGNITY OF LABOUR.

"We may talk about the dignity of labour, but all our practice denies such preaching. The manual labourer, both by himself and others, is considered socially the failure in society. Material conceptions of value deter- mine our actions, and both the working-man and the cther classes consider success rather by what a man has than by what he is."
CONTROL OF LIFE.
"In various ways middle-class people are

making laws for, and undertaking to manage, the lot of the working-man and his children. tut they are not always prepared to work with the working-man. The real object of all efforts should be to create such conditions as would enable the working-man to manage his own life, he wants to be a man and feel

that in a real sense le controls his own life. A man cannot be made good by mere outside effort or machinery. A man must make himself a good citizen by seeing for himself that the interests of his own personality require him to devote himself to the social good. And for the willing sacrifice of self the individual must have a self, must have those interests which make up an individual life before he can carry out his social and civic duties."

div.head: SHOOTING CORMORANTS.
div.p: SHOOTING CORMORANTS.

I had often noticed that the boatmen or lobster" fishers never failed, SS henever I employed them, to ask me to shoot them a cormorant, but I did not imagine that I would be persuaded to devote an evening to the pursuit of such leathy fowl. However, one lives and learns, and I now know that cormorant or snarl. shooting cqn be carried on in a manner which raises it 16 tie level of sport, and that the ungainly, long-necked "Isle of Wight" rarsons " can provide shooting which will tax the marksmanship as will that at really high pheasants. The crofters of the Hebrides seers all to have the peculiar taste which leads them to enjoy seart soup ; at any rate, it is indisputable that, how ever many of the fish-eating bi;ds you may bring in, all will be gladly seized and borne away. It i 3 these fncts which renders cormorant-shooting possible, for no one desires to kill birds which are useless, although, indeed, the cormorant family levy a terrible toll upon fisb,and come therefore to some extent under the head of vermin.— liesketh-Pritchard, in " Country Life."

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 8, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 8, 1913.
JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
THE HOLY LAND

The voyage is well calculated to benefit the health, of Mr Brighouse, the popular South-west Lancashire coroker who is just recovering from a trying illness ;, but if he intends to spend much time in the Holy Land I should doubt the wisdom of his choice. It is not the sort of country for an English convalescent. I have had the advantage of a little conversation with one who has been there with other tourists, and the common experience was that it was impossible to obtain good, wholesoms bread; in fact, indifferent diet had such an effect on my friend's constitution that be has even now barely recovered. JUDGE AND JURY.

"The judge is bound to accept a verdict whether he agrees with it or not." So I read in the " Examiner" legal column. When, as Mr Justice Ilowkins. the late Lord Broughton presideo in the Criminal Court at Leeds Assizes, I used to attend as the representative of a Yorkshire paper, and I well remember bow in one instance, plainly disgusted with the finding f the jury in a case which had occupied the greater part of the day, he promptly caused them to be empannelled for the next on the ca!endar,* and kept them sitting till 10 p.m. I suppose the judge found it a sweet bit of revenge; but it struck me as very like cutting off one's nose to spite one's face Only the other week a judge diqagreed with the verdict of a jury—which had the effect cf releasing one chargcd with a serious crime - and he told them so very distinctly. One •has repeatedly heard the significant comment, "Well, gentlemen, it's your verdict, not mine." REMARKABLE JURIES.

I read in my daily paper that at the Whitechapel County ,ourt last week no fewer tban twenty persons with the surname of Cohen were summoned to serve on the jury. I oas reminded of the tricks of a humorist in the North. In selecting men for jury service at Quarter Sessions, he once deliberately picked for a panel a dozen of the stoutest, "and•they were so fat that they could not find accommodation in the b-a! Then be went to the opposite extreme and the Court was entertained with the spectacle of a jury box containing twelve extremely thin, ill-looking men. But the climax came when the inveterate joker put before the Court a squinting jury!

THE ATHLETIC GIRL. In his address on " Athletics " before the Philo- mathic Society, the head master of the Lymm Grammar School took occasion to deprecate the excessive atten- tion given by some modern women to athletics. I was reminded of an incident at a girl's High School ,prin- giving not long ago The head mistress had eulogi-ed hockey, and a leading medical practitioner who followed said he was fully perm-Ey-led that hcck•y was not a desirable game for girls. 'He approved tennis, which taught girls to walk erect, but not to compete in a manni-h way wi h men. Hockey and its like had done much to Broil the feminine character of girls. He deprecated the swinging gait, the t•-•wzled hair, and the large feet of the modern athletic girl. From this point of view another authority comments that an assembly of the elder girls who have distinguished themselves at a troiern school is apt to be a lament- able sight, a) little has come to them of the graces of early womanhood. Scragginess, dull complexions, and ungainly movements are conapicious. Games which make the boy strong and graceful, being over- done in the case of the girl, have the opposite effect. Girls who are the victims of over-exertion, mental and physical, are clmmon nowadays. Exercise in moderation is excellent, but when a girl whose Mind is iNearied by work is driven into the playing field and encouraged to take part in violent games till her body is exhausted, she is being made to burn the candle at both ends. CONCERNING OYSTERS •

It may have been observed that I turn for a text to the Children's Corner of this journal, and "Uncle Caleb's" description of-the oyster brought to my mind many things. Disraeli is credited with haying first said "He was a bold man who first ate an oyster," but in all likelihood " Black-eyed Susan" was the source of his inspiration, for Jchn Gay has, therein some lines with reference to the " bras 3 or steel" constitu- tion of the man who "first broke the oozy oyster's peail coat, and risked the living morsel down his throat." " Uncle Caleb" will say that he was a grievously mistaken man too, and that he would have been less bold had he had any idea what a scavenger the oyster is But what a mighty host have followed the example thus set. From an oft quoted passage in one of the Satires of Juvenal it is clear that British oysters were eaten in Rome in very early times, and oyster shells from the Colchester beds were used in the building of the Coliseum. The same ancient writer has at least one other distinct allusion to the fact that British oysters were eaten and enjoyed in Rome in his day. But let me pass on to Dr A T Pierson, whose "Life Power" contains the following pass- age :—" Vitellius c-uld with beastly voracity exemplify the gluttony which prevailed in the time of the Crews by eating a round thousand of oysters at a sitting; and increased the heinousness of the offence by availing himself of the abominable fashionS then in vogue of tickling the palate with a peac-ok feather in order to make room for new indulgence. Even the wise and good Seneca, who praisei poverty but cauld not live comfortably on ten millions of dollars, ate a few hundred oysters daily, and then blamed the delicious mollusk for his indigestion." It is suggested as highly probable that the Roman epicuies valued this island of ours principally because of its oysters. Pliny says of a certain Sergius Grata, who lived in the time of Augustus, that he formed artificial oyster beds and "contrived to make a large income by the exercise of his ingenuity." So that artificial oyster culture was well known to our conquerors. Coming again to cur own times, Colchester annual oyster feast goes back to the reign of Charles 11. I have a relative in the United States who more than once or twice has sent over a small barrel of American blue points at Christmas. What am I to do with them in future— after reading that discomforting description of the anatomy of an oyster? It wouldn't be right-to give them to some ignorant person who hasn't read it, would it? BREAKING LAMPS.

The appearance of three youths before the Lynam Gas Committee on charges of breaking gas lamps recalled fcr me a period which I spent in a town on the Lancashire and Yorkshire border. The highway passing through the district was exceedingly busy, connecting as it did important industrial centres of the two great counties. There was a good deal of traffic by night as well as by day, and as teamsters often fell asleep, leaving their horses to blunder along at their own sweet will, lamp posts were constantly knocked down. When the responsible drivers were caught, there was no quesion of the Gas Committee usurping the functions of the magistrates or com- promising to let offenders down lightly. The police reported the cases in the ordinary way,and a summons followed as a matter of course,with the result that the costs were a good deal heavier than under the other plan. To be sure, I have often known Watch Com- mittees deal with cases of chimney firing and other minor offences. The practice was to give offenders an opportunity to appear before the committee and consent to a nominal flue, the alternative, of course being a summons to petty sessiolp. Needless to add, the great majority preferred the former course. INDISCRIMINATE ALMSGIVING.

At the Association of Guilds of Help the Rev. J. S. Hazeltine showed that the hardest problem of all is the indiscriminate philanthropist ; and there was an echo of this in the pro2eedings of the local Guild last week. For many years I have myself been hammer- ing away at the doctrin3 that philanthropists should regulate their almsgiving, that their zeal should be strictly according to knowledge, and that those who for any reason are unable personally to attend to these matters should avail themselves of the help offered by such organisations as the above montioned. To yield to the appeal of the fir-4 whining hypocrite who presents himself at one's door or is casually met in the street is not only sheer laziness, but misch;evous folly. There is less excuse for it now than ever there was, and there is reason to believe that those who have been systematically guilty of it are gradually breaking off the evil habit. AMATEUR, CASUALS.

There have been many of these since the time, which I well remember, when Ifr Greenwood spent a night in a W otkhouse as one of the tramping class, and made a fine journalistic "scoop " of it. One of the litest of them extended the experiment over a much longer period and published the results in book form. Therein Mr Crane, the author, confirms the popular impression that there is a sort of freemasonry among tramps and " downrighting " is a trade with recog- nised principles and rules. It is said the professic nal tramp does not make use of the casual ward when he can afford the common lodging-house. This 18 not proved. It seems to depend very much 'upon

the reputation of the casual ward. Different boards of guardians adopt different methods of making the casual ward uninviting, and it is unquestionable tha t the districts in which the merest payment is demanded in 'return for a night's lcdging get the fewest tramps. IMPROVED POOR LA.W METHODS. But *hat of the unfortunate honest out-of-work 'l' I understand that not long ago the Clerk ti the Warrington Guardians received from the Local Government Boaid a copy cf a new Order enforcing this and all such bodies outs de London to make arrangements for more uniform and systematic adminis- tration of casual relief. It was even thus early reported to.be already working or contemplated in upwards of h sc,re of English countries. This is the manner of it : Voluntary committees provide a mid- day meal for vagrants leaving casual wards in the morning. This mid-day meal rem yes the temptation to beg or steal a meal during the journey to the next casual ward, and thus demoliphes a reason for indis- criminate almsgiving. The Board urges the Guardians not already carrying out this arrangement to establish a committee comprised of representatives of different Boards of Guardians in the county, and, if possible, of a Standing Joint C,Eumittee, to arrange for the uniform administration of diet, detention, and tasks; discrimination (which may take the form cif earlier discharge and lighter tasks in favour of wayfarers genuinely in search of work), and the provision of the mid day meal Experience shows that the working of the scheme entails but small cost. One would fain hope that members of the Warrington Boat d of Guardians may presently be induced seriously to apply themselves to the sobilion of such problems instead of wasting their time in unfriendly personalities, and in quarrelling over trifles that :do net matter. IN LIGHTER VEIN.

Let us conclude with a laugh. I came across the following a while ago : A tramp rang the bell at a dcctor's house and asked the pretty young lady who opened the door if he would be so kind as to ask the doctor if he hai a pair of old,trousers to give away. "I am the doctor," said the smilirg ycung lady. It was a crestfallen tramp who t•ok his departure from that house.'

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held on IVednesday. There were present : Messrs ti Mather (in the chair), W Furness, A Brooke, J W Knowles, P Longton, W Houghton, J C Sutton (clerk), B 8 Newcombe (surveyor), H H Burnage (assistant surveyor), F Kerfoot (inspector), and Dr Sephton (medical officer).

div.head: WINWICK DRAINAGE.
div.p: WINWICK DRAINAGE.

The minutes of the General Purposes Committee con- tained a referen_e to the still existing troubles re the Winwick drainage and the alleged obstruction of Mill Brook. The Clerk had read a letter from the Law Clerk -to the Asylum Committee that the Council were receiving drainage water and untreated sewage matter into the highway drains which were connected with the Mill Brook on the Asylum Estate, from the estate of the Ecclesiastical Commissicners who,so far as the drain and storm water way concerned, had no rights reserved for the passage of such water through or over the Asylum Estate and so far as the untreated sewage matter was concerned the Council were receiving it into the drains rind turning it into the Mill Brook in contravention of the Rivers Pollution Act. The letter concluded that the Asylum Authorities could not allow the pollution to continue and they would be glad to know what the Council proposed to do in the matter. The Committee vie eed the u h9le subject of Winwick drains and Mill Brook obstruction to he one of com- plexity. The Cuncil had no part with the expensive litigation between the Asylum Committee and the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, the effect of which had been to show that if one sore was ,healed other sores might break out in fresh p'aces. A deputation was appointed to visit the Asylum to examine the alleged defective s: s'ems.

The CHAIRMAN (Mr Mather) said the deputation visited the Asylum on Monday last, but they were refused the opportunity of an examination. A letter from the Law Clerk of Winwick Asylum suggested th,tt a deputation from the Council should confer with the Asylum Committee on Thursday of next week. The Council decidei to fall in with the'sugges- ,ion.

SMOKE NUISANCE. The INSPECTOR (Mr Kerfoot) reported having taken observations of alleged smoke nuisances at Mr Gorton's works, Paddington, and the Warrington Corporation Water Works, Win:Nick. The Counc:l ordtred notices to he served to have the nuisance abated.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that there had been 29 births and 26 deaths in the district. The death rate from all causes was 22.3 per thousand of the population against 23.8 for the c,arresponding month last year.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF JUNIOR SURVEYOR.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF JUNIOR SURVEYOR.

Mr W k Sutton who is to sail next week for Van- couver, British Columbia, received testimonials of a high character under the signatures of the Chairman of the Council and Chairman of the General Purposes and Finance Committee. The Surveyor read from his reportlbook as follows :

"It is with feelings of regret that I have to announce to you the resignation of a much valued servant, Mr W R Sutton. ' He has been our assistnnt dow for practic- ally 13 years and during that time has been a very efficient officer on our staff and I cannut let this occasion pass without expressing befoie you my thank- fulness for his useful help, end my appreciation of his many good qualities. He is a first class surveyor now, with a valuable experience. I heartily wish him every success in his new sphere and hope that his many good qualities and genial personality will ensure him a lucrative furl useful career.
We understand Mr %V R Sutton accompanies a gentleman who is returning to British Columbia, where he has been resident for some years.

div.head: WEALTH OF SOCRATES,
div.p: WEALTH OF SOCRATES,

Socrates, who had 3. wealth of wisdom, was not possessed of much in the way of material riches. His proyerty was valued at five minea, which sum would be less than twenty pounds, and that included his dwelling. Yet folk were happy in those days. They lived plainly and simply, but wisely withal. The grape was the source of much enjoyment. It is really wonderful how the virtues and merits of the Grecian grape have survived to the present day. For do we not all know the delicious Currant—which is the Greek grape, rinened and dried by the glorious southern sun. To eat Currants i 3 to follow the example of the poor but wise and scholarly Socrates' for the Currant is the most wonderful nutrient in the world, and so savoury. An entirely new and inter- esting little book, telling you all about Currants, and giving recipes for a great variety of sweet dishes which can be made with Currants, has just been published, and your Grocer will give you a free copy on request. The book is called" Home Recipes for Cooking Currants."

div.head: ELECTIVE AUDITORS.
div.p: ELECTIVE AUDITORS.

The polling for the election of two auditors for the borough of St.Helecs, which took place on Saturday, resulted in the re-election of Mr J Francis (Labour) and the election of Mr T Dickinson (Conservative), Messrs W Holland and Darby, who came out as Independent candidates, were unsuccessful.

div.head: Messrs. Grosfield's Important Aotion,
div.p: Messrs. Grosfield's Important Aotion,

On Monday the Chaucery Division of the High Court reaches another stage in the action brought 11, mfy_sre Joseph Cnisfield and Sons, Limited, 01 Wart ing ton, against Techno-Chernics 1 Laborato.rieet Limited, and Nile Testrup, of London, to restrain the dafendants from infringing a patent for converting unsaturated fatty acids or their glycerides int° saturated compcur.ds. The defendants denied infringe merit and pleaded thst the specification did not fully' disclose the true nature of the invention. Mr Astbury, K.C. in opening the case for the defend' ants, said the first thing the patentee told them in 1110 specification was that the process might be worked bi creating a vapour from the fatty acids, but it wee now conceded that they could not make th vapour of a fat or fatty acid. If that was the true reading of the specification the patent was bad. Tire defendants had made experiments which showed diet the process carried out as described by the patentee failed. In every one of such experiments the nick'. used had been obtained in a perfectly honest way—hl reduction in a current of hydrogen. The plaintiff said they tad made experiments which had succeeded, but that would not do. If the prccess would only work in a particular way then the patent was bad, because the patentee did not tell them how to do it. The Judge said he felt no difficulty in construing the patent, except on one point, and that largely related to temperation. Counsel had not finished his opening when the Court adjourned.

div.head: TOLD IN RUNCORN.'
div.p: TOLD IN RUNCORN.'
The straightforward statement of a Runcorn resident like that given below, bears an interest for every maot woman or child here.

We are indebted to Mr. J. Mort, of 19, York-streeti Runcorn, the proprietor of the well-establishyd builder's business in Greenway-road, for permissioo to publish the following statements: Two years ago, Mr. Mort said :—" I caught a cold some time ago, which tattled in my kidneys sod brought on acute pains in the small of my back. They were sharp, cutting pains, and seemed to drag me down, so that I was almost bent double. "There was a sandy sediment in the kidnef excretions, and this cinvinced me that my kidneys were not in ,a healthy condition. I have a lot of walking to do in the course of my business, and after / I had finished for the day I often noticed that my feet were swollen.

div.head: MILITARY CONCERT AT THE PARR HALL,
div.p: MILITARY CONCERT AT THE PARR HALL,

It was surprising and disappointing that the militarf concert given at the Parr Hall on Saturday evenias by the band of the Ist Battalion " The King's (Liverpool Regiment) failed to attract more than a veil moderate audience. The opportunity of hearing first-class army band is generally seized with some eagerness by dwellers at a distance from the great military centres especially when, as was the case oi Saturday evening, the programme is of an essentiallf pop.ular. character. "'here VS as just the necessarf variety in the choice (I items to relieve the entertain- ' men.s. of any suspicion of heaviness, while their inter' pretation was in accordance with the traditions of the perfectly equipped and carefully trained bands which are the pride of our army. The tone produced by "the King s, with their splendid balance in brass and wood-wind instruments, is exceptionallY rich and in the quieter passages, organ' like, and the way in which all sections of the band worked together was marked by wonderful precision, accuracy and c!eartiess of detail wok. There was occasionally a tendency to exaggerate and, over-accentuate, while the tempo rubato was employed with more than usual freedom. These points were especially noticeable in the " Carmen" selection which, in our view, suffered to some extent in effective' ness on that account, although the crispness of itg, rendering was highly praiseworthy. The bana, acquitted itself with most distinction in the " Trovatore " selection, the solo passages particularlf in the Miserere Scene—being altogether admirablt?; The fantasias " Students' songs "and " Lohengrin were the most ambitious of the remaining items, and the popular fancy was captured by the one-step and two-step which went with a swing rarely experienced, except in a military band. The efforts of individual pei formers met with cordially-expressed apprecia- tion, the Xylophone solos by Lance-Corporal Edwards being particularly melodious in themselves and finished in execution. The same performer gave a cornet solo in admirable style although "I hear thee calling me" did not afford him all the scope one would have desired. A glockenspiel solo by Lance-Corporal Edwards was a pleasing novelty. The band was under the conductorship of Mr A E Halford, who is to be congratulated upon the. great success of his work ne bandmaster. Additional interest was lent to the pro- gramme by the vocal solos of Miss Nellie Anderton (contralto) and Mr J Rabbitt (tenor). Miss Anderton infused a degree of feeling and animation into her vocalisation of "Softly awakes my heart" which showed that that difficult song was well suited to her powers of expression. It would be difficult to suggeSt a reason for the displacement of "She wandered dowo the mountain side," the originally selected second item, in favour of" The blackbird's song "and" Mal.. Day," artistically interpreted though they were. Mr Rabbitt was in fine voice and gave "The trumpeter and " Lend me youraid " in his usual thorough-going and wholly effective style, two encores being enthusiastically accorded.

div.head: " The Pride of Byzantia."
div.p: " The Pride of Byzantia."

Fun, of the fast and furious order,is tue dominE. Cog element in th:s new and attractive novel pr duction, which has drawn large houses to the Royal Court Theatre during the week. " The Pride of gyzantia " is novel inasmuch as it is a capiial combinatioii of prntomimical comedy, good singing, and fine acting. It is staged in a gorgeous, but none the less, ari istic manner and the groupings of the 'millet are tastefully executed. Although the absence of a continuous story is to be regretted, one really enjoys to the full the abundance of good things provided in the way of fun and frolic. A most able company comedians ant comediennes has been secured and all unite, successfully, in one effort to keep the audience in good humour the whole of the time. Chief amongst the comedians is Mr Arthur \Vhite who as S immy Blenkinsopp, a typical Tyke, is simply irresitible. He is a clever dialect comedian, a past master in the art of facial expression and a smart punster. His witticisms and by-talk are up-to-date and ludicrous to the extreme. In the " stormy " pass- age with the conductor he sends the " house" into mcontrollable fits of laughter. He has a typical partner in Miss Madge Soutter who appears as Sarah Ann, Mrs Wenkinsopp's maid. Her eccentricities are exceedingly funny and one cannot suppress laughter as she makes her appearance in the tightest of hobble skirts.; and struggles up and down the stage in that light but troublesome garment. Mr Cliff Inman as Percy Rivers aids in keeping the ball of humour rolling. Then we have Miss Lucy Murray's excellent portrayal of the homely Mrs Blenkinsopp. The part is a difficult one but Miss Murray is perfectly at home and gives us a true representation of the York- shii e housewife who, through money, moves in a society not quite her own. The extravagrant grammatical eefecs are ye y humorously "pointed " arid create much mirth. Mr J P Marsden makes up well as Mr o,fjenstein, the fawning jaw, and is a smart comedian. Miss D.rothy Vero appears in the title role. She has a breezy style and is equally success- ful in song and dance. Along with Mr Reg. Matthews, the dashing raval officer, she provides a number of capital vocal items The duets in _which they took part were a feature of the production. Little Elsie Pennell and Little Mary O'Hara as Harry and Winnie, London waifs, are a couple of the smartest juvenile entertainers we have seen for some time. Strongly pantomimical in character, the turn they provide is quite smart and Miss OTlara's rendition of an Irish song met with unstinted approbation. She gave the accompanying dance in a pleasing manner and was an easy favouri!e with the audience. Mr James Chippenda!e is succes-ful in his representatio of the character of Sir Jospph Rivers, the bankrupt barer' et, who tries to win Vire Blenkins pp in order to share her wealth. He made his position appear as obnoxious as was necessaiy. Thee is an extensive ballet, and a visit to the theatre should not be missed.
NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. RETURN VISIT OF HINDLE WAKES."

There can be no better proof of the success of Stanley lloughtm's wonderful Lancashire drama " Bindle Wakes," than the fact of its re-apperance at the Court Theatre next week. It is very unusual for a play to make such a quick return visit, but that this will be justified we have not the slightest doubt. Mr Edwin T Heys is bringing an exceptionally strong company, every artig being a native of Lancashite so that it will have the real local flavour. As Mr Heys was lusiness manager for six years for Miss Horni- man—by arrangement with whom the company visits kVarrington—this is sufficient proof of the thoroughness of the production. At the present time there are fur companies touring Hindle Wakes, and three more will start in the autumn. There will be the usual Thursday nyttinee at 2 39. Hindle Wakes is one of those rare plays which do not suffer in being played twice nightly, and it will be produced twice nightly next week without the slightest condensation.

ME KING AND A STAFFORDSHIRE CHOIR. The North Staffordshire District Choral Society has received a command to sing before the King and Queen on the occasion of their visit next month to Crewe Hall as the guests of the Marqu!s of Crewe. Shortly before the late King Edward's death the Hanley Glee and Madrigal Society and the North Staffordshire Choir were in turn cilled upon to give command performances at Windsor Castle. King George, as Prince of Wales; was present on both occasions. The actual eate of the concert has not been fixed.

The Bench granted the application.

the car. Both doors in the bottom of the car were thrown open to allow passengers to alight. Mary Ellis, a domestic servant, 13, Springfield-street, deposed to giving her ticket to the inspector when he asked for it. One passenger had left the car before the checker hoarded it. Cross-examined by Mr Madden, she said she did not know how many people were in the car. Madden: Were there any ?—Yes. You were not thinking about tickets ?—No. Mr Madden said the conductor started on the left- hand side of the car. They were not in Liverpool. They had an admirable system in Warrington. See how they preserved their tickets. Witness continued that she held her ticket in her hand but did not know whether the prisoner punched it or not. Mr Madden: You were thinking about something else ?—Yes, but I did not let the ticket go out of my hand. Where had you been ?—To Liverpool-road. Is that where " he" lives. Yes. (Laughter.) And when on got in the car you were dreaming? I might trove been. (Laughter.) It was an interruption the conductor coming along with his bell, &c., and as soon as you got your ticket you went back into that dreamy state ?—I may have done. , by Mr Madden : She might have been mistaken when she said that the checker got on at the Ship Inn She could not say where the passenger got off. Mr Wooll : Do you see that your sweetheart has anything to do with this case ?—No. Mr Wooll : No more do I. Mr Wooll : Did you pick any tickets up before going in the car ?—No. When George Washington Pendleton, a checker, was called and sworn, Mr Wooll said that (meaning the swearing of the prisoner) wes a most superfluous performance for a George Washington ?—Witness : I thought so. Witness said he received the ticket 383 from Miss Ellis. Mr Wooll : Did anything pass between you and the prisoner in connection with the number of passengers? —No. By Mr Madden : There were occasionally tickets lying about the car, but not always. It just depended on the tidiness of the conductor. When he was a
Photo Burnlt CONDUCTOR HORTON.

conductor he always made his way bill up within 200 and 300 yards of the terminus. Mr Madden: 200 or 300 yards, and you should have done it within 200 yards. There were, oontlnu.d witness' passengers who jumped on the cars within 300 or 400 yards of the terminus.
Mr Madden : Hsve you any way bills which have been altered ?—.
YO3, but I-ha.ve not got them here. Mr Madden : :they are like the tickets ; they are lost.
NNitness knew that the two clerks were on the car, and we knew about the pin pricks. He knew of all the arrangements which had been made.
ANIMOSITY DISCLAIMED.

By Mr Wooll : I have no animosity against the prisoner and I have not manufactured any evidence. When he boarded the car the prisoner did not deny that the ticket had been sold to Msry Ellis by him. John Robert Wilson, a clerk, in the tramway offices, and Ernest Sbepperd, clerk, also gave evidence. 'the former witness did not recollect the prieoner once coming to him with a half-sovereign which he had received for a sixpence but he would not deny that such had been the prisouer's conduct. Detective Sergeant Holland, who arrested the I prisoner, said that in auswer to the warrant the prisoner said " It is not true." Mr Madden : Who laid the information? Mr Telfer, tramway manager. That closed the case for the prosecution. The court adjourned and on resuming the prisoner was called into the box and stated that he la,d been married since his arrest. During the ten years be bad been in the employ of the Corporation there had never been a complaint against him to his knowledge. He had been offered a. position as driver. That was promotion, but he declined it for health reasons. When they were on the trams their meals had to be obtained when they could get them. On January 17th he had no chance of finishing his tea at the proper time and was eating what, he had left over from his tea. The 300 yards limit was Dever strictly adhered to, and under all circumstances it wss not possible to adhere to it. He had known cases where tickets had blown from the top of the car to inside. When the car reached the terminus he had to hold his money in one hand and pick up the tickets with the other hand. It was quite possible that he might have dropped some of the tickets. When the clerk got into the car he had made his way bill up. On the return journey he issued proper tickets to the passengers and did not issue the tickets in question twice. The ticket the woman gave to the checker wasl not given to her by him, When the checker told him the ticket was punched the wrong way' he said ! is it. 1. had not noticed" and thought no more about it. The checker never gave him the slightest indication that it was a wrong ticket, He did not remember anyone getting off the car before the checker got en. The tramway manager told him there was something wrong with his way bill, but that he would be given an opportunity of explaining, but in the meantime be would be suspended. If be had been asked for an explanation he could have given one. He had not had the slightest chance to go before the tramways Com- mittee. In re-examining prisoner, Mr Madden said the rules and regulations of the Corporation sere more honoured in the breach than in the observance. Thomas Davenport, employed at the Patten Arms, and formerly employed on the Corporation tramways, said the prisoner was a very trustworthy and honest servant. When be, witness was an inspector the men were subject to strict supervision. He should not say there was anything extraordinary in a ticket blowing from the top of the car to the inside. Air ‘Vooll : Don't you think it was unusual for this ticket to have been blown all the way round into Miss Ellis's hand ? Witne.s : Did it blow into her hand ? (Laughter). Mr Wooll : For my part I don't think it did. Witness said that if a passenger dropped a ticket and got excited she would probably pick up the first ticket she saw. George Alolyneux, conductor in the employ of the Warrington Corporation, said the regular practice was to make way bills up at the Coach and Horses but he had never made the way bill up before he had reached Tbewlis-street. Walter Rowe, conductor in the employ of the Co r- poration, said he worked the Cemetery route and made nis way bill up 500 yards from the terminus and the checker, Pendleton, had s'gned it. He had never been accused of issuing the wrong tickets. Mr Madden : What were the facts of that case..

Mr Wool! : That is not evidence as that case hss nothing to do with the present case. The Chairman: Ws don't see, Mr Madden, how it affects the case. By Mr VVooll : He had never made up way bills 1100 yards from the terminus. Mr T S Steel was called to Rive evidence and he sai he was a former member of the Warrington Tow()

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 8, 1913,
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 8, 1913,

Council and had been a member of the Tramways Com- mittee for five years. He bad known Horton, as a very straightforward honest and reliable man. The prisoner did not explain himself in the Police Court because of an intimation that a prima facie case had been made out He had seen passengers pick up tickets from the seats which they had thought were the tickets which had bean issued to them.

div.head: COMMITTEE NOT CONSULTED.
div.p: COMMITTEE NOT CONSULTED.

- - - - Councillor George Archer, a member of the Warring- Town Council and on the Tramways Committee said he had not been consulted about that particular prosecu- tion and neither had the Tramways Committee so far as he knew. To his knowledge the Tramwa3s Committee had not instructed that prosecution. Edwin Plinston, Insurance Inspector and secretary of the Tramways Union, also gave evidence. Mr Madden in his statement to the jury said that the witness Pendleton would net admit that Davenport passed him time after time when he had made the same mistake or irregularity of that kind and Davenport said he did. He might have called half the conductors in Warrington if it were not for disturbing the traffic and they would all tell the same tale that the wretched regulatl'on of 200 yards was a rule honoured more in the breach than in the observance. It was an impossible regulation as a great number of those regulations were impossible. There was no touch of humanity about those rules. There was no provision of time for the man who left his home in the early dawn to get his food. Work all hours, get your meals when you can— throw a bone to a dog—you are only working men, you are only a conductor, only so and so, get your meals when you can, and the public must be looked after. It is in keeping with the electric cars— all to be done on the rush. The man Horton, had passed Thewlis-street and thought he would snatch part of his meal. As set down in the Corporation rules, the position to be observed by the conductor was something like a Gilbertian opera. When he said it was a miserable charge to bring against the prisoner he did not say that there was not a big prin- ciple behind the charge. He did not for a moment contend that it was not a serious thing for a tram conductor were he found and caught in the act of issuing a ticket twice and keeping the penny for himself. It would Le a reasonable assumption if be was caught doing that once that it was part of a system. Such was not the case they were trying. The Corporation was so irregular in what it did that they could not pro- duce the tickets which were such important evidence. Did not the jury think that the prisoner should have been given an opportunity of explaining himself. They set a trap, the reason for setting which had not come out that day. Whether there was any underhanded robbery going on amongst conductors he could not say, but the Corporation started out with a ready made plan. It was never intended to give Horton an opportunity of explaining himself. They sent two detectives up to arrest him. That was all part of the pin pricking plan. He was not to be given a chance to explain himself. Tram tickets were like leaves and were found in all sorts of places. It was not impossible for the woman to have picked another ticket up. Mr Madden then emphasised the fact that the evidence he had called showed that the prisoner bore an exceptionally good character. Horton ,had admitted that it was an irregularity but he did not think it was a criminal offence. If he thought he would have had his character tested he would have searched the car and examined every ticket religiously and probably would have found 0U0385. Horton distinctly said he issued a new ticket to the woman, Ellis, and no doubt the other ticket was blowing about the streets yet. In conclusion Mr Madden pleaded in most eloquent terms for the prisoners discharge and said that if there was any doubt they ought to give the prisoner the benefit of it. The man had an exceptionally good character and they should take that into account. Mr Wooll said the defence of the prisoner was not that usually put forward for innocent men. They taxed a witness's character and slung mud at the Cor- poration. The prisoner was not charged with breaking regulations of the Corporation but with embezzle- ment. The Criminal Courts would not allow singula. cases of a meritorious nature being called in as evidence on behalf of a prisoner. They could find cases of the most confirmed criminals doing acts of kindness It was not right that witnesses should have been called to prove that the man had given milk to a cat or a penny to a beggar. Those were singular cases but did not affect the present case at all. The Corporation had not the least prejudice against the prisoner and had the least desire to hound him into gaol. They had one desire, to protect the interests of the ratepayers for whom they were trustees. The case for the defence in regard to the tickets was one long tissue of extra- ordinary things. The jury found the prisoner not guilty and he was discharged.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

TRANSPORTER BRIDGE FATALITY. BRAVE EFFORT THAT FAILED. At Widnes on Monday, the Deputy Coroner, Mr F A Jones, held an inquest on William Porritt, who fell from the 100 feet span on the Widnes Transporter Bridge, and was drowned. Robert Connor, who was working on the bridge at the time of the accident, said when Porritt came to the surface of the water he appeared to be stunned, but later commenced to swim. A strong ebb tide was running at the time, and he' (Connor) shouted to Porritt to swim to the buttresses of the old bridge. Porritt made a brave effort to reach the buttresses, but failed to do so by about three feet, and then disappeared from sight. In reply to the coroner witness said the scaffolding boards were perfectly dry, and were composed of 9 by 3 inch timber. He considered nets and handrails would be most inconvenient and useless for that par- ticular class of work. A verdict of" Accidental death" was returned the jury suggesting that it was necessary that a boat shouid us kept near to the approach during tide time.

RUNCORN DRINK LICENCES. TWO REFERRED FOR COMPENSATION. The adjourned annual licensing sessions for Runcorn were held on Monday, Mr F Norman presiding. The renewal of the licences—the Moulders' Arms, Mill-brow; Queen's Head Vaults, High-street ; and the Forester's Arms, Canal-street—u ere objected to by the police. With regard to the Moulder's Arms, Superin- tendent Ennion said the house was licensed prior to 1869. It was a beerhouse situated in a working-class neighbourhood. The plaster was falling off the bedroom walls, and the licensee's wife said : "If you only look at it it falls off" (laughter). There were three fully licensed houses within a circle of 200 yards, and he con- sidered that if this licence was taken away there would still be sufficient to meet the requirements of the neighbourhood In answer to Mr Knowles, Widnes, who appeared for the owners, witness said he would be surprised if the house was selling per annum 160 barrels, and 882 dozen of bottled stuff. It had always been well conducted. Mr Knowles submitted that a house doing such a business could not be considered redundent. With regard to the Queen's Head, Superintendent Ennion said this house was also licenced prior to 1869. It was a poor house, frequented by a few young men and young women. There were five licensed houses within a radius of 200 3ards. In reply to Mr Knowles, witness said this licence was considered by Quarter Sessions last year, and renewed. Superintendent Ennion said the Forester's Arms was situated in a working-class neighbourhood, and was the property of Messrs Greenall, Whitley, and Company. Intreply to Mr Greaves Lord (instructed by Mr J W Knowles), who appeared for the owners, witness said he was not aware that the house was selling over 200 barrels a year. The licence of the Forester's Arms was renewed, and those of the Queen's Head Vaults and the Moulder's Arms referred.

WIDNES LIBERAL CAMPAIGN. MR. J. B. MARTINDALE AND THE CONSCRIPTIONIST AGITATION. Mr. J. B. Martindale, the prospective Liberal candi- date for the Widnes Division addressed Ward meetings in Farnworth North and South on Monday evening, and was received enthusiastically. Speaking at Farnworth South meeting Mr Martindale remarked that the Tories said that the Liberals had been working too hard during the cast seven years. But, as a democratic party, be could assure them they were going to work still harder in the future for the benefit of the great masses of people of this country. The people were very much better off to-day than they were seven years ago. Even to the smallest hamlet in the country they could observe striking examp:es of the good accomplished by Liberal legislation. There was also a great decrease in pauperism in the country during
