div.head: DISTRICT NEWS. LYMM.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS. LYMM.

HOSPITAL S UND A Y.—ln connection with Hospital Sunday, services were held in Lymm Parish Church last Sunday when the preacher in the morning was the Rector, the Rev G B Thurston, M.A. The evening sermon was delivered by the Rev and Hen C F Cross, Vicar of Stretton. The offertories throughout the day which amounted to £l5 9s.7d.,were devoted to the funds of the Warrington Infirmary. SHOP ASSISTANTS VISIT THE " SOAPE It Y."—On Wednesday afternoon about forty members and friends of the Lymm Branch of the National Amalgamated Union of Shop Assistants, Warehousemen and Clerks went to Warrington, where they were conducted over the extensive soap works of Messrs Joseph Crosfleld and Sons Ltd. Many expressions of approval for an enjoyable and instructive visit were recorded. COUNTY COUNCIL LECTURES.—TweIve months ago the Cheshire County Council kindly provided the local poultry fanciers with well-delivered lectures by Mr H Paget Easten. This time they are giving gardening enthusiasts a turn by sending Mr R G James of the Holmes Chapel College, to give a series of lectures on horticulture. At a gathering last night in the Girls' Schoolroom, Pepper-street, Mr James spoke on" The propagation, pruning, and management of bush fruits." His subject for next Friday is " The culture of apples, and pears." DIED ON THE WA Y TO WORK.—Shortly before 6.30 last Tuesday morning, Mr John Eaton of Rush Green, an employee of Messrs Charles Moore and Co, Ltd, was hurrying to his work when he felt a rather sharp pain in his side. As he was approaching the railway crossing he was overtaken by a fellow workman who offered assistance. He had not helped Mr Eaton many moments when the latter collapsed in his arms. The doctor was immediately sent for but on arrival pronounced life to be extinct. Mr Eaton, who was sixty-nine years of age, was a Latchford man but lived with his daughter at Rush Green, and was quite well when he set out to go to work. He Was highly respected by all who knew him. The inquest was held at the Lymm Police Station on Wednesday, when the coroner Mr T J Ridgway, returned a verdict of death from natural causes. ENTERTAINMENT AT BROOM ED G E.—On Tuesday night the workers and scholars of Broom Edge Primi- tive Methodist Sunday school held a successful enter- tainment. The assembly was formally opened by the Rev RW B Whiteway with a hymn and prayer, after which a miscellaneous programme was entered npon. Recitations by Miss Amy Brazendale, Joe Blease and J Gibbs were well applauded, as were the solos by the Misses Lucy Leigh and Eva Perrin—" Grandmother's Dream " ; and Jennie Reed, "Roses underneath the snow." Action songs, "House Mairis " and " Pina- fores " (the latter being encored) were given by the Misses Bessie Brazendale, Nora Brazendale, Dolly Chorlton, Ethel Cowap, Bessie Gibbs, Annie Moss and Elsie Scott. Perhaps the main item of the evening was the amusing dialogue "Honesty is the Best Policy," in which the respective parts were well sustained by the Misses Jane Blease, Amy Brazendale, Lilian Chorlton Jennie Reed and Mr John Hayes. Two shorter dialogues were" Selfishness," performed by the Misses Mary Blease, Lucy Leigh ann Mr J Perrin ; and " A lesson in charity," contributed by the Misses Mary Moss, Gertie Talbot, and Mr John Hayes. Further variety was afforded by Mr Perrin's humorous reading " The butcher's daughter," and the gramaphone selections provided by Mr A Champ. The duties of alcompanists were ably performed by Miss M Champ and Mr A Champ, who also contributed a pianoforte duet. On the motion of the Rev R W B Whiteway a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the workers and the Chairman (Mr A B Edwards). FORTHCOMING ELECTIONS.—AIong with the march of time and the signs of another Spring, comes the signal that the Lymm elections are drawing near. In fact in the case of the County Council Election it is a thing of the past for though to-day was the date set apart for the contest no poll will take place, as the popular retiring member, Mr Samuel Walker Gould, J.P., of Bridge House, Oughtrington, has been declared by the deputy-returning officer, Mr W Mullard, as returned unopposed. Mr Gould now represents the wide- spreading district composed of the parishes of Lymm, High Legb, Agden, Bollington, Millington Rostherne, Ashley, Warburton, and Partington, The statutory notices in connection with the Bucklow Union Election of Guardians, and the Lymm Urban District Council Election of Councillors have been published this week. Nominations for both elections can be handed in to Mr W Mullard, the returning officer, up to 12 o'clock noon on Thursday, March 13th. Should any candidate nominated for election wish to withdraw his candidature, he may do so before 12 o'clock noon on Tuesday, March 18th. The polling for both elections is to take place on Saturday, April sth, 1913. The retiring members of the Board of Guardians are Messrs S Davies and S W Gould, J.P. In connection with the Urban District Council there will be opportunities for five contesta caused by the following retirments :—Booth's Hill WsrA, I,Mr W G Groves, J.P. ; Heatley Ward, Mr S Davies; Lvmm Ward, Rev G B Thurston, M.A. ; and Statham Ward, Mr F Lockyer. There will also be the election of a second representative for Statham Ward in accordance with the recent County Council grant.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PRESENTATION TO MR. W. W. SRA W.—An interesting event, surrounded with rathor sad circumstances, took place on Friday, February 28th, in the afternoon at the Council Sono°ls. Mr Shaw, having for some years now been assistant schoolmaster at the above school, has unfortunately had to relinquish his post owing to ill-health. He has won the appreciation both of the teachers and scholars and they felt they would like to give him some small momento on leaving. The presenta- tion cook the form of a gold-mounted umbrella and silvermounted walking stick, both suitabably inscribed. The gathering took place in the large schoolroom, when a large number of scholars were present. Supporting the teachers were Dr Murray (manager), who presided, Mrs Murray and Mr E Foster.—A letter was received from Mr .1 G Withinshaw, regretting his inability to attend, and wishing Mr Shaw happiness and health in his retirement.—Mr Griffiths, the headmaster, paid a warm tribute to Mr Shaw's work in the school, also to his sociability with his colleagues and expressed his regrets on behalf of himself, teachers and scholars at the cause of Mr Shaw's retirement. The Chairman, as manager, also spoke words of appreciation and hoped the scholars would remember in after years what Mr Shaw had taught them in the school. Mr Shaw suitably replied and encouraged the scholars to learn all they could. The scholars right heartily applauded Mr Sha w several times, also all those who took part in the proceedings.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A COLLIER'S SWINDLE.

At St. Helens on Monday, William Bevan, collier, 16 Emily-street, Thatto Heath, was charged with obtain- ing 9d by Wee pretences. Mr Kelly prosecuted for William Jessop, a collier, employed at the St Helens Collieries, and explained that it was a case in which Bevan, who worked in the mine not far from Jessop, changed the tally on a full box of coal, and so was credited with having worked this coal, and was paid for it. The colliers as a body behaved very honestly and straightforwardly to their mates, but the Cheokweigh Society knew that, unfortunately, there were a few black sheep in the pits, and they alleged that accused was one. Accused, who protested his innocence, was convicted of attempting to obtain 9d by fraud, and was tined £lO and costs, or two months. sr. HELENS FINANCES.

CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT TO INVESTIGATE The St Helens Corporation Finance Committee has decided to engage a Liverpool chartered accountant to investigate the books of the Corporation, the methods of keeping the acoountr, cash, and stores, &c. The committee has balances in hand amounting to £2,542 on loans borrowed from time to time for tram- way and other purposes, and has decided to pay the amounts into the sinking fund of the accounts concerned. The Local Government Board states that the total amount of the capital grant available to the Council based on population is £2,916, for the purposes of deal- ing with tuberculosis under the Insurance Act.

div.head: Buckley-street Sunday School.
div.p: Buckley-street Sunday School.

A free tea party was given to the children on Satur- day, when 350 scholars sat down for tea. A very enjoyable time was spent. After tea a short con- cert was given which was very much appreciated by the children. Great credit is due to the teacher's for the manner in which they catered and arranged the pro- ceedings. The evening's enjoyment closed by singing the doxology. As the children left the school to go home each child was given an orange.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

Pteaching on Sunday evening last from the prophecy of Zaahariala concerning the day, the light of which as neither clear nor dark, the Rev W Reid stated that the description corresponded with to-day's experience of life. Both in the inward hidden life and in its outward expression, there was very much which was not light. neither was it quite dark. Around Holy Scripture, and especially around the Person of Jesus, and His work of atonement, had criticism waged its controversies, and still continued to do so. The evacuation of interpreta- tions previously held proved how far from clear was the light, and yet the power of Scripture, and the Christ it presented in the life of to-day, proved that it was not dark. This sense of twilight might be said also to pervade the work of the Church. Her work at home, in regard to the circumscribed area that it vitally touched, abroad likewise, owing to the scarcity of men and burden of debt, showed how tar from clear was the light, but on the other hand many tokens proved that I the day was not altogether dark.

div.head: Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.
div.p: Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.

In connection with the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, the married women's quarterly effort, which took the form of a tea and meeting, was held in the school-room on Thursday. Preaching in the afternoon on "The plea for the sacrificial life," the Rev .1 Bradbury (Blackpool), dealt with the thought that Christianity was pre-eminently the religion of the print of the nails and its distinctive note was redemp- tion. Christ was the eternal Saviour and the sacrifice of God was an everlasting one. That was the (Bs- ' tinguishing mark of Christianity from all the other religions of the world. The second thought was that the universal test for discipleship was that it should bear the print of the nails. It was the one test Christ always put ; it was the test that the world still put to the Church and it was the test which every Christian should put to himself—was he swayed by the sacrificial spirit. rhe last thought was that the bearing of Vile print of the nails was the secret of the world's conquest The day had gone, hen there would ever be a response from the best soul of the church to a selfish religion.— The tea was greatly enjoyed and at the evening meeting Mr G Faulkner presided. The Rev. Bradbury gave an interesting discourse on "Frank Crossley, the merchant saint." The meetings were greatly enjoyed.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. " Self – Denial."
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. " Self - Denial."

The service on Sunday evening was conducted by the Rev H Williamson, 8.A., who spoke on " Self-denial." To some people, he said, Lent appears to be a period of something less than joy and gladness—a time when they must give up certain luxuries and pleasures. It is their belief that Christ expressly commanded such a course, and because of this view their conduct is com- mendable. But such a line of action does not harmonise with the character of Jesus Himself as the Gospels reveal it. The Jews called him a gluttonous man and a wine-bibber. He could attend and even enjoy a marriage feast, and Ile showed little respect for the laws about fasting. Then what did Christ mean by self-denial. To deny oneself is not to deny something to oneself. Peter denied Christ. That is to say Peter ignored Elio; end treated Christ as though He did not exist. Similarly in self-denial the man must ignore himself by refusing to make himself the centre of his aims, thoughts and ideals. So Charles Lamb forgot his personal preferences when he undertook the guardianship of his sister Mary Lamb, giving up, as he did, literary companionships that appealed to him, as well as the thought of marriage. Lieutenant Oates, no doubt anxious to live, forgot self and went out into the solitude to save his companions. So it is seen that self-denial is something greater than the denying of oneself certain luxuries for a period of 40 days. It is the counting of oneself as a cipher, as a mere nothing. But self-denial is only a foundation and not a building. There must be present in the individual something which is to take possession of the empty space created by the self-abnegation. Lamb would have achieved nothing by tty)re self-denial. The love
for his sister ocC-up-ied the vacancy that self once filled. So in the Christian life, having

swept out self, we must make Christ the centre of our life. There is nothing forbidding in such a programme, for in reality it is a profound act of self assertion. In all of us there are two selves, one of these is in sympathy with the lower things of life, whilst the other self is in sympathy with the ideals and principles of Jesus Christ, and to deny oneself and follow Him is to say that the self which sympathises with Him is our real self, and that the lower self does not truly represent what we in heart are.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a good gathering on Sunday at an open meeting in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the Society. In the absence of Mr John Taylor the chair was taken by Mr Hedley Taylor who in a very appro- priate address upon the anniversary said the word was from the Latin -4nnus, a year, and Versus a turn. He took the seven year periods of a child's life :—Firat home life, second, school life, third, the period of development of character. He wished the society well in the 21st year. Rev T T James M.A. gave his pre- sidential address upon "The foundation which is Jean Christ." Wherever we went and wherever we looked, in art and literature we found under all, Christ. In music and painting Christ was the great theme ; the speaker's reference to Charrington' the converted brewer was very telling. He facrificed a tremendous fortune for the sake of Christ and man. The Brother- hood movement was founded upon Christ and their efforts must be for Him. The new president referred to the retiring president,Mr Farrar.He felt it was fitting at this time to acknowledge his earnest, continuous and faith- ful work in connection with that Brotherhood,and they hoped for many years of service from him. The Secre- tary read a letter received from the Secretary of Wycliffe Brotherhood, Sheffield, sending hearty greet- ings upon the 20th anniversary. They thought with loving memories of their late president amongst them ; and would be pleased to hear from time to time of the Warrington Society's work. Five new members received a hearty welcome. Votes of sympathy were passed with Mr Beddard, who had met with a severe accident and now lies in the Infirmary; to Mr Meachin on the death of his mother; and Mr Taylor, who was prevented attending the meeting in consequence of the fire at Stockton Heath. Mr F Fieldhouse sang two solos in a pleasing manner. Mr W Rutter rendered a cornet solo, " Largo," which was greatly enjoyed. Mr Payton, Mum. Bac., welded at the organ. Mr J W Travis read the lesson. Mr Farrar led the prayer. Unfermented Wine. Lancashire Church People's Movement.

There was a lively controversy in the Manchester diocese some time ago owing to the action of the Bishop (Dr Knox) in declining to sanction a Blackburn vicar (the Rev George Denyer) using unfermented wine at Holy Communion. On that occasion evidence was forthcoming from Mrs Lewis, a local temperance worker' ana others as to the lamentable results which follow the tasting of wine at Communion on the part of reclaimed persons who, once addicted to drink, had become total abstainers.

Tne Archbishop C-1-.170rk has now consented to receive a deputation on April Iltb, with a view to hearing their views on the optional or permissive use of unfermented grape-juice at the Lord's Table. Mr Denyer is taking an active interest in the movement, and is trying to obtain a representative assembly to wait on the Archbishop. Possibly no one could provide more concrete facts and losses than Mrs Lewis, who has conducted a special temperance mission in Blackburn for over twenty-flve years, and has been brought into close contact with many cases where the use of fermented wine at these services has aroused a dormant craving for strong drink.
For playing football on Sunday afternoon in a Kingston street, William Eveleigb, a local youth, was fined Ll and costs.

Licence of Waggon and Horses, Buttermarket- , street, to be surrendered. Licence of King's Arms, Battermarket-street, to te referred for compensation. Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay, to be rebuilt cn the q – opposite side of Liverpool-road. . . Licence of Railway Tavern, Factory-yard, to be . referred for compensation (on reduced terms). Off-licence at the corner of Powys-stieet and Baxter- • • , street, to be surrendered. • I Royal Arms, Bank-street, to be closed and ale-house licence transferred to the Old House at Home, Friars' • Green. The magistrates on the Bench were :—The Mayor (in tne chair), Aldermen BennettVames Evans and Pierpoint, Councillor Roberts, Messrs John Fairclough, S Wright, C Jackson Holmes, A J Jolley, W Roberts, W Furness, T Locker, J W Hayward, W Richardson, G Pilling, T Peruber ton and W T Williams. All thiS houses mentioned above belong to Messrs Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd. Mr Greaves Lord (instructed by Messrs Arthur Browne and ('o), on behalf of the firm, submitted that their scheme with regard to the rebuilding of the Britannia Inn, was a reasonable one. It was propose to surrender the licence of the Waggon and Horses In which, when the rebuilding had been carried out, woul be almost adjoining the Britannia Inn. Notice o objection had been served by the Chief Constable ur the licensee of the King's Arms and, if the pree application was granted, the firm proposed to a' that house to be referred for compensation, wit opposition. div.head: BREWERS' BARGAIN.
div.p: THE BREWERS' BARGAIN.
FIVE LICENCES ABOLISHED AND TWO HOUSES REBUILT. Temperance League's Opposition.

As the result of an arrangement which received the approval of the justices at the Warrington adjourned Licensing Sessions yesterday, the following reductions of licences and rebuilding of houses are to take place : Britannia Inn, Butterruarket-street, to be rebuilt. Licence of Waggon and Horses, Buttermarket- street, to be surrendered. Licence of King's Arms, Battermarket-street, to te referred for compensation. Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay, to be rebuilt cn the opposite side of Liverpool-road. Licence of Railway Tavern, Factory-yard, to be referred for compensation (on reduced terms). Off-licence at the corner of Powys-street and Baxter- street, to be surrendered. Royal Arms, Bank-street, to be closed and ale-house licence transferred to the Old House at Home, Friars' Green. The magistrates on the Bench were :—The Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen BennettVames Evans and Pierpoint, Councillor Roberts, Messrs John Fairclough, S Wright, C Jackson Holmes, A J Jolley, W Roberts, W Furness, T Locker, J W Hayward, W Richardson, G Pilling, T Perubei ton and W T Williams. All thiS houses mentioned above belong to Messrs Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd. Mr Greaves Lord (instructed by Messrs Arthur Browne and ('o), on behalf of the firm, submitted that their scheme with regard to the rebuilding of the Britannia Inn, wss a reasonable one. It was propose to surrender the licence of the Waggon and Horses In which, when the rebuilding had been carried out, would be almost adjoining the Britannia Inn. Notice of objection had been served by the Chief Constable upon the licensee of the King's Arms and, if the present application was granted, the firm proposed to allow that house to be referred for compensation, without opposition. Undoubtedly the alteration of the Britannia Inn would be some improvement to the road frontage and the licences would now be concentrated in one house instead of in three. A DANGEROUS CORNER. Mr Greaves Lord, in mtkiug the application for the rebuilding and removal of toe Bowling Green Inn, Liverpool-road, said the house stood at a dangerous corner and he was told that since the last annual licensing sessions no fewer than six accidents had occurred there, owing to the great difficulty ini manipulating traffic. Two had happened within the last fortnight. From the public point of view, it was eminently desirable that there should be a stringent alteration in the position of affairs. The house presented a curiosity in licensing matters, inasmuch as the premises occupied two sides of the roadway. Arrangements had been made to dispose of the land on which the inn sow stood. Part of it would go to Messrs Crosfield whose works practically shut in the place on every side except that facing the roadway, and the other portion would go to the Corporation for the purpose of making a reasonably safe corner. The inn would be re-built on the opposite side of the road, the firm having, at con- siderable cost, obtained the cottages at the corner of Powys-street and Liverpool-road. The new house would be in immediate connection with the bowling green which was part of the licensed premises. If the scheme were approved the firm proposed to surrender, at the end of two years, the off-licence at the corner of Powys-street and 13-ixter-street, which was of some considerable value. Notice of objection had been served with regard to the Railway Tavern and the firm proposed to consent to its being referred, the compens- ation payable to be £l,OOO less than the sum agreed npon as reasonable by the Bench or the Inland Revenue Commissioners.

REMOVAL OBJECTED TO. Mr Lord next applied for the removal of the ale- house licence to the Royal Arms, Bank-street, to the Old House at Home, Friars' lireou. The Warrington Corporation had given notice to treat, with a view to acquiring the Royal Arms for the purpose of improv- ing the narrow roadway leading out of one street into a much broader street. If the scheme for removal were sanctioned, it would mean that the Corporation would be treating simply for an ordinary dwelling house and not, as now, for licensed premises with the value which attached to them. It v.its proposed that the Old House at Home should be so altered and reconstructed as to make it commensurate with the class of trade which would be attracted when it became a full ale-house licence. The Chief Constable said the police did not oppose any of the applications. Their only regret was that an application similar to the last one was not made more frequently. They would be pleased to have two or three a year. (Laughter.) The Rev W Cooper objected to the transfer, first as a citizen of St Austin's Ward and secondly on behalf of the Warrington Band of Hope Union and the Wart ing- ton Citizens' remperance League. Previous attempts had been made to secure a wine and spirit licence for the Oki House at Home. Mr Browne: Nothing of the kind. The Magistrates' Clerk : There have not been within my knowledge. The Mayor: That objecticn evidently falls to the ground. The Rev W Cooper: Then I withdraw it. Continu- ing the rev gentleman contended that it was a most undesirable neighbourhood for a wine and spirit licence as there were so many lodging houses in the vicinity. The existing facilities were ample,for between Itylands. street and Bridge Foot there were seven fully-licensed houses. Rougly speaking, they would be within 250 yards of the Old House at Home. Moreover the Hippodrome and the Royal Court Theatre had each three full-licensed bars. It had been contended that the transfer would materially facilitate a street improve- ment but, on the other hand, the °position suurnitted that the Royal Arms was now at its minimum surrender value whereas, if it were removed, a considerably enhanced price might have to be paid for it at a later date. Mr Greaves Lord said it was quite obvious that Mr Cooper was speaking without any information as to the condition of affairs. He (Mr Lord) was instructed to give an absolute denial of his statement with regard to the Royal Arms. It was a very good and valuable house. Mr W Roberts : You don't mean to Bay that the Royal Arms is as good a house to-day as it was prior to the removal of the County Court. Mr Lord : My experience is that the proximity of a County Court hss very little intkence on the business of a public house. In reply to the Mayor, Mr Lord said the firm con- sidered the house to be in average condition. THE POLICY OF THE BElsiurf. The Mayor, in announcing the decision of the Bench, said they thought it was their duty to the public to declare their policy, which they believed was a very sound one. The policy adopted had been diminution, as far as it could legtimately be carried out,of licences, especially in the cases of houses which were old and badly constructed, and the substitution of better adapted premises. With that object in view, the Bench had decided to grant the present application. They wished to point out that the effect would be that five licences would be abolished, two with and three with.rut compensation,while the compensation in one case was to be .£l,ouo less than the amount agreed upon by the authorities. Under all the circumstances, he would say to Mr COoper that, although the decision in one case might disappoint him, the position and policy on the whole, must be satisfactory to the town in general and to the cause which he advocated. The Bench were perfectly unanimous in their decision and in the sentiments %hich he (the Mayor) had voiced. They made it a condition of the rebuilding of the Bowling Green Inn that the abolition of the off-licence in Powys-street should be simultansous with the com- pletion of the new inn. Mr Lord : We will give that unflertaking. BILLIARDS LICENCE REFUSED. The Bench refused an application by Mr Amos (Messrs Robert Davies and Co.) on behalf of Mr John D Horan, of Preston, for a billiards licence for the old music hall, Market Place.

div.head: GUARDIANS' ELECTIONS.
div.p: GUARDIANS' ELECTIONS.

Up to the present very little interest is being shown in the triennial election of members of the Warrington Board of Guardians which will take place on Monday, April 7th. Nominations must be handed in not later than 12 o'clock noon, on Thursday next, at the office of Mr Arthur Bottotnley, clerk to the Board, 12, Bewsey-street. Any candidate nominated for election may withdraw his candidature not later than 12 noon, on Tuesday, March 181. So far there appears to be small prospect of exciting contests, the only Warrington Ward in which a fight is at present assured being Orford Ward, Here the retiring member (Mr J A Rnshworth) is to be opposed by Mr Francis M McKinley, 208, Orford-lane, (insurance superintendent). A third candid at 3 is spoken of, in the person of Mr E Horrocks, a Labour man. In the country parishes the office of Rural District Councillor is associated with that of Guardian. We hear that Mr E England has consented to seek the suffrages of the electors of Poulton-with-Fearnhead, in opposition to the retiring member (Mr G Mather.)

Royal Theatre of Varieties. "Life's Darkest Hour," is the title of a bighl:- sensational drama written by Mr Manville Morton, the new manager of the Royal Theatre of Varieties, which has been successfully presented during the week by the " Royal" Stock Co. Each artiste acquits himself or herself in a creditable manner and the play is well enacted.—Next week the " Royal " Stock Co. will appear in a drama" Every Inch a Man."

div.head: itxaminer, Saturday, March 8, 1913.
div.p: The itxaminer, Saturday, March 8, 1913.
MR. BOTTOMLEY AND THE PARISH COUNCIL.

Mr Bottomley is naturally indignant at the inexplic- able supineness of the village authorities in neglect- ing to provide proper means of giving an alarm of file. The misleading notice in Victoria-square, directing people to ring a bell which is not there, was his chief ground for criticism and complaint, in the course of a chat with a representative of the " Examiner" on Thursday. Asked for an expression of opinion on the arrange- ments existing in Stockton Heath to cope with out- breaks of fire, Mr Bottomley said: "The reason I rushed down to Victoria-square, was because Iliad seen daily, a notice to this effect: 'ln case of fire ring the bell which hangs at the corner of the Police Station.' After going to Mr Taylor's house for the purpose of telephoning to the station, and Miss Taylor having promised to send the message for me, the first thought which came into my mind was as to the notice which I had so often seen. I hurried off, with a view to ringing the bell, but found to my dismay, that DO such bell existed at the place indicated. Consequently I lost ten minutes of very valuable time—so valuable, in fact, that I am satisfied I could have got the whole of the furniture out of one of the bedrooms, which con- tained all the wearing apparel,bad I not been engaged in this futile errand. "I have since been informed that the bell is not in the place indicated on the notice board, simply because no definite understanding had been arrived at with the police authorities. But that, in my opinion, is no excuse whatever. The members of the Parish Council knew full well that the bell was not hung, and I say it was their duty to take away that notice and replace it with another informing residents that, for the time being the bell was not available at the police station—in fact it would have been far better to have removed the notice altogether. As it stands at pre- sent, it is altogether misleading, and, had there been a notice which told the truth—or no notice at all—l should never have gone down to Victoria Square to give he alarm. .` I have every praise for Mr Mclntyre for the great kindness he extended to me. He personally has nothing whatever to do with the bell question, and I shall never:forget his considerateness towards me from the moment he heard of the catastrophe. "What makes the position more extraordinary is that, after the disclnsures of this week, the notice is still there. I am surprised that some member of the Parish Council has not thought what a ridiculous position that body was liable to find itself in, by allowing a notice to be exhibited, the contents of which they knew to be absolutely misleading. It passes my comprehension why some action was not taken the moment the bell, which was hung on the old police station, was removed."

div.head: PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE IN TROUBLE. The Why and Wherefore of the Silent Bell.
div.p: PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE IN TROUBLE. The Why and Wherefore of the Silent Bell.

As a sequel to the disaster, the fire brigade arrange- ments obtaining in the village were the subject of severe criticism in the district during the week-end. The question raised in all quarters was " Where was the alarm bell ?" There were only one or two people who really knew, and even some members of the Parochial Committee at the monthly meeting on Tues- day evening, had to ask where the bell was. Then came the answer from the Chairman of the Fire Appliances Committee : "It is in my charge, in the stable." The question which puzzled nearly the whole of Warrington was answered; the mystery was solved, Then came the next important query" Why, seeing that there was a box at the police station, was the bell lying useless in a stable ?" The County Council were blamed for that, and after a lengthy discussion it was decided again to approach that authority with a view to getting a bell fixed on the police station. This, coupled with another resolution that was passed, to the effect "that temporary arrangements be made .to put up the bell until it could be placed on the police station," looks uncommonly like "locking the stable dcor when the horse has been stolen." As to why this temporary arrangement was not made before, no answer was forthcoming. At the Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday, there were present : Messrs G Pilling (in the chair), J H Clarke, H J Westbrook, F Pearson, J Whitley, F Rose, C Hallows, W Mclntyre, J R Wood, J McDermid, G F Ashton (clerk), and S L Wright (surveyor.) One of the lengthiest discussions there has been for sroine time at a meeting of this body commenced on Mr W Mclntyre (chairman of the Fire Appliances Com- mittee and captain of the Fire Brigade) iaying before the committee a plan of the proposed standard for the fire bell. He stated that at the last meeting a eub- camrnittee was formed and they endeavoured to find a suitable central site for the erection of the bell. First of all it was thought to put it in the back passage leading to Gaskell-street, immediately to the rear of the police buildings. They considered that position not sufficiently to the front and ultimately decided on a site near the trolley pole attached to the shop of Mr Dutton, butcher, London-road, which would not only be central but prominent. Mr Mclntyre proceeded to refer to the disastrous fire on Sunday morning, and to explain why there was no alarm bell. Tee late Chief Constable gave them permission to erect a bell on the old Police Station, but ttey had failed to obtain the same privilege for the new building. They submitted a plan which they con- s'dered reasonable,and with fittings adequate to support a bell weighing about one cwt. This was not approved and they felt they could do nothing else but endeavour to look out for another site. Time had gone on and up to the present they had no alarm bell erected in the village. There was a s2heme, the plan of which he submitted that night, to erect the bell in London-road, and possibly they might approve of such a course being adopted. Of course it was very neces- sary that'they should have the bell erected, because as long as they had the apparatus they might as well make what use they could of it, With regard to the fire, he was informed of it at 3.15 a.rn.,end immediately after he heard the Warrington fire Lrigade pass. He quickly left the house for the scene of the fire, but on his arrival he saw there was no hope of saving anything. It was beyond all doubt that what- ever could have been done had been done. He did not think there would have been the slightest possibility of saving any more than had been saved. Three of the brigade men turned out, and some articles of furniture were saved even after the whole building was enveloped. There was no negligence or carelesine-s and nothing further could possibly have beendone.The whole question rested upon the point that they had no alarm bell. He understood Mr Bottomley came down the village to the Police Station. Naturally he saw the cupboard was there, and that was further evidence that the most suitable place for the erection of the Fell was the Police Station. Naturally, of course, everyone ran to the Police Station, when any- thing of that kind happened. He did not know whether they thought further representation should be made to the County Council for the bell to be erected there. There was evidence that Mr Bottomley, not knowing the district and not being fully acquainted with all the circumstances, immediately went to the Police Station and expected to fled the bell either on the station or somewhere near. He did not find it, so he telepto ned to ‘Varrington. The result was disastrous to him sod his next door neighbour. (Hear, hear). Mr Pear Eon had received a oommunicition from Mr Roger C Parr, their county councillor, who had requested him to read a resolution which was passed at the meeting of tne County Councii, that permission be I granted to the Stockton Heath Parish Council to fix a tire alarm bell in a certain position in the yard to the rear of the Police Station, provided that the Parish Council entered into an agreement securing to the county the payment of a nominal rent, and also guaranteeing till expenses incurred in connection with the erection and upkeep of the bell as the Chief Con- stable might consider necessary, and further, upon the condition that the existing bell could be removed to a position at the rear of the Police Station site. Mr Parr, their county councillor, had Informed him that both he and his tether were under the impression that that resolution had been carried out. They were unaware there was any dilliculty being put in the way of erecting the standard either for height or anything else.

Correspondence with the County Council was read by the Clerk in regard to the fixing of the bell. Mr Clarke said Mr Parr informed him that it was his own and his father's wish that the bell should be fixed on the building. If it had not been for the officiousness of the officials it would have been on the building. He suppobed the architect thought his handiwork would be disfigured by the bell being attached to the building. As a ratepayer and a county ratepayer be thought they would be right in expressing tbeir dissatisfaction with the treatment they had received from the County Council (Hear, hear.) They were responsible for the officials, and if they did not carry out what the ratepayers required it was time they dealt with the officials. Although they had another site for the bell, which would suit to a great degree, everyone would admit that the proper place was on the Police Station. (Hear, hear). Mr Whitley: I cannot understand how it was the officials could over-rule the decision of the County Council. I raise my protest against the ungentle- manly treatment we have received and I move-- Mr Mclntyre: I move that we bear in mind this disaster and that we appeal to the County Council for permission to erect this bell and attach it to the police station. Mr Whitley: I second that. At the same time we have every sympathy with Mr Bottomley, Mr Mills and the owners of the property. (Hear, hear.) It was a

serious and disastrous fire and it is very unfair to the ratepayers of the village that this committee should have been placed in the position they were by the County Council. Mr 3 Hallows : I move that the bell he fixed at once in the place decided upon. If we approach the County Council more time will he wasted.
Mr Westbrook : Can the bell be temporarily fixed Where is the bell ?

The Clerk : It is in the charge of Mr Mclntyre. Mr Westbrook : Under the bed or where? (Laughter.) Mr Mclntyre : It is in the stable. Mr Wood : What is the objection to the standard being erected in the Police Station yard? The Chairman : It was said the height wes ridiculous Mr Wood : And what height will this be? The C airman : Eighteen feet. Mr Wood : Is that the principal abjection? The Chairman: They have not given us any assist- ance whatever. Mr Westbrook T Why do they object to it being fixed to the now police station wuen it was fixed on the old one? I wish to make it clear that our officials on the County Council have done nothing but their duty. Tb3y told him that when they got to Chester or Crewe they were only two out or so many who were probably not so sympathetic as they ought to be, and they were out-voted. Supposing there had been a boll there and the brigade had been called out would they have been of any assistance? Mr Ntclntyre : I cannot think so. Mr Westbrook said it was a strange thing the Wilderspool brigade were not called out. Mr Pearson : Mr Taylor attempted to get the te sI Wllderspool brigade Ly telepherA I-. • „° no It was quite necessary that sor brigade houdbe there as two pairs of houees,one on eau,. ueen burned down.

Mr SMlestbrook : The police station is paid for by the ratepayers and I think we might hold our,rneetings in it. It seemed to him that one policeman might be told off to ring the bell when necesEary. Mr Mclntyre : We are going to have three more. Mr Pearson : There were none in at the time of the fire. None on the ptemises. Mr .1 Hallows : I agree that the best place for the bell is the police station. I suggest that Mr Mclntyre make his proposition read that the hell he fixed there for the present. They could then wait until they met the County Council. Mr Pearson : We have lost six months already and we cannot wait another six months. Alr Mclntyre's resolution " That we apply to the County Council for permiEsion to put the bell on the police building " wigs unanimously carried. A resolution proposed by Mr J Hallows,and seconded by Mr Westbrook, that temporary arrangements be made to put up the bell until it could be placed on the Police Station, was also carried. Mr Westbrook asked if the brigade had had any practices lately ? Mr C Hallows : Two years ago. Mr Whitley : Is the apparatus in working order ? Mr Wood : There has been no fire practice for two years. It is the duty of the Chairman of the Fire Appliances Committee to call the men out for practice. Mr Wood was continuing when two members said he was out of order. Mr Wood : I appeal to you, Mr Chairman. Am I not in order. 1 The Chairman : Hardly, but go on. Mr Wood : There ought to have been practices. Mr Westbrook : I think we ought to take care we are not suddenly interested in this matter now the elections are coming on. Mr C Hallows said the matter had been mentioned at previous meetings. They had always been ready to attend the meetings of the Fire Appliances Committee if tbey had been called. The discubsion then terminated.

div.head: STOCKTO)I HEATH'S RECORD FIRE
div.p: STOCKTO)I HEATH'S RECORD FIRE
TWO VILLAS GUTTED.
A VIEW OF THE GUTTED VILLAS

A disastrous fire, attended with exciting scenes occurred at Stockton Heath in the early hours of Sunday morning, one semi-detached villa being com- pletely gutted, and the upper part of the adjoining residence destroyed. The original scene of the out- break was the villa, Ballantrae, Grappeuhall-road, in the occupation of Mr. Arthur Bottomley, clerk to the Warrington Board of Guardians. It appears that Mr. Bottoml,7 had stayed in the dining-room reading until 1.15 in the morning, and when be retired to rest the fire in the grate had died out. At 2.55 he was awakened by his wife, who told him she had been aroused by a noise downstairs. Immediately there was a loud crash and, thinking that burglars were in the house,Mr Bottomley prepared to investigate. On opening the bedroom door, he was met by an inrush of dense smoke. lira Bottomley at once rushed downstairs while het husband, with considerable difficulty, rescued their son Alan, aged ten years, from an adjoining bedroom. He got the boy in his arms but, owing to the blinding smoke, father and son were in such a dazed condition that they were in imminent peril until Mrs Bottomley returned and taking her husband by the arm, guided _ .

him below and safely into the roadway. So rapidly had the fire been gaining, that the family had to make their escape, clad only in night attire. Tbe house was heavily timbered and, fanned by a southerly gale, the flames soon had a strong hold on the building. The alarm was given to Mr John Taylor, who resides in the next house, and from his residence immediate efforts were made to telephone to the Warrington Fire Station. Fifteen minutes, however, elapsed before the brigade could be communicated with. in the meantime Mr Bottornley, deceived by the obsolete notice be had so often seen in Victoria-square, had rushed barefooted to the Stockton Heath Police Station, with a view to ringing the bell which—so the legend ran—was to be found at the corner of the build- ing. To his consternation, however, the visit was futile, for, since the erection of the new police station, the bell has not been re-hung and at present reposes in a stable. Returning to his home, Mr Bottomley
Mr. A. Bottomley's Heavy Loss.

div.head: -MR. BOTTOMLEY'S TO THE LEFT.
div.p: -MR. BOTTOMLEY'S TO THE LEFT.

entered the drawing room, by means of the window, and, with the help of a few residents, succeeded in saving a piano and other valuable effects. On receiving a telephonic summons the Warrington Fire Brigade promptly turned out, under the command of Deputy-Snperintendent Turner. When t'Aey arrived lt Stockton Heath, however, Mr Bottomley's house was burning fiercely from top to bottom, the roof having already collapsed. In spite of the strenuous work of the brigade and a plentiful supply *f water, the flames travelled to the adjoining villa, tenanted by Mr Thomas F Mills. Mrs Mills awoke shortly after three o'clock and, seeing the reflection of fire in front of the house, gave an alarm to the house- hold. Mr and Mrs Mills and their children—Arline (14), and Clifford (6) —very lightly clad, quickly escaped to a place of safety. Before the brigade could get the fire in hand, great havoc had been wrought. Mr Bottomley's villa, with the greater part of its contents, was c( mpletely burnt, out, only the baro walls remaining. Furniture jewellery and clothing alike fell a prey to the flames, the valuables destroyed including the Warrington Academy Golf Cup,which Mr Buttomley recently won, and a presentation gold chain and marble clock. Mr Bottcruley succeeded in saving the replica of the cup with which he was presentea. Mr Bottomley's loss, which is not covered by insurance, amounts to upwards of :F.600. The upper portion of the house of Mr Mills was gutted, but the firemen succeeded in saving the lower rooms, although the furniture was damaged by water and fallinp debris. Mr Mills, who fartunately saved a considerable portion of his furniture, sustained damage to the extent of £2OO. He was, however, fully insured. The origin of the fire, which began in the dining- room, is a complete mystery, in view of Mr. Bottonaley's conviction that there were neither fire in the grate nor matches in the room when he retired to rest. The causes suggested are that the fire is the work of a burglar or incendiary, or that burning soot had accumulated in the chimney and been blowp on to the carpet.

div.head: Photo Bi 4 rrett. STOCKTON HEATH "FIRE STA TION " AND (inEet) THE FAMOUS ALARM-BELL NOTICE.
div.p: Photo Bi 4 rrett. STOCKTON HEATH "FIRE STA TION " AND (inEet) THE FAMOUS ALARM-BELL NOTICE.

So much comment having been aroused in Stockton Heath by the revelations in regard to the missing fire bell, and the emphatic but useless notice with the injunction to ring the bell in case of fire, a representa- tive of the " Fxaminer " took the opportunity this week of having a quiet chat with a respected member of the village fire brigade, who proved to he not at all shy in expressing candid opinions on the state of the fire brigade and its uselessness in the recent crisis

For a couple of years or thereab,uts the inhabitants of Stockton Heath have been lulled into a feeling of security by the following striking notice which appears conspicuously on a board attached to a wooden building which has been specially erected t.) house the fire appliances of the local auttiority:—
"IN CASE OF FIRE RING BELL WHICH HANGS AT CORNER OF POLICE STATION."

In order that posterity may have a full and accurate conception of the means for dealing with conflagra- tions in the village in the year 1913 our representative took a passing snap-shot of the notice which says so very much but means so very little. The snapshot

appears herewith and ought uliimately to be enshrined among the archives of the embryo municipality on Warrington's southern border. I called on my fireman at a most opportune time, (says our representative,for he was discussing the recent disaster with a brigade colleague of his, when I entered. the workshop with a cheery "good afternoon." I had little difficulty in getting the sturdy fire-fighter to "talk,"for, like all the villagers he was full of the recent ctisis.

"What," I queried, "do you think of Sunday's fire?" to which he replied "It was most disastrous" I continued suppose you were there as a member of the brigade," and really I thought something was radically wrong with my informant when he received my natural question with boisterous laughter. " No," he laughed "I was not there." Why ! did you not receive any call? No, I did not get to know until ten o'clock on Sunday morning that there had been a fire, and then a tram conductor told me.

What was the signal of alarm prior to the building of the new police station ?—Oh ! we had a bell fixed there, but it had to be knocked with a clothes prop. Do you mean to say that since the bell has been off the police station you have not had any intimation from the Fire Appliances Committee as to what call you shall receive ?—None whatever, we have to rely on someone coming to the door and knocking us up. How many firemen are there in the village ?—Eight. How often do you practise ?—Again he laughed, as he informed me that they had not had a practice since the last fire in the village, nearly two years ago. "Two years ago," I exclaimed. "why that is ridiculous. How do they expect you to act then, in

case there is a fire? "—"lt may seem,and is ridiculous, but nevertheless such is the case. And," be added, " we have, at least I have not, got paid for the last fire, and we were there six hours and saved a great deal of the goods. As a result of the fire the damage was only .£5O. " If the bell was fixed and an alarm given, how soon do you think the men could be on the spot? - Oh, well within 15 minutes.

And have all your apparatus fixed ?—Yes, we could be playing em the fire in a quarter of an hour. Sure ?—Perfectly. Then, probably, if the bell had been fixed on Sunday morning and the alarm had been given, you could have rendered valuable service to Mr Bottomley and Mr 11 ?—Yes, a great deal could have been done and a lot of the furniture would have been saved. At least we could have held the flames in check until the arrival of the Warrington Brigade. How many men of your brigade rendered assist- ance on Sunday morning ?—Three, and they saved some of the furniture.
Are the appliances in working order ?—Well, they have not been used either for a fire or a practice for over sixteen months, so it is a great _question whether

the hose pipe would carry water. No.doubt if it were put down and tested, the water would probably burst through the sides rather than spurt out at the nozzle. If the thing is not used the elasticity goes out of it and it is then practically useless. Don't you think the bell ought to have been fixed, if only temporarily, on some prominent site ?—Most certainly. It is a gross case of neglect that some arrangement had not been made. Despite the fact that,as a member of the fire brigade, he would receive some of the ridicule which has been levelled at that organization, my informant displayed hi 4 loyalty to the Parish Council when he remarked " I am not going to find fault with anyone in regard to the bell not having been fixed somewhere, but I am going to find fault when I do not get paid for what I have done."

In conclusion the fireman tendered several sugges- tions, leading off with the one that the bell ought to be fixed on the police building and made part of it. In the event of that not being possible for the present he suggested fixing the bell on one of the Corporation standards in the square with an attachment no that any.one could ring it and with a list of the firemen and their addresses in a case. A fine could be imposed for misuse of the bell and a notice affixed to that effect. Then again there ought to be some mat k of distinction, a band on the arm or something very noticable, so that the firemen could exercise their authority at a fire. Now, people who did not know them, were rather inclined to treat them as interferers and meddlers. What was needed was more encouragement for the firemen, who gave their time willingly to practides, if they were called, and faced danger in the interests of the villagers.

MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. RYLANDS' RECS v. EGERTON. Rvlands' registered an easy victory at Gorsey-lane on Saturday, when Egerton were the visitors. In the first half the home team had to fmce the wind. ?lay was keen, the tackling on both sides being a feature of the game. After a spell of attacking, Rylands' scored through Gallop, from a passing bout,after all the backs had taken part. On resuming, Egerton took up the attack and from a penalty Dii Bevan dropped a splen- did goal from half-way. A few minutes after Bevan repeated his performance. rhis roused the borne team and close on half-time, from a pass by Carter, Horrocks dashed over at the corner for Leah to add the extra points. Half-time arrived in favour of the home team by 6 points to 4. On resuming, the Wiremen quickly assumed the upper hand, the forwards, led by Stretford, getting possession of the ball. The backs, being well fed, made most of their chances, and tries were scored by Gallop, Warren, Slater and Horrocks (2), from which three gopls were kicked. In the closing stages of the game Egerton were well beaten, Rylands' winning by three goals seven tries to Egerton two dropped goals (four points). Just on, time Gibson, one of the opposing forwards, in trying to stop Slater, was so badly hurt that he bad to be attended to at the Infirmary. MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. FIRST DIVISION. RYLANDS RECS V CLIFTON.-At Clifton. A Bramhall, full back; G Warren. W Leah, S Carter, A Horrocks, three-quarter backs; G Floyd, J Gallop, half hacks ; Stratford, J Brandwood, H Morris, A Beth, .1 Broadlaurct, B Slater, forwards. Reserves, P Mason, Jolley and Barton.

The first item, the rambling match, it was decided to travel by motor char-a-bane to Nlickle Trafford ; start at 8 a.m., have dinner at NI ickle Trafford or Chester, and to have three hours' fishing. Members must be paid up in entrance and char-a-bane fare on the Saturday week before tho match. This will give the secretaries time to guirantee the number for catering, and it was unanimously agreed that this ruling must he carried out for at least this match. it was also passed at this meeting to pool all the entries for this match, it being the first occasion of an affiliated society joining in the match. The Executive Council being the next business, it was gone through in quick style. One society had had a general meeting and had selected their members,this cut the selection down to six. The following names were the members selected, Messrs J Warburton,J Cox, T Singleton for the Headquarters, J Potter, F Jolley, J Bryers for the Bay Horse, J Bradshaw, W Lester. F Trigger for the Coopers Arms, along with the ccntre secretary. As regards holding the seinon open at the Gowy it is wider consideration and will be known in due course. NOTICE. Secretaries will receive any part of the fee for the rambling match any Monday night up to the time of closing same. A.S.

Thesearrangements indi- cate that the Royal progress on this occasion will compensate largely for the public disap- pointments which were as unavoidableas regrettable in 1909. July 7th next should be a real joy-day in the ancient borough.

Pure Indian Tea commands the markets of the world. India exports in a year 249,000,000 lbs. of well manufactured tea of which the United Kingdom consumes 169,000,000 lbs. So keen is the desire for the delicious teas from India that the de- mand has out-run the supply, and the dealer is tempted to keep down the price of his blends by substituting inferior teas from foreign countries for the genuine Indian product. These substitutes have neither the richness nor the purity of Indian tea. It is therefore desirable for the purchaser to obtain a guarantee that the tea sold her is genuine Indian. Considerations of economy, of health, and of comfort, unite in recommend- ing this course.

the last few years. To his (the speaker's) mind the Government had done something supreme by their defence of the Free Trade system during the last seven years. Mr Boner Law had said that if they did not have Tariff " Reform " where were they going to get the money from to provide old-age pensions? Liberalism liu‘d provided the money for that much-needed reform from the proper sources. He (the speaker) was quite in favour of the Naviteing kept within the proper limits. A short timeago the Tories were crying out for Dreadnoughs,and they,now wanted conscription in the land. He thought they could rely on the sturdy British sentiment for the defence of their native land. He greatly disfavoured a military system that took men away from their employment at thei* most impressionable age. They had riddled the Tories' arguments with regard 'to food taxes, with the result that that policy had been dropped. By the reception he had been accorded at the meetings he had addressed in the constituency he considered Liberal- ism was a driving force of enthusiasm in Widnes. At Farnworth North Mr Martindale urged the com- mittee to work hard in future, when he hoped by their aid to win Widnes for Liberalism. He reviewed the Liberal programme and said the Liberal Government e,as not a spent force. DANGEROUS COBBLESTONES. INQUEST ON RUNCORN WOMAN. At an inquest in Runcorn, on Monday, on Martha Johnson,eixty-six,a widow, of Heath-road, it was stated that she went outside her house for" fresh air" early last Wednesday morning, and slipped on cobblest'eaes in the stieet. She broke her thigh-bone, and died in the Cottage Hospital on Saturday from lacmrt failure following the injury. Dr Sim said three people had recently injured them- selves to his knowledge at the same spot. The jury found that the deceased had died as the result of the accident, and they recommended that the authority responsible be asked to undertake new street making at this point.
